## Canon established by Batch 0002 (Volume 04, Chapters 161–170, prose on the page)

**Items 1–418 are the record of Volume 01, of the Volume 02 plan, of Chapters 51–100, of the Volume 02 close, of Chapters 101–150, of the Batch 0015 review repair pass, of the Volume 03 close and of Volume 04 Batch 0001, and none of them is renumbered by this section. Items 393–418 are Batch 0001 and are not repeated here.**

419. **THE FIFTH THING IS THE HEAD LINE OF THE NINTH SPREAD, AND IT IS A DAY AND A HAND AND NO MARK, FOUR DAYS BEFORE THE FIRST BIRTH ON THE PAGE.** Chapter 161, in a room over a byre on trestles, in the fifth hour of the tenth week of a cold in its ninth generation. **A keeper opens a spread when there is a first thing to put in it; that is the rule, it is not written anywhere, Sarr has done it four times and his father did it twice, and there is no reason on earth to rule a page, put a day in it and a hand in it, and no mark, four days before there is anything in the book at all.** He has checked it every winter for six years and has run out of things to check it against. **He has not told his wife, has not told Wystan Roole, and says there are four other people alive in this valley who would understand exactly what he has just said.** His reason for not telling them is not trust: **a man who has had a thing like that for six years and has not told anybody cannot tell the difference after about four years between wanting to tell somebody and needing to, and the day he cannot tell the difference is the day he tells a man off the road.** His three terms for the reading: **the ninth spread may be read in that room on those trestles while he is down at the byre; no name is to be read out loud, not one, not to himself, not under his breath at the ninth hour on that leg; and there is no page — not a leaf, not a corner, not the back of the last leaf — because a second copy of that book is the thing the book has been doing for nine generations without ever being asked to do it.** The three readings are now fixed: **a man who came through with a cart in the third year of his keeping, who read four spreads in an evening and got the fifth generation wrong in a way that has been in a copy ever since and is dead; a woman four valleys off who read it over two nights, came down on the second morning and said she had been wrong about the first, and has written once a season for six years about the weather and has never once asked him about the hand; and Aren Kest, who read the ninth spread for an hour and about ten minutes and wrote nothing.** **A later writer may not make a fourth reading and may not supply the missing one.**

420. **A PRESS-MARK PROVES A BOOK AND NOT A MAN, AND A HAND IS NOT A PRESS-MARK, AND THE VOLUME KNOWS THE DIFFERENCE AND DOES NOT ARGUE IT.** Chapter 163. **There is a depression on the back of the last leaf of the ninth spread, the size of a thumbnail, low down and a little to the left, and it came off a mould while the paper was wet and it is as old as the leaf.** The man with the cart called it a press-mark and said the book was printed at a house two valleys over, and he was right about the paper and wrong about everything people do with a mark once it is in a copy: **there is a paper house about four valleys over and Sarr has been down to it once in his life in a warm week.** The distinction, said once, in full, by the man off the road: **a press-mark is the mark of a thing that was made, and you can hold it up and say what made it, and when the making stops nobody is anybody's business; a hand is a person, it is the one mark in the world that cannot be made by a machine, and that is exactly why you cannot get a person out of one.** Those two marks are on the same leaf four inches apart, **and the one that proves a house is in a copy four hundred miles off being the reason a valley is somewhere it has never been, and the one that proves nothing is the one Sarr has been looking at for six years.** He is not going to guess and the guess is not going on a page, in his words, because **a guess in a copy is a name in a column with a different kind of face on it, and the wrongness was never the damage, the damage was that after the eleventh it was in eleven places and not one of them could be checked against the other ten.** **That is the volume's mystery and it is a mystery about a hand, and it is not explained in this volume and nothing in this volume may schedule an explanation, a flashback, an origin, a maker or a deathbed.** The bundle of about forty leaves tied with tarred hemp stays in that room, and the fifth generation stays wrong in it, and Sarr's own reason is on the page: **a copy that is right about the fifth generation is a copy, and there is no way on this earth to get a wrong fact out of a book that is right about a hundred other things, and he let a man have a false fact about his valley for about nine years of his life because the other option was that he had both.**

421. **THE NINTH SPREAD READ IN DETAIL, AND IT IS NOT A PAGE OF NAMES, AND THE NINTH GENERATION IS TWO HUNDRED OF ONE MARK.** Chapter 162, an hour and about ten minutes, three columns, about a hundred and ninety ruled lines. **Three marks exist in nine spreads: a small barred T for a person in this valley who has not gone out of it; the same mark with a stroke under it for a person who has gone out and not come back, and the stroke is the only part of it that means anything; and the same mark with a stroke through it from the top for a person who went out and came back, and there are nine of those in the whole book and the last is a hundred and forty years old.** **The whole of the ninth spread is the first mark, two hundred times, and the mark says nothing about any of them except that they are here, which is the answer to why there has never been a third reason in nine spreads and it is not a reason anybody had to look for.** The day column **runs down and never goes back up, and a man can take the order of a whole valley off that page without reading one thing on it that is a person.** The hand in the third column does not vary, and does not go small or fast at the foot of a page of two hundred lines, and is the same size on the first and the last, and the pen and the ink are not ones he knows. **The fourth spread has two hundred and eleven names in the column at the right-hand edge and about thirty of them are people who have been in a room with him, and he read all of them and wrote none of them down and the not writing took him forty minutes longer than the writing would have taken.** The name column **stops in the middle of the fourth spread and does not begin again above it, and it stopped because that is the last year anybody went out of this valley and was gone long enough for a name in a book to be a fact about where they were rather than a fact about a family.** After the two hundred names the last leaf of the ninth spread is **ruled the same way with no lines in it, an empty ruled space at the top for a heading, and the first ruled line below it is the first place a person could be put; and the day has never been written at the head of it in nineteen years by a man who knows the rule better than anybody alive.** **He found the day a girl of about nine was born, four lines up from the foot of the ninth spread, in a small mark, with a hand in it that is not the hand of anybody alive; he had not asked for it, nobody had offered it, he told nobody and told the girl nothing, and he could not ask the woman over the byre because a woman looking in a book to check a thing about a child is the whole of what this valley has done to itself for nine generations.** **The roll must stay a roll of persons. A later writer may not turn it into a device and may not have him tell anybody that day.**

422. **THE MECHANISM, ONCE, IN TRADE TERMS, BY A PERSON WITH NO STAKE IN THE MARCHES, AND IT IS NOT RESTATED AND IT IS NOT IMPROVED ON.** Chapter 164, on a bank, the third day of a wall, to a stranger, in about eleven hundred words, and no person in that valley has ever repeated it. **A wall is not a promise: a wall is built once, goes in the ground, stands there in the dark at three in the morning doing nothing, and has never once asked anybody for anything, and that is the whole of why a wall lasts and a promise does not; it is not better, it just does not want feeding. And that is what is under this valley's winter, and he has never seen it and neither has the man of eighty-eight-year-old's contemporaries, it is not a promise, it is nine generations old, and it does not want anything, and that is why nobody in this valley has ever found a hole in it. So: a promise has to be renewed or it stops, a working does not, and the reason the ninth generation is asked to keep the winter every year is not that the asking holds anything up — the asking is what we pay for the privilege of it being a promise instead of a working, and the price of a working being a promise at all is that somebody has to keep saying it out loud, and nobody in that valley has ever costed it.** He has counted the rooms: one at the top of the cross and about forty people stand in it and he has been one of the forty for nine years and could not say out loud in front of them what they are paying for. **No narrator may underline it, no later chapter may restate it, and no character may summarise it.**

423. **WYSTAN ROOLE IS NAMED, 34, A BRIDGEKEEPER OF THE NINTH GENERATION, SIXTEEN MEN AND NO WORK, AND THE WALL IS THE WRONG WALL AND IT IS THE BEST WALL ANYBODY IN THAT VALLEY HAS SEEN.** Chapters 163, 164, 166, 167, 169 and 170. **He is the man of about thirty-four of Chapter 159 who showed three faults in a floor in about four seconds and said that finishes the first day and that he was not going to ask him to do anything and wanted it understood that he had not asked; he has now asked, and he says on the page that it took a stranger in a room with a book in it, and he asks the room and not the stranger to be noticed.** His want, in his own words, and spent: **a road is not a thing you are given, a road is a thing you dig; and a valley that cannot leave is a valley that cannot argue with anybody about anything.** **He is also the man who takes the return stitch down at the end of Block 4, with an explanation, and the volume does not make him wrong to do it, and nothing in this batch foreshadows it.** The wall at the Low Holm: **asked for in the middle of the week, not granted and not refused, about four hundred feet, double-faced, a batter, laid dry in lime putty and stone because quicklime in a cold week is a powder that will set in the spring and squeeze the course out, the string down on the fourth course and up on the ninth and down twice more, a plumb bob of wrought iron and a length of string, nine through-stones the length and depth of the wall, and a notch in the third course with a dressed lintel over it cut by his own hand, out of a stone off the byre coping that is a hundred and forty years old and squared, four inches wider than the hole on each side.** **He cut a hole in the wrong place first, in the second course, about two feet out, on purpose, in about nine minutes, and knocked it out and dressed it, and there are four men alive who know.** The wall is eleven days and about four hundred feet and the other two things it could have been are about nine weeks of causeway out of that gate to the ford and a dinner-plate hole in a byre floor. **He said the best-wall sentence out loud on the ninth day in front of nine people, once, and that it was the last time he was going to say it.** The woman of the Low Holm never thanked him, moved a pail four inches out of the wet place twice, and said she would like both the wall and the hole in her floor to be in the world at the same time and would like neither of them to be the one who gives. **No money was named, asked for, owed or refused for any of it.**

424. **NEV TREEN IS NAMED, 66, OF THE EIGHTH GENERATION, AND THE ROOM OVER THE CROSS HAS TWENTY-NINE BENCHES BOLTED TO THE FLOOR IN FOUR ROWS WITH A NUMBER CUT INTO THE END OF EACH, AND THE BACK OF THE RIGHT-HAND ROW HAS A HUNDRED AND FORTY ON IT, AND NOBODY HAS EVER BEEN STRUCK OFF A BENCH.** Chapters 165, 166, 169 and 170. She gives her name before anybody asks. **She was asked what she swore in the winter her generation came of age, in the room over the cross, in the cold, with the whole valley in it and a man at the back with a slate; it took nine minutes and it was the worst nine minutes of her life; she will not say what she said and has never said it in a room.** She told the ninth generation about it because they were owed it, and she told them it was survivable, **and it was survivable, and she was wrong, and she knows she was wrong, and what was wrong was not the asking: the asking was right and had never been done, and what was wrong was the man with the slate and the book behind him and the fact that a book does not know the difference between what a person said and what was true.** She says it out loud once, to a stranger, and **it is not an apology for anything and she says so in her own words: there is nobody in this world she owes an apology to.** **Nine of the thirty-one in the aisle are left: four have said for forty years that it was the worst thing that ever happened to them and one of the four is her, and five have said it was the best and two of those five have never said a word about it to anybody and she has never asked them.** Her reason the ninth generation has not been asked is her reason and not his: **there is no other way to ask anybody in this valley; you can have a thing happen in a room over a cross in the cold in front of the whole valley with a man holding a slate, and whatever is said there is the thing that happened, and in about nine years nobody will ever know that you and she said a thing in a cheese house.** The back row is at the back because **you can get out of a room at the back in about a second and a half, and it is not a custom, it is an arrangement, and she has wanted somebody to ask her to have it changed for about twenty-five years and nobody has.** The hundred and forty is the number of strokes, put on a bench by a man with a slate every time anybody has stood in that aisle, and there is a woman of twenty-two in this valley who has never stood in that room and whose family has a bench, and **nobody has ever been struck off a bench, and that is the entire difference between what she went through and what is about to happen: a hundred and forty strokes on a bench is not a column of names, it is a bench, in a room, in a building, and a building is a thing that falls down, and a thing being in a house is not a thing being in a hand, and nobody in nine generations has worked that out and she has had forty years and two bad hands and has not worked it out either.** **In Chapter 169 she gives up standing in the aisle and to be asked again**, and says so out loud and says there will not be a page for it. **In Chapter 170 she comes as a person in a room, puts her hands flat on the end of a bench for a minute and takes them off again, and the only person in that room who knows she has not done that in forty years is the man off the road, and he does not nod.** She has not asked for anything else and has no want beyond the two statements on the page.

425. **THE VOLUME'S FIRST ASKING, AND IT IS REFUSED IN ABOUT FOUR SECONDS BY A YOUNG MAN OF TWENTY-TWO, IN A DOORWAY OFF THE WIDE PLACE, IN FRONT OF ABOUT NINE PEOPLE, ON A MARKET DAY, AND THE REFUSAL IS CORRECT AND IT IS THE ENGINE OF THIS VOLUME AND NOT A DEFEAT.** Chapter 166. He asks whether the young man has ever been in the room over the cross, and then whether he would like to be asked what he swore, **and the young man puts a hurdle down on the step, which is a thing a man does when he has thought about something for a long time, and says no, and not in that room, and does not raise his voice and says it to the man and not to the market.** The reason is one sentence and it is the benches: **when a person stands in that aisle and says something, a man puts a stroke on a bench, and that is the only way it is known, and it is the only reason anybody in that valley has ever believed anybody about anything.** **The refusal is of the form of the asking and not of the question, and that is the volume's argument: he is not refusing to be asked what he swore, he wants to be asked what he swore, he has been in that book since the day he was born and has never been asked anything at all — and there is nowhere to put an answer that is not a page, and a page is a column, and in nine years there will be no way anybody is ever going to know that the two of them said it in a doorway.** **He puts the second half on the step between them and the man who asked him says so: *You have got a book in a bag at the Low Holm* — and the answer is that it is in a room over a byre, the man who keeps it will not have it out of that room, and if you and I say a thing in this doorway then in nine years there is no way anybody is ever going to know that you and I said it.** Iven Sarr is standing at the edge of the wide place with a slate under his arm, having come down on purpose, **and says both halves of that are right and that he has been on the wrong side of the second one for nineteen years, and that he had been asking this valley for things in a room with a bench in it since the day he was nineteen years old, and that he is not going to be the man who kept a book of what this valley said and never looked at it, because there is already one of those in a copy four hundred miles off.** **He is not asked anything and nobody asked the ninth generation anything in that wide place.** The sentence about the leaf is **said once and is the Marches' own plant, cited as a story rather than as a document: there is one man in this kingdom who ever got out of a column, and he did it by writing on the back of a leaf, two years before anybody came for him, that he did not put his name there, and by the time anybody looked it was already written.** **He says the leaf is the story of a man in a book, and that it is the reason he is asking, and that he has had about a week and has not thought of a better one.** The refusal is not improved on, not restated and not turned into a defeat anywhere in this batch.

426. **THE FINDING BEGUN: FOUR WORDS FOR A PERSON, NINE GENERATIONS, AND A CARRIER IS NOT THE CROWN'S FOURTH WORD.** Chapter 166, at the cross, to about four people, and **no character in this batch calls a carrier a custodian and no character calls a custodian a carrier.** **A carrier is a person who has gone out of this valley and been named for it, a fact about a road and nothing else. The hand is a person who keeps a thing that is not made of words, a fact about a wall and nothing else. A keeper is a person who maintains a place or its records, and that is employment and not authority over anybody, and Iven Sarr has not been able to tell anybody what to do in nineteen years because he is good at it and not because anything in this valley gave him the right. And there is a fourth word in the county he came from, and it is for a person a community appoints to speak to one other person, and it carries consent inside it, and it is the only one of the four that anybody can be sorry for.** The finding: **a man in a market in this valley had been called a carrier to his face by a woman at a gate, no person had appointed him to do anything and no person had asked his leave, and there is not one form in that valley on which to enter it, and that is not a gap in the form — it is nine generations of a valley using one word for four different jobs and being careful, in the way a valley is careful, never to look at all four at once.** **The fourth word is described in its own words and is not named in this batch, on the Chapter 156 precedent, and the description is not a mirror of the first not-asking and no character notices a resemblance.** Block 3 completes this finding and does not re-derive it.

427. **THE WALL'S MONEY, FOOTED IN PENCE ON THE PAGE, AND THE VALLEY'S OWN PRICE REFUSED AND ADDED TO NOTHING.** Chapter 167. **Quicklime, three loads, at sixpence a load: six, six, six, and six and six is twelve and twelve and six is eighteen. A barrow of sand, fourpence. Eighteen and four is twenty-two pence, which is one shilling and tenpence.** Under it, in his own hand: **the above is a figure in a county's money and is not a figure in this valley's money; the valley has no coin; the price of three loads of quicklime here is nine bushels of barley and a peck, and that figure is on the back of a slate and the man who wrote it there is a woman of about thirty who does the births and has never argued with anybody about a number in eleven years, and I have not added her figure to mine and I am not going to, and there is nobody alive who could.** The two are the same three loads of lime, one is what the man from the low country asked for and one is what he took, and the difference is four bushels and nobody in this valley will ever find out what they were for, and **the lime came out of the same sack as the barley that a family puts in a byre roof in the warm week because there is nowhere else in this valley to put it.** The woman with the slate finds her figure on his own arm and says **that is not a place anybody keeps a figure, and that it is right, because she is not a place a number lives in, she is a person who happens to have one.** **He could have had paper made four valleys over and given her a second copy and did not, because a thing written down twice is a thing two people can be got at, and a person is not a place a number lives in.** The valley's actual ledger is on the page in full: **four seed houses, two families counting twice a winter and never comparing in a book, one slate, one woman, and about four hundred people.** **No 456, no 254, no 2,450, no 2,906, no 9-4-1, no hearth figure, and no Marches figure is set beside a valley figure in any chapter of this block.**

428. **THE FIRST DRIFT FIGURE OF THE VOLUME IS REFUSED IN HIS OWN NOTEBOOK, AND THE REFUSAL IS NOT CHAPTER 158'S REFUSAL AND IS NOT IMPROVED ON.** Chapter 168, the tenth night of the wall, in the valley's own register, in italics on the page. **Out at the fourth hour on a day this county does not use, from a sill with no glass in it, on a line made up in nine minutes with the hour against each of the nine; the office's printed figure is three weeks, three weeks in an office's hand for two years, and the office cannot say whose figure it is and he cannot either.** His own count was three weeks and two sleeps at the fourth week and he stopped counting at the ninth; the valley's count is now the fourteenth week of the cold; the two have never agreed and he has not tried to make them agree. **And the finding, which is the new one: the error is not the difference between three weeks and the time he has been here, because the time he has been here is not the absence; the absence is a number in a country that keeps its days and is not his and will not be his until he is standing on the other side of a line again; a sum done here gives a figure with no meaning in it, and a figure with no meaning in it is worse than nothing, because it looks like a figure and he will believe it in about four months and put it in a return.** So: **three weeks printed, unchanged, in an office's hand two hundred miles off, and a valley that keeps no months, and a man with no frame; and he is not going to write a figure, and this is the third time in this case he has got to that page and not written one — the first time he threw the paper away, the second time he left the two numbers side by side and did not add them, and this time he has written down why, and he does not know yet whether that is a better thing or a slower way of failing.** He left the page alone afterwards, which is the first time in this case he has done that. **The only figure that is his is four lines long: went out at the fourth hour, a line made up in nine minutes, and no name in it anywhere.** And: **nobody in that valley knows there is a figure at all, and no person in it has any reason to suppose that there is a piece of paper about four hundred miles behind him with a number on it, and that is the only thing about this crossing that is actually his.** The printed warning is three weeks and has not moved, **no character in this block uses the word *failed* about a road, and the ratio is error over absence and never over the warning, and the path interval is nowhere in it.**

429. **THE HEARING WAS HELD ON ITS OWN DAY AND NOBODY CAME AND NOBODY WAS SENT, AND IT WAS NOT ADJOURNED AND NOT REFUSED, AND THE DOCUMENT THAT DECIDES WHAT A BODY CORPORATE DOES WITH A HEARING AGAINST NOBODY IS NOT WRITTEN AND IS NOT BLOCK 2's.** Chapter 170, in a room of its own, the ninth of Rainmonth of the year after, a Tuesday and not a market day, at the second hour, the scales under that room not used since the fourth of it. **The keeper of records sat in one of two chairs and the second copyist in the other with fair-copy paper and a rule, because a hearing that is not minuted is a thing that happened, and the day-book is the only book in that office nobody can be served with, and the copy goes on a shelf with the number against the office and nothing against a person. The junior clerk came up the two flights with the ordinary post of a Tuesday.** Nobody came. Nobody was sent. The resolution of the twentieth of Hearthmonth says both, and the road at the other end had been shut in four lines of writing and the person who used to hold that end had been struck and the county did not replace her in time, and none of that was in dispute. **The finding, said out loud once in that room: a body corporate that is sued is represented by a person, and if this office hears a thing then this office is a party to it, and a party can be sued, and she had just made this office a party to a matter against a county that is not on any map because she agreed eighteen months ago to hear a delegation, and there is no instrument in this kingdom for hearing a thing without becoming one of the sides of it.** She wrote **four** lines — the date, the claim number against the office, that no person came, and that no person was sent with the resolution that says so and the day it was entered — and **she did not write a fifth line, and the second copyist asked her to, and the reason she gives is that what a thing means is not a fact, and this office is for facts, and if she puts a meaning on that page then in forty years somebody will read the meaning and skip the fact.** The day and the hour went in as two things and not one. **The hearing is neither held nor not held; it is recorded, and the decision-document is Block 4's and `outline/volume-04.md` §8 Block 4's page, and it is not written here.** He is not in that county, has not sent anything, nothing has come from him, **she has not asked, and it is not a question for a minute, and no number is entered and the ninth not asking is not re-touched.**

430. **THE OATH IS NOT IN THE BOOK AND NOT IN THE FRONT ROOM, AND THE FIFTH PLACE IS A DOOR FOUR STEPS DOWN IN THE BACK WALL OF THE BYRE, AND THERE IS A FORM ON A BOARD IN IT, AND NOBODY IN THIS VALLEY HAS READ IT.** Chapters 169 and 170. Sarr's four places are found and empty and he has never said where they are. **The fifth place is under the eaves of the byre, four steps down, a room about four feet by six with a board floor and stone walls older than the byre, and on the board there is a sheet of paper under a stone, and the sheet has columns ruled on it, and it is a form.** What he knows and does not know is on the page and is exact: **it is ruled, and ruled in more columns than his book has, and there is writing on it and the writing is dry and is not his writing and not his father's writing, and he does not know what is in the columns, does not know who ruled it, and does not know how long it has been on that board, and he stood in the doorway holding a lamp and did not go four feet into it.** His reason, in his own words: **a form is a thing with columns in it that somebody else made, and when a thing arrives in this valley you put something in it, and he has watched four people in his life answer a form and has not one of them still living in this valley.** He forbids the stranger from asking him one word about that room, having decided that a man who has had a thing for six years cannot tell the difference between wanting to tell somebody and needing to. **THE FORM IS NOT OPENED IN THIS BATCH. Its office is not named, its hand is not described, its age is not given, and nothing on it is read. That is Block 3's, and the office's hand on it is Block 3's beat, and `outline/series.md`'s Volume 4 escalation line and knowledge-control row remain unsatisfied and are carried forward as an open item.**

431. **THE READING HAPPENED, IN A ROOM OF NINE AND A STRANGER, AT THE THIRD HOUR OF A MARKET DAY, AND WHAT WAS READ WAS FOUR WORDS, AND THAT IS THE BLOCK's COST.** Chapters 169 and 170. **The thing on the leaf is *Next market day*, in his own hand, on the back of it, written on the eighteenth evening, with no month and no year and no hour on it, because this valley has no months and no years and no hour anybody keeps. The leaf went back under the book and the book went over the leaf.** On the market day **ten people came into a room of twenty-nine bolted benches in four rows with a stove at the front, and a man of thirty-two read four words off a leaf in the voice of a man reading a figure off a board, and then said out loud, in about four seconds, in his own words, that that was all of it and that he was not holding anything back that anybody handed him. The man of eighty-one asked for it to be read again, and the second reading was slower and was not better, and about three people understood that he had not asked for the words.** Sarr's want, changed and stated as changed: **six weeks earlier he wanted the oath read in that room all of it and not the parts that have held; now he wants the reading to be four words long, and he has worked out that if he tells a roomful that he has looked in a fifth place and there is a thing in it, this valley will talk about a thing in a room for a year, nine of them will be right about it, and in four years there will be nine accounts of a form behind a byre and not one of them checkable against the other eight — and a thing four hundred people can check is worth more to him than a thing they cannot.** He says the second half of his want himself: **he thought there would be forty people in that room and there were nine and a girl, and there is no version of the forty in which any of the nine is there, and he did not know until that morning that wanting forty was the same as not wanting the nine.** He answered eleven questions in about half an hour and did not improve on one. **The woman with the slate took the slate out, looked at it, and put it back, and did not write on it. Wystan Roole counted the room twice, said nine of us and a man of thirty-two who is not of this valley, and said the figure of about four hundred out loud in that room for the first time in his hearing, and offered to cut it in stone, and was told no.** **The ninth generation was not asked anything. The young man of twenty-two was at the back of the right-hand row from the start to the finish and was not asked, had not asked to be asked, and nobody went near him, and the reason the man off the road stayed at the front is on the page and is that a man of thirty-two standing four feet off a boy in a room where nobody has asked the boy anything is a man arranging himself.** **Nev Treen was in the room as a person and not in the aisle and was asked nothing.** The girl of about nine asked one question — *Is that all of it* — was told *No*, waited four seconds, said *All right*, and went and got her barrow out at the ford, **and the arrangement that has been standing between her and the man off the road since the ninth week survived her asking a question of a third person inside four feet of him.** **Sarr shut the low door with his palm flat on the wood, which is a thing everybody in that valley does to a door, and the two of them went up a stair of nine treads of which one is soft, and the fourth one said so under both of them.** The chapter ends on the wall outside in the dark, four hundred feet of the best wall anybody in that valley has ever seen, holding up a byre instead of being the first four hundred yards of a road, and on a shut door, and neither man said anything about the wall on the stair.

## Relationship state at the end of Chapter 170

- **Aren Kest and Mara Vey: the breach open, worked on in public in Batch 0001, untouched in this block, and further away than at the end of Chapter 160 by four hundred miles and a closed room.** He is not in this county. He has sent nothing and nothing has come from him. **On the ninth of Rainmonth of the year after, at the second hour, in a room over a weigh-house, she said out loud in front of the second copyist that hearing a thing makes this office a party to it, and that the only thing she has got is a room a person can be turned out of by a person with a door, and that she found that out four years and a half in, and she did not say a word about him except to say that she has not asked and that it is not a question for a minute.** The ninth not asking stands and this block does not enter a tenth and no number is put on the page. **He is on a bank in a valley and she is at a table in a fen town at about the same hour, and the two of them are not in one sentence anywhere in these ten chapters and no instrument in this case can put them in one.** The third rule's final clause is still about him and neither of them has said so. **The intimacy is not bought and nothing in this block touches it.**
- **Aren Kest and Iven Sarr: a man who told a stranger his whole want and then gave it away and got a smaller one, and has not been asked one question about the room at the back of his byre.** Sarr's want is now four words long and he said so himself before anybody could. **He has read a roll nine generations deep in a room over a byre for an hour and ten minutes and wrote nothing, and he found out that a birth is not a unit, and he put a man off the road on the stage at the third hour of a market day and said *that is all of it, and I am not holding anything back that anybody handed me*, and he did not improve on it, and he has not explained a hand and will not.** He has refused the man a question about the back room and the refusal is not a defeat: **a man who has had a thing for six years cannot tell the difference between wanting to tell somebody and needing to, and Sarr has said that out loud and it is the fifth thing and the last thing he has.** He has given the reading and not the oath, and the oath is not in the book and not in the front room, and he did not go down four steps.
- **Aren Kest and the ninth generation: refused in about four seconds, and the refusal is the engine.** A young man of twenty-two put a hurdle down on a step in a doorway off the wide place and said no, and not in that room, and then said **he wants to be asked what he swore and has never been asked anything at all**, and that a page is a column and there is nowhere to put an answer that is not a page. **Aren Kest did not argue with him, had an argument ready about two hundred and eleven names in a column, and did not use it because the young man did not know there was a column and the argument would have been about a book and not about himself.** He has said the thing stands and that he is not going to come back with it in a week in a different coat, and that this is the first time in four years and a half he has heard a no he was not going to argue with and he has not got a better reason for that either. **And the young man gave him one: *you have not written it down* — and he said that was the first honest thing anybody has said to him in a doorway in six weeks.** They have not spoken since the market day except that the young man was in the room over the cross and nobody asked him anything, and Aren stayed at the front on purpose.
- **Aren Kest and Wystan Roole: an ask, and a wall, and no road.** Roole asked him to do something for the first time in four years, in a room with a book in it, and it was to come and look at a footing at the fourth hour. **Three faults in a floor in about four seconds finished the first day in Chapter 159 and he was told so and he came anyway.** He said the mechanism out loud once, on a bank, to the only person on it who builds anything, and has not said it again to anybody. He said the best-wall sentence once on the ninth day in front of nine people and said it was the last time. **The woman whose byre it is has never thanked him and has never refused him and has twice moved a pail out of the wet.** He is also the man who takes the parapet down at the end of Block 4 and the volume does not make him wrong, and nothing in this block foreshadows it.
- **Aren Kest and Nev Treen: a woman of sixty-six who gave him the valley's position before he asked for it and then gave up the one thing she had.** She told him to ask her the right question and he did not, and she told him anyway. **She said out loud, once, that she told nine generations of her own family that being asked was survivable and that it was and she was wrong and she knows it, and she said it is not an apology for anything.** She told him the room over the cross in full, including that the numbers on the benches are strokes and that nobody has ever been struck off one, and that the difference between what happened to her and what is about to happen is that a bench is in a house. **In Chapter 169 she gave up standing in the aisle and being asked again, and said there would not be a page for it, and in Chapter 170 she came as a person in a room, was asked nothing, and put her hands flat on the end of a bench for a minute.**
- **Aren Kest and the man of eighty-one: one exchange about a stick, and then a second reading.** The old man said he had brought that to work with, was told it was to get about in, said there is no road, was told there is no road, said **then you have brought it a long way for it**, and went down the bank, and it was the only thing he said to anybody in that yard that week. **In Chapter 170 he asked for the four words to be read again and said he has been in that room sixty times and has never once heard what is in it, and he is the only person in that valley who is pleased about a stranger reading a thing out in the cold and nobody has asked him anything and he wanted it that way round for once.**
- **Aren Kest and the woman with the slate: a number on his own arm, and a page he did not write.** She told him a week early what the word was going to be. **He wrote nine bushels and a peck of barley on his own arm instead of on her slate, and she said that is not a place anybody keeps a figure, and that it is right, because she is not a place a number lives in.** He could have made a second copy on paper from a house four valleys over and did not, and the reason is on the page and it is four years and a half of learning that a thing written down twice is a thing two people can be got at. **In Chapter 170 she took the slate out in a cold room, looked at it, and put it back, and did not write on it, and nobody asked her why.**
- **Aren Kest and the girl of about nine: an arrangement that has survived two tests.** She will not give her name and gives a place instead. She counted four hundred and six stones in a wall in two goes round it and would not ask anybody, because then she would have to be told. **In Chapter 170 she asked a man of fifty-eight one question in a room of ten people and was told *No*, and waited four seconds, and said *All right*, and went and got her barrow out at the ford — and neither of them asked the other anything, and he noticed that the arrangement survived it and did not improve on it.** He knows the day she was born, from the ninth spread, and told nobody and told her nothing and could not ask the woman over the byre, and there is nowhere in four hundred miles to put it.
- **Aren Kest and the woman of the Low Holm: a door, a drain and a floor that is still a dinner plate.** She told him about the square mouth in the byre wall and that the drain has come out under the wall for sixty years, and said she was saying it to him because he had asked her one question and she would rather it was the right one, **and she has not said it to the man who is building the wall and he has known since the middle of the week that he asked her for a thing before he had worked out the bottom of it and says so out loud.** She would like the wall and the hole in her floor to be in the world at the same time and would like neither of them to be the one who gives.
- **Aren Kest and the man of fifty-eight's copy, the cart, and the forty leaves tied with tarred hemp in a room over a byre:** a fifth generation that has been wrong in a county four hundred miles off for about sixteen years, uncorrected on purpose, and a second letter that said a person who has got a thing wrong in a copy ought to say so in the copy, which Sarr has never been able to decide is the best sentence anybody has ever written about a book or the worst, and has had sixteen years. **The copy does not leave that room.**
- **The valley: the wall, the notch, and the asking that was not made.** A retaining wall that is the best wall anybody in that valley has seen, eleven days, sixteen men, and a hole in the bottom of it with a lintel over it, and about eleven weeks off a thaw nobody in that yard is going to be told about. **The ninth generation was not asked anything, in a market and in a cold room, and about nine people know it and no form in that valley exists to enter it, and the first three questions the block answers are all about a page and not about a person.**

The forty-five ceiling in the Batch 0003 prompt is not lowered by this; Batch 0002's own worst chapter sat exactly on it.**

437. **CHAPTER 170 IS 4,970 WORDS, AND THE BLOCK IS 33,385, VOLUME 04 IS 66,430 AND THE MANUSCRIPT IS 668,072.** `logs/batch-0002.review.log` finding 3 was a self-contradiction and not an arithmetic error: `state/batch-summaries.md`, `state/current.md`, `state/chapter-summaries.md` and `state/continuity.md` each printed **4,958 in the per-chapter column and 4,956 in the prose of the same sentences.** The true count before any repair was 4,958. **The four prose repairs of items 438 to 441 then moved it, because a repair pass that fixes sentences is obliged to re-foot every figure that sentence feeds, and a figure left standing after the sentence it counted has changed is the same error wearing a different hat. Chapter 170 is therefore 4,970 and the block is 33,385, per chapter 3067 / 3185 / 3545 / 3140 / 3204 / 3135 / 3016 / 3128 / 2995 / 4,970, and the ten columns foot at 33,385. Volume 04 is 33,045 + 33,385 = 66,430 in twenty chapters and the manuscript is 601,642 + 66,430 = 668,072 in one hundred and seventy chapters.** **Chapter 170 remains the second-longest chapter in the manuscript after Chapter 149's 5,136 and remains untrimmed**, on the Volume 03 close's §10 item 4, and no scene was cut to move the figure. **Every other count in the block is unchanged: `about` 383, `the whole of` 36, `about N seconds` 5, `cut` 21 and all ordinary, `---` rules 11, bolded line-openings 53, semicolons 0, em-dashes 0, straight double quotes 0, curly apostrophes 0, and the nine whole-word fillers `nodded` 1, `held` 10, `wrote` 27, `stood` 30, `plain` 0, `counted` 8, `breathed` 0, `steady` 0 — all nine identical, because not one of the four repaired sentences used a counted word.**

438. **THE NARRATOR DOES NOT REPORT WHAT SARR IS THINKING, AND CHAPTER 170 LINE 5 NO LONGER DOES IT.** `logs/batch-0002.review.log` finding 4. The line read that a man not returning to a thing for half an hour is *a considerable piece of self-knowledge for a man of fifty-eight, and he did not appear to think of it as any kind of achievement* — **a verdict on another character's interior in a book that otherwise keeps interiority with Aren, and the same construction occurs zero times across Batch 0001's ten chapters.** It is now *and he did not appear to know that he had said it twice or to think anything of having said it*, which keeps every observable fact on the page — he said it twice, he did not come back to it, and nothing in his face showed that he had noticed either — and hands the reading of it to the reader. **The neighbouring line at 39, *he did not look like a man enjoying it*, was inspected and left alone, because it is external and correct.** This is the finding the "record POV honestly" instruction exists to catch, and it is now canon: **the narrator in this volume may report what a room does and may report what is written, and may not report what a person thinks unless that person is Aren or is in the first person.**

439. **THERE IS NO THERMOMETER IN THE VALLEY, AND CHAPTER 170'S COLD ROOM IS LOCATED BY A BODY.** `logs/batch-0002.review.log` finding 5. The room over the cross was *cold at the door and cold at the back and four degrees less cold at the front* — **the only `degrees` in Volume 04, and the only prior use in the manuscript a lean angle in a main-world hall, and the one figure in the block with no hedge and no instrument, in a valley where the volume's whole method is that nobody can give a figure exactly.** It is now cold at the door, cold at the back, and less cold at the front, where the stove is, **and a man coming in off the dark can tell which end he is in before he can see a bench.** The room's measurements that were already on the page — an aisle four feet wide, forty people is what the room takes, ten is what was in it — are untouched. **A reader is not to expect a temperature in a valley scene, and a later writer is not to introduce an instrument that nobody in that valley owns.**

440. **THE CHAPTER'S LAST LINE NAMES THE TREAD AGAIN.** `logs/batch-0002.review.log` finding 6. The chapter established at line 71 that *the fourth tread said so under the second boot*, and ended at line 219 with *and the fourth one said so under both of them* — **three lines after two men have gone up a stair, so *the fourth one* reads as a third person rather than a board.** The callback is the good part and it stands; the pronoun was the defect and it is now *the fourth tread*. **Nothing else in the ending was touched, and the chapter still ends in a yard on a shut door and not in a room, which is hard requirement 10 of Batch 0002 and was verified by the reviewer.**

441. **"I HAVE NOT ONE OF THEM" IS NOW "AND NOT ONE OF THEM IS STILL LIVING".** `logs/batch-0002.review.log` finding 7, an elliptical construction that read as a dropped auxiliary. The sentence is a man of fifty-eight enumerating exactly, so the fix is the plain one and the enumeration is untouched: **I have watched four people in my life answer a form and not one of them is still living in this valley, and I am not going to be a fifth.** The four is not altered and neither is the refusal that follows it. **That is seven findings, ten repairs in the block when the phase's own six are counted with them, four of the seven in finished prose and each of those four one sentence, and no scene rewritten, no thread closed, no date moved, no name changed, no money figure touched, no calendar touched and no device added or removed.**

## Canon established by Batch 0003 (Volume 04, Chapters 171–180, prose on the page)

**Items 1–441 are the record of Volume 01, of the Volume 02 plan, of Chapters 51–100, of the Volume 02 close, of Chapters 101–150, of the Batch 0015 review repair pass, of the Volume 03 close, of Volume 04 Batch 0001, of Volume 04 Batch 0002 and of the Batch 0002 review repair pass, and none of them is renumbered by this section. Items 419–441 are Batch 0002's and are not repeated here. This batch closed no thread and answered none of the nineteen the Volume 03 close handed over, none of the nineteen Batch 0001 carried forward and none of the nineteen Batch 0002 carried forward.**

442. **THE FORM IS READ OUT LOUD, IN A ROOM ABOUT FOUR FEET BY SIX, ONCE, TO A STRANGER, AND NOT ONE WORD OF IT IS WRITTEN DOWN, AND THE OFFICE IS NAMED AND IT IS THE ANCESTOR OF THE OFFICE IN THE FILE TWO HUNDRED MILES OFF, AND THE TWO ARE NOT JOINED IN ONE SENTENCE BY ANYBODY.** Chapters 171, 172 and 179. The sheet is a printed form under a squared stone on a board floor in a room four steps down under the eaves of a byre, and it is headed **Office of Quarters, at Grayford**, and it is a **Return of the quarter, to be sent round once in every seven years, and returned to the same, and not to be sent on.** Eight numbered columns, printed in a small even type, and two hands have answered three of them. **1. The quarter. 2. The book of the quarter, and the name of the keeper of it. 3. The number of men going out of the quarter. 4. The number of those that have gone out and not come back. 5. The name of the person appointed in the quarter to answer for the men that go out. 6. The year. 7. Withdrawn. 8. Answer received.** **The third column is answered *four in this year*, in a slow careful hand, in a reckoning this valley does not use and cannot convert into anything. The fourth is empty. The fifth is answered *none appointed*, in the same hand. The sixth is a number of years in the office's own count from a year this valley has never heard named, and it is not turned into a length of time, and the reason is on the page. The seventh is a ruled space with a rule drawn across the head of it that has not been ruled across. The eighth is an inch and a half of ruled space with nothing in it and a rule at the bottom of it no more faded than the rule at the bottom of the third.** **The finding of the two hands is said once, in full, in Chapter 172: the slow careful one wrote three answers and got tired in the last word of the second and came back up in the first word of the third, which is a person, and the other one is identical across two answers written on different days, which is not a person, and the way a man knows is that nobody chose it.** **The form's age is two hundred years and it is given on the page as an experienced reader's finding and not as a figure derived in the valley: laid paper with chain lines about an inch apart where the roll has none, ink gone through the strokes, four folds gone soft like cloth, a furry stub out of a pad, and a man of fifty-eight who has handled paper all his life putting it above the trough in his wife's mother's yard and above the lintel over his own door. No chapter converts the sixth column and no character describes a form's origin, a maker, a year of setting or a deathbed, and the office itself has never had a letter sent to it and never will.**

443. **THE COUNT IS OF CARRIER OBLIGATIONS, IT WAS NEVER ANSWERED AND IT WAS NEVER WITHDRAWN, AND AN OFFICE THAT WILL NOT PASS A FORM ON HAS BUILT A FORM THAT A VALLEY LIKE THIS ONE CAN NEVER ANSWER, AND THE OFFICE WAS RIGHT, AND THE OFFICE HAS NEVER BEEN TOLD THIS VALLEY EXISTS.** Chapters 171, 172, 174 and 179. **The finding that carries the volume, said in the middle of a room in Chapter 174 and not as a chapter's last line: an office is the most durable thing in the book, because a county can break an oath in public and a family can burn a roll and an office waits — and the proof of it is a column headed *Withdrawn* with a rule drawn across the head of it that has not been ruled across in about two hundred years.** **The document's own design is the century: *returned to the same, and not to be sent on*, and a valley that cannot carry a sheet to Grayford because it has no road and no cart and has not had either for nine generations.** **And the count the third column asks for has been kept four years in chalk on the back of a stall at a market by the man who makes nails and cannot sell them, because there is nowhere in the valley to keep a figure, and he has never heard of the form and nobody is ever going to tell him, and that is the whole of the finding in one object.** **The consequence in one sentence, said in Chapter 174 and corrected twice in the same room: a valley of four hundred people has been keeping a winter that an office asked it to keep, for about two hundred years, through nine generations, in a form, because a form is a form — and the correction is that the form does not ask about a winter, it asks for a figure of men going out, and the valley answered it the only way it knows how, which is with a book, one line at a time, over a generation.**

444. **THE WINTER BOOK IS A FORM WITH ABOUT FOUR COLUMNS TAKEN OUT OF THE MIDDLE OF IT AND A COLUMN OF NAMES PUT IN ON THE OLDER SPREADS, AND THE RULING OF THE TWO IS THE SAME WITHIN A HAIR, AND NOBODY IN NINE GENERATIONS HAS EVER RECOGNISED IT BECAUSE THERE IS NOT ONE FORM IN THIS VALLEY FOR IT TO BE RECOGNISED AGAINST.** Chapters 172 and 174. **Found on a physical thing: two sheets lying side by side on the boards of the floor of a room over a byre, one of them the only roll in a valley of about four hundred people, and a man who has pegged out nine hundred yards of approach and a mile of boundary in four counties can see it from a foot off with his hands behind his back.** Three columns on the ninth spread are ruled to the same widths as three of the eight numbers on the form, and the margin on the left is the same margin, and the depth of a ruled space on one is the depth of a ruled space on the other. **The name column of the older spreads is a fifth column and it is the only place a name has ever been in nine spreads, and the person who made the book that way did it on purpose and did not write down that he had done it, and the reason is the four lines at the head of the first spread.** **The chapter ends on the question the block does not answer: *then who took four columns out of it.* Nobody answers it by Chapter 180 and a later phase may not answer it either without a decision that this volume has not earned.**

445. **THE FOUR LINES AT THE HEAD OF THE FIRST SPREAD ARE READ OUT FOR THE FIRST TIME IN A HUNDRED AND FORTY YEARS, AND THEY ARE A RULE ABOUT KEEPERS, AND THEY ARE THE ANSWER TO THE FORM'S FIFTH COLUMN, AND THAT IS WHERE NINE GENERATIONS OF A CONFUSION BETWEEN FOUR WORDS FOR A PERSON WAS WRITTEN DOWN.** Chapter 173, and Chapter 169's promise that they would not be read is discharged here and is not improved on. In a man of fifty-eight's own hand, a hundred and forty years old, and read out twice: *This book is kept and the room is kept. The keeper of it is a man and not an office. The keeper of it answers for the book and the room and the day and the mark and the hand. The keeper of it answers for no person in this valley and speaks for no person in this valley and has been appointed by no person in this valley. Where a man is named in a book of this valley it is because he did it himself and not because anybody asked him.* **He read them about nine hundred times and never once knew what they were a rule about, and the man who wrote them read the fifth column of a form on the floor of the back room and wrote the opposite of it at the head of his own answer, and signed nothing and dated nothing and told nobody, and it has held for a hundred and forty years and it is the best thing anybody in this valley has ever written down.** **And the finding is completed in this block and is not re-derived: a carrier is a person who has gone out of the valley and been named for it, a fact about a road; the hand is a person who keeps a thing not made of words, a fact about a wall; a keeper maintains a place or its records, which is employment and not authority; and a fourth word, for a person a community appoints to answer for one other named person, who answers to the people who appointed him and can be relieved by them. THE WORD `CUSTODIAN` DOES NOT APPEAR IN CHAPTERS 171 TO 180. The fourth word is described in its own words in Chapter 173, on the Chapter 156 and Chapter 166 precedent, and Batch 0003's prompt allowed it to be named and this batch did not name it. No character in this batch calls a carrier a custodian and no character calls a custodian a carrier. The second not-asking, a man at a gate who will not say what a word means, was not turned into a mirror of the first and no character in this batch noticed that the two resemble anything.**

446. **OSGAR VELL IS NAMED, 22, OF THE NINTH GENERATION, ON THE ROLL FROM BIRTH IN A HAND NOBODY ALIVE CAN NAME, AND HE IS THE YOUNG MAN OF THE DOORWAY IN CHAPTER 166, OF THE MARKET IN CHAPTER 166 AND OF THE BACK OF THE RIGHT-HAND ROW IN CHAPTER 170, AND HE COMES UP NINE STEPS TO SAY HIS OWN NAME BECAUSE NOBODY HAS ASKED HIM A QUESTION SINCE A MARKET DAY.** Chapter 173, and `outline/volume-04.md` §13's Batch 0003 row. **The name budget is one new name of six and five slots unfilled, so Volume 04 stands at four names of six and twenty-two of twenty-four slots unfilled: Iven Sarr, Wystan Roole, Nev Treen, Osgar Vell.** He is the volume's instrument and not its symbol. **His eight spellings, said once, in a room, and the eighth is not a word: there are seven ways of saying it in nine miles and the eighth thing is a description printed on a form under a byre, and it is the only one of the nine that is true about anybody, and nobody has ever used it, because it describes a thing that happened to a man and is not a name for a person. His mother and his aunt, who live eleven yards apart and have not spoken about it in nine years; the woman at the mill, who has said it to him since he was about seven; a fourth version he made up himself at seventeen in a doorway; the girl of about nine at the gate, who will not give her name and gives a place instead; the man who makes nails, whose is the only one that makes it sound like a job; the man of eighty-one, whose is the only one that makes it sound like a debt; and the printed description.** **He says the two accounts of where a word came from have never been in the same room and that no instrument in this kingdom could put them in one, and that a man of thirty-two is the only person he has met who could check either and cannot check a word out of a man's mouth. He is going over the pass on the fourth day of the next cold, with about eleven others, and has never had an answer he could hand a person. His four seconds in the doorway are spent and are not improved on and are not restated anywhere in this batch, and the refusal stands.**

447. **WHAT A CARRIER WAS FOR, AND THE NAMING WAS NEVER DONE BY THE VALLEY, AND THE STROKE IN THE WALL IS CUT BY A BROTHER WITH A COLD CHISEL OFF A ROOF SLATE IN NINE MINUTES IN A WET WEEK.** Chapters 175 and 176, and `outline/volume-04.md` §8 Block 3's texture card. **The third generation's house, two steadings up the bank from the Low Holm, a woman of sixty-eight married in forty-eight years, a man of the seventh generation in the byre, and a man of seventy-four at the table by the fire who has not said a word for an hour.** Nine stones in a corner of a byre yard with a barred T cut on each and a stroke through one of them, and the one with the stroke is the newest because the cuts are sharp. **The story is four generations old: a man of seventeen went out and was gone fourteen months and came back in the warm week with nine beasts that were not this valley's and with a word in the low country's language, given to him by a stranger who did not ask his name and went on down the valley the same afternoon, and the family's own correction, made forty years ago by a grandmother now dead, is that it was not a stranger but somebody in the valley who had it off one.** **And the finding: nobody in this valley named you, and there are two accounts of where the word came from and one of them is in a room under a byre and one of them is in a yard, and the two have never been in the same room. And a man of seventy-four says the whole of it once, at the age of seventy-four, about fifty-five years late, and says that there were three of them that week and that the two people who have cut a stroke in a wall in that valley in a hundred and forty years had between them not one idea.** **A knife and a cold chisel in a yard is the only instrument in this volume that anybody has ever used to say a true thing, and it is said once, and it is not improved on.**

448. **THE COUNTERWEIGHT IS A TRADE FACT AND NOT THE MECHANISM: A THING IS NOT KNOWN TO HOLD UNTIL IT IS PUT UNDER A LOAD, AND EVERYTHING IN THIS VALLEY HAS BEEN UNDER A LOAD FOR NINE GENERATIONS AND NOT ONE OF IT HAS EVER BEEN TESTED, AND A THING THAT HAS NEVER BEEN TESTED IS NOT A THING THAT HAS PROVED IT HOLDS, IT IS A THING THAT HAS NEVER BEEN ASKED.** Chapter 177, said once, in a yard and on a bank, in the language of a valley that builds roads, and it is **not** the mechanism said in Chapter 164 and it does not restate it and no narrator underlines it and no character summarises it. **The mechanism remains spent: a wall is built once and does not want feeding and a promise has to be renewed or it stops, and the asking is the price of the privilege of the working being a promise at all. Wystan Roole is shown knowing it in Chapter 176 by beginning a sentence and stopping, and the reason he gives is that he said it once on a bank in the eleventh week of the first cold to the only person in that valley who builds anything and he is not going to say it twice.** **The strain itself, as far as the page takes it and no further: a bridgekeeper of thirty-four can put his hand on a nine-week-old wall and know it and cannot put his hand on a stone he laid four days ago, and the ninth generation's grandmothers have been saying *the water has gone quiet* about the Burn since the first winter, and about four hundred yards below a ford have gone quiet and it has not stopped above the ford, and there is no figure in that valley to be had for it and a man with a cart is coming over the pass in the warm week and nothing is expected of him. Nobody in this block names the working, nobody explains it, and no character says what is under the winter.**

449. **THE SECOND ASKING, AND THE WORD, AND THE NOT-TRANSLATING, AND IT IS THE CORRECT ACT AND THE VOLUME SAYS SO IN A DOCUMENT.** Chapters 178 and 180. **It is about a different thing from Chapter 166's asking and it is not a cut and no character puts the two together and nobody describes what anybody is going to do in terms a reader could repeat.** They are told, at about nine hundred doors, in eleven days, four men and a woman at a door, the same six things in the same words in the same order: **one,** there is a thing under this valley nine generations old and it is holding; **two,** it is straining, said by a bridgekeeper and not by the man who is asking, and it is going to go on straining, and there is no way in the world to put a load on it; **three,** there is a man here who can take it out, and it would be done in a season, and the winter would come down; **four,** about two hundred of them are in a book from the day they were born and it says they are the people of a winter and they are not, and there are eight columns on a form under a byre and four lines at the head of the first spread saying there is nobody appointed to answer for the men that go out; **five,** it does not make them safe, and a count in a file in a county about two hundred miles off is the only thing in the world anybody could produce against anybody in this valley, and a figure is the only kind of paper that cannot be refused, and it will still be there in nine years whether the winter is here or not; **six,** it has to be stood to, by the about two hundred in the book, and nobody is to be put in a column about it and nobody is to have a stroke cut on a bench about it and nothing is to be written down.**** **The word they use is the word this valley has for a bridge, introduced in ordinary trade use in Chapter 176 and not explained, in about forty mouths in nine miles and in no book, and it is not translated, and the reason is given in his mouth and it is that every thing that has happened to him in this valley has been done in a word that is not his and he is not going to be the first person in the history of this valley to say a thing in his own language and have it be the thing on the page. He runs out of it at a gate in Chapter 178 and a man of thirty-four tells him to use the valley's, and the reason he gives is that the man at the gate has never been to the county he came from and is going to hear a word and hold it and that not one of the four of them will ever be able to say what he heard. The volume says so in a document in Chapter 180: a leaf torn out of the back of his own notebook, nine lines, given to the man of fifty-eight, the first page he has given to anybody in four years and a half, and the line about the word is on it, and he asks whether it is a bad idea and is told that it is a bad idea and that there is one reason it is worth doing, and it goes on the seat of the bench at the back of the right-hand row, folded once, and there has never been one thing on any of the twenty-nine benches that has ever been put on one, and there is one now.**

450. **THE CONSENT IS NOT UNANIMOUS AND THE NUMBER AGAINST IT IS NINE, AND THE NINE IS THREE HOUSEHOLDS CONVERTED INTO PERSONS BY A MAN WITH A ROPE-BELT IN ABOUT NINE SECONDS, AND IT IS WRONG, AND IT IS THE FIRST ARITHMETIC ANYBODY IN THAT VALLEY HAS DONE ON ITS OWN PEOPLE.** Chapters 179 and 180, and this reconciles `outline/volume-04.md` §8 Block 3's *the number is small* with Block 5's *the nine not-unanimous people named in the book before it is done* and with the close's *the first three families to go are the three who said no*. **Three and nine are both now canon and neither may be changed by a later phase.** The three reasons, given at three doors and nowhere else, in about four sentences, a minute and four, and one sentence. **A man of about fifty at a gate: his grandmother stood in that aisle when the benches were put in and it took nine minutes and it was the worst nine minutes of her life, and he has a bench with a hundred and forty cut into the end of it that his family has never been struck off, and he is being asked to agree to a thing that will not go in that room, and he has not got a better reason and it took him about four seconds. A man of about forty of the ninth generation: he has been in that book since the day he was born and has never been asked anything, and he will not be the first in nine generations to be asked, and you may write him down as one of three and you cannot write down why, and if you write down why he will change his mind, and he has decided he does not want to be a man who changes his mind for a piece of paper. The man who makes nails: he has wanted to go out of this valley for nine years and has said so out loud, and the first family out is going to be a family with a reason and a place to go, and he will not stand to a thing that puts him at the front of that queue, and he would rather be one of the three than be the first, and he says it at a market two days later in front of eleven people because he is a nail man and a nail man says things at markets.** **The count: about four hundred people, about four hundred households, a hundred and ninety-four of the ninth generation in the valley, eleven of the ninth over a pass and not able to be asked, and the difference between the roll's about two hundred and the a hundred and seveny-nine who were asked done by subtraction off a number nobody can check. Not one figure of those is in a book and the four who made them worked it out in about nine minutes in a cold room and none of them wrote it down.**

451. **THREE FIGURES GO IN THE BOOK AND NO NAME GOES BESIDE THE NINE, IN THE DAY COLUMN OF THE LAST LEAF OF THE NINTH SPREAD, WITH A MARK UNDER EACH AND A HAND OVER THE TOP, AND THE HAND VARIES.** Chapter 180, the twenty-fourth day of the second cold, at about the sixth hour, with four people in the room. *About four hundred. About a hundred and seveny-nine. Nine.* **A figure of people is the same kind of thing as a day in a valley with no months, no years and no hour anybody keeps, and there is no other column for it, and a line without a mark in that book is a line that has never happened.** **And the reason there is no name against the nine is the reason for the four lines at the head of the first spread, and the man of fifty-eight says in the room that he did not know that until this afternoon and that it is the first time in nineteen years he has had a fact in his book with a person on it and left the person off.** **And the three figures are the first figures in that valley's book in a hundred and forty years, and the finding is that a figure of people goes in the book and a figure of money goes on a trestle in chalk, and the trestle falls down and the book does not, and that is the first distinction anybody in that valley has ever drawn.**

452. **THE MONEY, FOOTED IN PENCE ON THE PAGE BEFORE THE TOTAL IS SAID, AND THE VALLEY'S OWN PRICE REFUSED AND ADDED TO NOTHING.** Chapter 180. *One man, one day, at three pence. Sixteen men: three, sixteen times over, is forty-eight. Forty-eight a day for eleven days: forty-eight eleven times over is five hundred and twenty-eight. A barrow of salt at fourpence. Five hundred and twenty-eight and four is five hundred and thirty-two pence, which is eleven marks and fourpence.* **It is in a county's money about four hundred miles off where an unskilled day is three pence, written in a notebook and then on the end of a trestle in chalk about eleven inches high, and not in the book, and the trestle has been the same trestle for nineteen years and the chalk will be off it inside a year and neither man wrote a second copy of it anywhere, deliberately, and the reason was a rule about a thing written down twice.** **The valley's own price of that fortnight is eleven kitchens and about four barrows of salt and nobody's figure, and the two are never added and there is no way on this earth to add them and a person who tried would be doing arithmetic on a thing to make it go away.** **The form's own printed figure is *four in this year*, in a reckoning the valley does not use, and it is not converted into anything, and it is the only figure anybody has ever given this valley by anybody from anywhere.** No 456, no 254, no 2,450, no 2,906, no 9-4-1, no hearth figure, and no county figure set beside a valley figure in any chapter of this block.

453. **THE COUNT IN THE FILE TWO HUNDRED MILES OFF IS CITED ONCE, IN HIS MOUTH, AS THE ONLY THING IN THE WORLD THAT CAN BE PRODUCED AGAINST ANYBODY IN THAT VALLEY, AND IT IS 2,640 IN A WOMAN'S HAND WITH NO SEAL, NO NUMBER, NO RETURNABLE DATE, NO SIGNATURE AND NO ADDRESSEE, AND IT IS NOT RE-DERIVED, AND TAKING THE WINTER OUT OF THE GROUND DOES NOT TOUCH IT.** Chapter 179. **The finding in a room, said once, out loud: a count is the only paper that survives, and everything else in that valley falls down — a bench is in a house, a book is in a room, a form is on a floor, a slate is round a woman's neck, a stall is at a market four times a year, and a thing somebody said at a gate is gone in about nine years. The nine words at the foot of the modern printed paper are the same nine words as at the foot of the form under the byre, and he says the wording and says *I have read that wording before* and does not describe the other one, and the reason is that a man who describes a document to nine people has made nine copies of a thing nobody in that valley can see. The Office of Provincial Registration is an office, it is dangerous because it is doing its job, and it does not appear. Its ancestor is named and it is a different office two hundred years older. `outline/series.md`'s Volume 4 escalation line and knowledge-control row remain unsatisfied and are carried forward as an open item and no later phase may read this batch as having satisfied them.** The marginal instruction is not explained and is not in anybody's mouth. The crown's fourth word is described and not named. No name is written in any Crown's hand and there has not been one in that county since a day at the end of a month it keeps, and this volume has never heard of that month.

454. **STAGE 3 IS NOT REACHED, NOT ATTEMPTED, NOT OFFERED AS A PLAN, NOT PRICED AND NOT DESCRIBED AS AVAILABLE IN THIS BLOCK, AND NO LINEAGE IS READ AND THE WORKING IS NOT NAMED AND THE CUT IS NOT NAMED.** **The `cut` string occurs twenty-one times in Chapters 171–180 and every one of them is ordinary** — a trough cut in one piece, four numbers cut into the ends of benches, a hundred and forty cut into the end of the back bench three times, a mark cut on each of nine stones in a wall, a bar across the top of a T cut nine times, a stroke cut through one of them from the top, the same stroke cut with a knife by a grandmother and cut with a cold chisel off a roof slate by a man of nineteen, a stroke cut with a pen by an office two hundred years ago, another cut in a wall two steadings up the bank, a cutting in a beck four times, an offcut of a byre roof — **and the twenty-first is in the sixth thing said at a door, which is the *negation* of the mark, and the working is not among any of the twenty-one and is not named.** **No bodily cost is added: the limp stands as Volume 03 left it, in the right leg, and the stick is four hundred miles for four hundred yards and is useless in a valley with no road, and that is a fact and not a cost and it is not said as a discovery in this block. No melody cost is added and the word does not appear. The Many-Handed stage's worsening belongs to Volume 15.** The return stitch is not mentioned in any of the ten chapters. The refusal in Chapter 166 stands and is not repeated and not improved on and is not restated. The not-askings stand at nine and this batch enters no tenth and there is no main-world room in the block and the two of them are not in one sentence anywhere in it. No apology in any form and no mistake has been made available to anybody.
