and any volume-wide use of it is wrong.** §2.1, §2.3 and §2.10 of the close.

647. **FIVE PAGE FIGURES IN VOLUME 05 ARE WRONG AND ARE NOT REPAIRED, AND THE CLOSE NAMES ALL FIVE.** (a) **The refusal count.** `214:3`, on the sixth day of the city's count, says the city *has been asked nine times in four hundred years and has said no nine times*, and `220:3`, `220:37` and `220:43`, on the nineteenth day, make the ninth asking and the ninth refusal the child's, and `220:5` says a man of sixty-six *has entered eight refusals in a book under a board* — eight before the ninth, which foots. **Eight plus one is nine, the ninth is the nineteenth day, and the sixth day cannot already have nine.** Every other statement of the count in the volume and in items 606, 609, 610 and 623 agrees with eight on the sixth day. (b) **An age.** `226:25` sets *a man of sixty-one at a bench with a book on it* and `226:31` reports that *a man of sixty-six* said a figure out loud in that yard for the first time in nineteen years; the man is Osmund Cusk, sixty-one, and Dermit Crane, sixty-six, is four hundred yards away in a bindle yard. (c) **A date.** `210:43` and `214:98` call a page dated the fourteenth of Harvestmonth thirty-five days old on the eighth of Embermonth, and the carried thirty-day month makes it **fifty-four days elapsed**, and the thirty-five is the path figure he is about to spend inside the city. (d) **A duration.** `231:35`, `231:39`, `232:69` and `233:19` say **forty days** for his time inside a city that keeps a count of days, and `233:29`, `233:45`, `233:61` and `233:69`, **in the same chapter and on the same day**, say **thirty-five days** four times. (e) **A calendar token.** `204:67` has *a leg that is the same leg it was in June*, and there is no June in this kingdom; the month's list is Thawmonth, Mudmonth, Greenmonth, Longlight, Rainmonth, Harvestmonth, Fallowmonth, Embermonth, Wolfmonth, Frostmonth, Hearthmonth, Goatmonth. **All five are recorded and none is repaired, because this phase writes fiction-plan and manuscript-state files only, and all five are carried to Volume 06 as figures a batch must not treat as canon. The fifth is a one-line repair and is the only one of the five that is a calendar token.**

648. **A PARAGRAPH IS ON THE PAGE TWICE, IN THE SAME ROOM, FORTY-TWO CHAPTERS APART.** *The clerk read that back and entered it and read it again, and the second reading was slower and not better, and that has been the practice of that room since the first year.* — a whole paragraph at `203:33` and again at `245:41`, both in the long room over the wharf, both the clerk of about sixty. **The Batch 0005 block sweep was scoped to the ten new chapters over 319 paragraphs of twelve words or more and returns clean, and 319 is what that basis produces on the page, and a sweep across the fifty chapters of the volume returns this one.** The motif is longer than the volume: `189:47` and `189:49` in Volume 04 have the second reading slower and not better, and `208:5` has the same clerk reading a whole minute back twice with the same clause. **So the house practice of reading a thing back twice and finding the second reading slower and not better is delivered four times in fifty chapters and a Volume 06 batch may not deliver it a fifth time in a room.** The standing rule this establishes, and it is the close's third half of the rule item 584 already carries: **a check scoped to what was just written cannot see what was written before it, and a sweep that returns clean is a statement about a scope and not about a book.**

649. **THE VOLUME NAMES THE LENGTH OF ITS OWN SPEECHES WITH FIGURES THAT ARE NOT THE LENGTHS OF THE SPEECHES, AND THE RULE IT LEAVES.** The volume's signature move is to give a speech and then to say how long it was, and **with the number words counted, seven of the eleven instances do not match:** `230:41` *answered it in nine words* against 78 words at `230:39`; `231:79` *in about nineteen words* against 60 at `231:81`; `233:13` *said nine words* against 18 at `233:15`; `234:25` *it is about nineteen words* against 64 at `234:27`; `234:53` *said nine words to nobody* against 14 at `234:55`; `227:29` *about twenty-two words* against 86 at `227:27`; `233:69` *the answer was six words* against 92. **Four check out exactly: `234:47` nine, `230:15`'s opening sentence nine, `231:75` three, `224:7` four.** **The one place the mismatch is earned is the eleven-word things, which are a man's own claim about his own practice and which Chapter 236 corrects on the page — about four hundred of the eleven-word things are not eleven — and says he is not going to lengthen a no to make it match a shelf. That is canon and it is the volume's best joke. Every other instance is the narration asserting and not counting.** The rule for Volume 06 and every volume after it: **a speech-length figure is either footed, or it is inside a character's mouth as a claim about that character, and the two may not be confused.**

650. **THE TWO COUNTED FIGURES IN `outline/volume-05.md` CORRECTED IN PLACE, AND A THIRD FOUND AND DELIBERATELY NOT CORRECTED.** §9's *the third refusal in a document in **four** volumes* is corrected to **three**, because the page says three at `250:21` and item 643 footed the chain: Chapter 148 in Volume 03, then the fourth route refused in writing in Volume 04, then this one, and Volumes 01 and 02 contain no refusal in a document that any later document counts. **§8 Block 5 and §10's *a bench of nine is asked a **seventh** thing* are both corrected to the eighth**, because the page says the eighth and the arithmetic is footed on the page at `245:37` and entered by a clerk of about sixty on a page under that stair: five askings for the crossing, four answered yes and one brought up two flights and not put, a sixth in a Harvestmonth with a figure of forty marks, a seventh on the thirtieth of Fallowmonth with the word consent in it four times, and now this; **five and one and one and one is eight**, and the prompt for Batch 0005 also said a seventh and the prompt is the thing that is wrong. **A third instance of the same wrong ordinal is in §11's concrete hand-off and is left standing, because the instruction that produced this close bounded the correction to §8 Block 5 and §10 and said correct nothing else in that file, and a close that widened its own brief to fix a third instance of a figure it had been told to fix twice is a close that has decided the plan document is wrong in a way its owner has to decide. A Volume 06 phase reading §11 must treat the eighth asking as the count and §11 as carrying a stale ordinal.** §14's *fourth refusal in a document in four volumes* is a different figure about a different thing and was not touched.

651. **THE VOLUME'S UNATTRIBUTED TWO-LINE STATEMENTS ARE FOUR AND THE LEDGER SAYS ONE, AND VOLUME 06'S OWN BUDGET IS FOUR.** At `209:58` *A road needs a person at the far end, and the person has to be able to say no. Nobody has told you whether it can.* · at `214:9–10` *Nothing here is owed to you and nothing has refused you.* and *You have not been told which of the two you are in.* · at `227:51–52` *Read it as far as it goes and then stop.* and *It does not go further for anybody, and the part that is left is not being kept from you.* · at `237:67–68` *You have said no twice tonight and both of them were yours to say.* and *There is no figure for what either of them cost and there is not going to be one.* **Four, all two lines, none with a number in it, one per chapter, and `209:58` is followed by the sentence that establishes the series: he has had four of those in four years and has written one down, and the one he wrote down has no hour against it and no name in it.** `AGENTS.md`'s at-most-one-per-chapter rule is satisfied four times out of four; the volume total in the plan and the ledger was one and it is wrong. **Volume 06's budget is four: one in each of Blocks 1 to 4, none in Block 5, two plain lines each, no number in any of them, none of them naming a path, the roadmark, the light or the mechanism, and none of them written down by anybody.**

652. **THE VOLUME 06 DAY MAP, THE WEEKDAY CHAIN, AND THE YEAR LABEL, COUNTED FORWARD FROM DAY 150 AND FROM NOTHING ELSE.** **Volume 06 runs day 150, the twenty-fifth of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Thursday and a market day, to day 390, the twenty-fifth of Embermonth, YR 316, a Saturday and a market day, and the year turns inside the volume at day 156, the first of Thawmonth: two hundred and forty days elapsed, two hundred and forty-one inclusive, eight months on the carried thirty-day rule, matching the Volume 6 row of the ledger. Blocks are 150–190, 191–231, 232–272, 273–313 and 314–390, which is forty days elapsed and forty-one inclusive for each of the first four and seventy-six and seventy-seven for the last, and the four and seventy-seven foot at the two hundred and forty-one, and no block boundary falls inside Mudmonth, which is carried at thirty days and is fixed by three of the table's own rows and is not an open month. All of this was recomputed again by the close's review repair pass and every figure reproduced.** Recomputed here from day 0, and every day and every weekday in `outline/volume-06.md` §17's table reproduces: **day 13 is Embermonth 8, day 103 is Hearthmonth 8, day 131 is Goatmonth 6, day 150 is Goatmonth 25, day 246 is the first of Longlight, day 253 is the eighth of Longlight, day 284 is the ninth of Rainmonth, day 390 is the twenty-fifth of Embermonth.** **Seventy market days fall in the two hundred and forty-one, and the blocks carry twelve, twelve, twelve, twelve and twenty-two, and the four and twenty-two foot at seventy.** Volume 05's forty-three market days were verified the same way and foot as four before the crossing, twenty-five in the ninety days away, and fourteen after the return. **And one year label in this chain is still open and the close records it rather than choosing a side: `outline/volume-05.md` §17's day 0 is the twenty-fifth of Fallowmonth, YR 314, and the year turns after Goatmonth in the month's order, so by that anchor the twenty-fifth of Goatmonth one hundred and fifty days later is in the same year, while all fifty chapters and the close's own instruction say YR 315. The outline follows the prose, because the prose is closed prose, and labels day 150 YR 315 and every day from the turn at day 156 onward YR 316, day 390 included. The day numbers, the month names and the weekdays are exact; the years are the one part a later audit has to settle, and a phase that settles them moves the two audited chains together and restates the last date of each volume and says that it has done so.**

653. **THE HEARING'S YEAR IS FIXED, AND IT IS FIXED BY THIS BLOCK.** The hearing was entered in Volume 04 for **a delegation that cannot arrive**, heard with nobody in it, not adjourned and not refused, and every state file since has given *the ninth of Rainmonth of the year following* while the page gives *a day in Rainmonth*. **The year is YR 316, and that was corrected in place by the close's review repair pass, which is the only thing it changed in this item: day 284 is one hundred and twenty-eight days past the turn at day 156, so a YR 315 label on it is a year out. The older reasoning reached YR 315 by counting from `outline/volume-05.md` §17's own day-0 label, the twenty-fifth of Fallowmonth, YR 314, while this volume follows the closed prose and calls that same day YR 315, and the two conventions differ by exactly one year at every point, so one sentence gave two years and the prose governs. The date is otherwise unchanged: day 284, a Friday, not a market day, one hundred and thirty-four days after Volume 05's last day, and inside Volume 06's Block 4.** The hearing was reached in Volume 05 and found empty and it stands. **The Crown's proceeding sits on the same date in the same province and it is a different proceeding, and the two are joined by a companion file of one sheet with a district on it and by nothing else, and no Volume 06 batch may merge the two hearings into one hearing.** The delegation does not arrive and is not sent for and no delegation is put in the room. The companion file is not removed, not corrected, and not asked after by anybody who knows what is in it. **And the fourth of Goatmonth, YR 316 is the next ninth of Rainmonth and is out of Volume 06 entirely.**

654. **THE CONTACT THAT ENDS IN VOLUME 06 IS IVEN SARR, 58, KEEPER OF THE WINTER BOOK, AND THE OUTLINE DECIDES IT AND A BATCH MAY NOT DECIDE IT DIFFERENTLY.** `outline/series.md`'s Volume 6 escalation row requires a cut on a forged main-world witness record, the cut tearing the local anchor instead, the path community surviving and losing all contact, and `outline/series.md` line 133 says an unconsented failure in Volume 6 ends one live contact, and the close's instruction requires the contact to be **a person and not an abstraction and decided in the outline.** Four reasons, and they are the reasons. **First, he holds the only document in the book that names a keeper, and the loss permanently closes the form's three questions, the origin of the subscription sentence, and the two unreconciled figures of the ninth generation — three live threads, which is what makes the loss a political fact and not a death scene.** Second, he is not the bridge, so the physical anchor can be a crossing and the man need not be a symbol. Third, the series needs Wystan Roole alive and building for Volume 8 and needs the mill man and the man of eighty-one and the girl with the barrow. **Fourth, and this is the reason the outline fixes the order as well as the name: the volume pays his want first.** He has wanted his book read for six years. **In Block 2, a man of thirty-two goes up a road nine days each way with a witness at each end and a date, and Iven Sarr stands in an aisle four feet wide that has gone three generations without being used, with a hundred and forty cut into the end of the bench behind the right-hand row and nobody struck off one of them, and is asked what he swore, and the answer goes into his own book in his own hand, and it is the first finding in that book in a hundred and forty years. The cut is in Block 3. A finding cannot be asked a second time. The volume's own mechanic is what makes the gift into a loss three chapters later, and the book does it anyway, because a man of fifty-eight has wanted it for six years and nobody asked whether he could stand it afterwards.** He is not dead. The valley is not closed. **Nobody in the valley is told, and the not-telling is held for eight months and is not resolved and is not scheduled.** `bible/power-system.md`: recovery requires accepting the loss and rebuilding trust outside the path, **so the recovery is with people who can be reached and it is not another crossing and no Volume 06 batch may schedule one.**

655. **THE FORGED RECORD'S GROUND IS THE *Keeper* COLUMN, AND THE PERSON THE LIE IS ABOUT IS SABIN DAIN, AND WHAT VOLUME 06 MAY NOT DO TO HER.** The Culling Order's classification of a crossing rests on a main-world witness record, **and the record is a *Keeper* entry, and the *Keeper* column is a column with a head on it, and the head is the office's own construction, and the name in it is a name nobody put there.** It is built out of three real things: a form of the office's own printed series, a hand nobody questioned, and a date that is somebody else's, **assembled by a person doing ordinary work who has never been asked what is in the four places and does not ask.** The name in it is a woman of thirty-three who fills that column about two hundred times a season and has been afraid of it since she was twenty-two, **who on the fourth of Goatmonth, YR 315 wrote a figure of persons in the second of four places on a return in about a minute and a quarter without looking up and read it back afterwards and the reading was slower and not better.** She finds out in Block 4, from a piece of paper somebody else has carried in. **She may not be thanked, may not be converted, may not be told she was right, may not be the person who explains the marginal instruction, and may not change her want, which is four or five words: nobody enters a family by a name nobody entered.** Her note of nineteen words stays face down in a book on the second shelf and **no Volume 06 batch may turn it over.** Her third speech is a refusal of kindness and it is the last time a kind thing is refused at that table: she would like somebody to write down that she did not stop it and there is nobody in that building she can ask, and nobody asks. **And the volume's argument is exactly this: a cut made on a forged record is a cut made on somebody's lie, and the argument is not the cut, it is what the lie costs the person the lie was about, and both of the entries in that column are in the same hand and neither of them is a decision.**

656. **THE LOCAL ANCHOR THAT GOES IS THE OLD TOLL, AND A SECOND SEAM IS IN THAT COUNTY, AND NEITHER IS MEASURED.** The anchor is **a dressed block in the abutment of a crossing four hundred yards up a fen county's own road, with forty yards of tarred hemp in it, put there on the fourth of Hearthmonth of the year before by four men and a boy, and dug for by nobody in that county, and put there by a man of thirty-two with a limp.** The crossing has **no owner, no money, no tolls, no seat on that bench, no glass in the sill and no third seat**, and it has carried nobody for four years, **and the thing it is for is a thing that has to be agreed.** `bible/power-system.md`: every cut leaves a visible seam in the current world and gives the affected path a lasting memory of him. **The Volume 04 cut's seam is the line about nine inches long in the third course of the fourth bay of the Sedge Reach under about half an inch of lime that has not moved and that nobody in that county has measured in five volumes. This volume's seam is a second one, in the dressed block, about the same length because the work is the same work and the hands are the same hands.** The bell above the crossing is nine stone of green-black bronze with a band of forty-one rivets and a dull red seam split lip to shoulder, **rung at the fourth hour and a half by a boy who has been the steward's apprentice for two years and three months and is still not good at it and by a carpenter who is a hand and not a keeper, neither paid by the guild and neither a member of anything, and it is a hundred yards off the cut and is not touched and goes on being rung, and nobody in that county hears anything happen.** The volume does not write the moment. **It writes the three days before it and the fourth day after it, and a man of thirty-two with a limp who cannot get up a bank, and a witness at an end who said the same four things he had said four times and was not asked for a fifth.** Neither seam is measured, ruled across, pointed at, or used as a door, a key or a mark, and **the two crossings four hundred yards apart are not put in one book by anybody in this volume, and the volume's last fact is that a county with one of each has never done it and is not going to.**

657. **THE FIRST OF LONGLIGHT IS DAY 246, THE RENEWAL IS IN THAT WEEK, AND THE CUT IS DAY 253, AND THE ORDER IS FIXED AND MAY NOT BE REVERSED.** Longlight is the month boundary oath-stones are renewed and the year's promises are made in public, and it has not been on the page since Volume 01, and `outline/volume-05.md` §17 said a writer who wants the volume to end on a renewal has to wait for Volume 06. **In Block 3, a boundary oath-stone in a fen county is renewed for the first time in nineteen years, and the renewal is a public act, and a public act is written down by a clerk of about sixty keeping a second kind of minute, and the thing written down is a description of what is at that boundary: a crossing with no owner and no money, a sill with nothing in it, a dressed block, a bell. The description goes to a provincial table and into an object column, and the object column has a word in front of the place name, and the word is the office's own and has been in the type case for two years and has never been struck.** A bench of nine is not asked, because a bench of nine has no standing at a parish boundary and has never claimed any. *Object* is the column that got a city in the last volume; this time *Object* gets a bell, **and the bell is not explained and its device is not named and nothing about it is his and it is not going to be.** **The cut is eight days later, at about the second hour of the eighth day of Longlight, and it needs a real document to stand on and the renewal is the real document. A batch that reverses the two has written a volume in which a man cuts on a forgery that has nothing under it, which is a different failure and a smaller one.**

658. **THE STAGE 3 STATE AND WHAT THE CUT COSTS, DECIDED BEFORE A BATCH, AND THE FEVER AND THE STAGE'S STANDING LIMIT.** Stage 3, Threadkeeper, held going in. **Three paths open: Bellweather-Living, the Hearth Marches, the Ninefold Winter valley, and by the end of the volume one of the three is not held and it was never taken from him.** The lineage reading was made once in Chapter 227 and is not re-derived. The cut is made once, in Block 3, and **it is the first cut in the manuscript that is not consensual, and `bible/power-system.md` has a row for exactly this: a cut made on a false witness, the community's own anchor tears, contact ends, and the fee is another crossing — and a second row that says why the volume exists: *He learns to cut a forced cull in a training path with one living bridgekeeper, then fails the same cut in Volume 6 because he ignores consent.*** **The consent is missing in one specific way and the volume states it: there is no bridgekeeper at the shoulder of the man making it with a rope between them, and that absence is the whole difference from Chapter 195 and it is one missing person.** Costs, all four, and a batch may not substitute a fifth: **a second visible seam in the current world (item 656); the loss of a live contact, which is Iven Sarr (item 654); a week of fever, Stage 3's, the second in two volumes, and somebody else holds his tools for seven days;** and **the stage's standing limit, which nobody has ever paid before: *each additional cut makes the Gatehouse's preferred history feel physically plausible to him.*** He notices it once, in a room, on the eleventh day after the cut. **It is not a vision and not a voice and not a System panel: it is that a version of the last eight months in which he did not cut reads to him as the reasonable one, and he can see the shape of it, and it is the shape of a thing that would have worked. He tells one person. That is the whole of it.** **The fee row is refused: he does not make another crossing, and no Volume 06 batch may schedule one.** The limp does not worsen and the many-handed stage's worsening belongs to Volume 15. **No melody cost is added and the word does not appear.** The tax the volume already carries is unchanged: he cannot be given a thing without losing the thread.

659. **THE MARSHAL IS A RETURN AND COSTS VOLUME 06 NOTHING AGAINST THE NAME BUDGET, AND HIS NAME IS NOT WRITTEN IN THE OUTLINE.** He is named on the page in Volume 01, in a register column headed *tendered by*, and in Volume 02, and he is the antagonist of the whole book, and he is never surprised. `outline/series.md`'s Volume 6 row names him as the man who offers access to sealed personal records including evidence about a woman's unauthorized crossing. **He is not a new name in this volume, and `outline/volume-05.md` §13's rule about a returned face governs him exactly as it governed Halven, Sabin Dain, Mara Vey, Bram Ottery and Aren Kest in Volume 05.** The outline refers to him as **the marshal** and writes his name nowhere, and no chapter of Volume 06 carries it, and **thread 89 of `state/open-threads.md` and the Volume 02 close's §7.1 hold the second severance for Chapter 894, and the phase that eventually writes it checks the thread and the separate-sheet rule first and joins no two halves in one sentence.** He offers a sealed personal record in Block 1 and he is never surprised, and what is in it is a list of what was taken out of a valley in YR 301 with a boy. **And the sealed record and a book on a slope four hundred years deep carry the same shape — eleven hands and eleven roads, a woman and a boy, about a year between the going out and the coming back — and nobody in either place has ever compared them, and Volume 06's reversal is that the column with no outcome column is not a gap in a book but a decision about a person, four hundred years old, taken by eleven people in a room once who decided that a cost paid every day is better than a cost paid once. The reversal is a complication and not a vindication, her survival stays intentionally unknown, and the keeper of sixty-one said the shape of it out loud to a stranger in Volume 05 and has not been asked since and is not asked in Volume 06, because he is four hundred miles off in a city this volume does not go to, and the not-asking is structural and not a choice.**

660. **THE NAME BUDGET, AND VOLUME 06 PLANS FOUR AGAINST VOLUME 05'S FIVE, AND THE ARITHMETIC IS ON THE OUTLINE'S OWN FACE.** **Volume 05 spent five names of six and left twenty-four of thirty unfilled across its five batches, against a volume planned at five and twenty-four: twenty-nine of thirty slots, one under the cap. The five are Iselde Senn, named once in a main-world room in Chapter 205; Nesh Karrow, 28, named at `206:71`; Osmund Cusk, 61, named at `206:71`; Dermit Crane, 66, named at `215:7`; and Ivo Marrow, 52, named at `228:3`.** **Volume 06 plans four and leaves twenty-six of thirty, and the columns foot exactly at thirty, and the rows are 2 / 0 / 0 / 1 / 1 across Batches 0001 to 0005 with unfilled 4 / 6 / 6 / 5 / 5.** The four are **Ansel Rudd, 44**, the first named member of the Culling Order on a page, spent in Block 1 in a room doing the office's work; **Hester Cray, 38**, the Crown officer who convenes the proceeding, spent in Block 1; **Perry Hask, 34**, a second clerk of the returns in the provincial town, the first person in the book to be handed a document that joins two things by accident, spent in Block 4; and **Bessa Quill, 36**, a bridgekeeper in the Ninefold Winter who rides down a road nobody has come down and comes back with nothing, spent in Block 5. **The reason is Volume 05's reason applied one step harder: the tail of a volume is carried by people already in the room, and a volume whose antagonist finally walks into a room needs a face for the room and four and not six, and the other four things this volume needs are all returns — the marshal, Sabin Dain, Iven Sarr, and every face in Merefen.** The one slot most at risk of being spent wrongly is Block 5's, **because Block 5 is four documents and a bell, and the standing instruction is that it may not be spent, and a document block with a new face in it has been told it is a scene.**

661. **THE SEEDS THE CHILD IS NOT TO BE A SYMBOL FOR, AND THE CLOSE'S COUNT OF THEM.** The child is nine years old, is not named in Chapters 201 to 250, does not count against the name budget, and **is not a symbol, a sacrifice, a post, a rescue, a martyr, a message, an instrument, a test, a lesson, an inheritance, or a way of making a man better.** Seven seeds the close names and Volume 06 may not spend: **one, the mark in the corner of the strip is a line and a bar and a figure and nobody in that room put it there and nobody has looked at it since the seventh hour of a morning in the spring, and the child is not named and is not to be named. Two, the child is the volume's last image and the volume ends on a thing in a place and not on a man, and Volume 06's last image is a county with two seams and is a different shape again. Three, the child is the living anchor the return was made through and that is a mechanic and not a virtue, and no Volume 06 chapter may have anybody put a hand on the child for any reason. Four, the child is not the ninth refusal's author in a way anybody may improve on: the ninth refusal was given by a person and the person is nine, and that is the volume's argument and not the child's deed. Five, the child is not the post, and the city's own reason is that a name in a book in that city is a person somebody can be shown, and that reason is the city's and not the volume's and not a sentiment. Six, about four hundred people in a city of about nine thousand know what the child is for and about nine hundred know what it carries and not one of the two figures knows the other one, and the two figures are never added. Seven, the child did not go out on the thirty-first, thirty-second or thirty-third of a count and did not go out at all on the nineteenth and on the thirtieth, and the not-going-out is the reason the ninth thing that ever happened to that city was missed by the width of a breath, and that is the ordinary way a city misses a thing and is not carelessness.** **The child is behind the reader in Volume 06 and the city is four hundred miles off and this volume sends it nothing.**

662. **THE THREADS THE CLOSE DID NOT OPEN AND THE THREADS IT DID NOT CLOSE.** **The close opened eleven and closed none.** The eleven it opened are items 646 to 656 in this block, and they are findings, not threads: the ledger's basis and its three wrong figures; five page figures; the repeated paragraph; the speech-length device; the two corrections to `outline/volume-05.md` and the third left standing; the panel count and Volume 06's budget; the Volume 06 day map and the year label; the hearing's year; the contact that ends; the forged record's ground; the anchor that goes and the second seam; and the Longlight renewal and the order of the renewal and the cut. **The twenty-five threads in `state/open-threads.md`'s section *Threads Volume 05 Batch 0005 carries into Volume 06* are all still open and none was closed by this close and none may be closed by a Volume 06 batch except by saying on the page that a thing was closed and where.** The seventeen Batch 0004 carried are all still open. **And the volume's spine thread, item 25 of that section — *a city is a person and a column is not, and the proof of it is that a city's refusal went out of it as a figure and a figure cannot be refused* — is the sentence `outline/volume-06.md` is built on, and the close records it as the volume's whole argument and as the next volume's obligation and does not answer it.** A close closes nothing the last five chapters did not already close on the page, **and the last five chapters closed nothing.**

663. **THE THREE SERIES RESOLUTIONS, CHECKED AS A COUNT AND NOT AS AN IMPRESSION.** `outline/series.md`'s Volume 5 resolution row has three items and the count is three delivered and none of them a gift, a rescue, an improvement or a conversion: **the city remains sovereign and unreachable by the Crown, delivered in four chapters in a tray, a file, a drawer of type, a return and a district, and about four hundred people in a city of about nine thousand people do not know that anything at all has come back into it; Aren's understanding of consent changes and the change is a habit and not a belief, delivered in Chapter 247 in her words and in Chapter 250 in his not-writing, and it did not make him easier to be around; and Mara challenges his habit of treating refusal as failure and does not accept his answer, delivered in Chapter 247 in about a hundred and fifty words across three speeches, the last of which is a refusal of kindness.** **A close that reports the third of those as *he learned to accept a refusal* has reported the sentence and missed the woman, and the woman is the volume's argument.**

664. **WHAT THE VOLUME 05 CLOSE CHANGED, AND WHAT IT DID NOT TOUCH.** **It wrote no chapter prose, no scene, no dialogue and no narrative, and it made no line-level correction to any chapter in Volumes 01 to 05, because those chapters are closed prose and a close that tidies a finished volume is a close that has decided it does not like it.** It corrected **two counted figures on the face of `outline/volume-05.md`** — §9's volume count and the bench's ordinal in §8 Block 5 and §10 — and nothing else in that file, and it recorded a third instance of the same ordinal that it did not correct and why. It wrote `outline/volumes/volume-05-close.md` and `outline/volume-06.md`. It appended to this file, to `state/open-threads.md`, to `state/batch-summaries.md` and to `state/chapter-summaries.md`, and it updated `state/current.md`. **It touched no controller file: not `scripts/`, not `.github/`, not `.opencode/agent/`, not `AGENTS.md`, `PHASE_SYSTEM.md`, `REPO_PLAN.md`, `OUTLINE_GUIDE.md`, `opencode.json`, or `state/phase-ledger.json`.** It created **exactly one prompt**, at `workspace/volume-06/batch-0001/PROMPT.md`, and no Chapters 251 to 260 prompt anywhere and no second volume-close prompt anywhere. **And the hardest thing it had to say is this: the last ten chapters of Volume 05 are a document block, the volume's argument is that a document is not a scene, and the close has to hold both of those at once without letting either one off — and it can, because the two are not in tension. The volume's argument is that a document is a place where a refusal goes to be converted into a population, and the last ten chapters are that conversion happening in four rooms and a bench's minute while six scenes hold the volume's other half, and the block's own count proves it: five document chapters at a mean of 76.2 `about` a chapter and five scene chapters at a mean of 38.6, and every one of the second five at or under the house ceiling of forty-five. The failure mode was named in advance and the volume beat it, and the price was one chapter — Chapter 242, which had a man in a room with a decision in it and spent the decision on a table out of a press — and the price is recorded and not repaired.**

665. **THE VOLUME 05 CLOSE'S REVIEW REPAIR PASS, ITS SIX FINDINGS, AND THE ONE THAT WAS RULED OUT.** A review of the close phase returned six defects. **Five were applied and one was ruled out of order, and the ruling is the item a later reader needs, because acting on it would have corrupted arithmetic that was right.** The five applied: **(1)** `outline/volume-06.md` asserted the year turn at day 156 and then printed YR 315 on the far side of it in the header, all five block headers, §15 item 19 and §16 item 5, and the batch prompt contradicted the outline, so a writer reading the outline and a writer reading the prompt would have printed different years out of one binding document; every date from day 156 onward is now YR 316 and no day number, month or weekday moved. **(2)** Four of five block frames were off by one, reading forty-one and forty-two and seventy-seven and seventy-eight where the true figures are forty and forty-one and seventy-six and seventy-seven; the totals were right and the per-block phrasing was not, and it is now footed. **(3)** An eleven-token bold span on `outline/volume-06.md` line 187 had a marker inside the sentence and an orphan at the end, and `state/current.md` line 17 ended on an orphan, so two files of the phase failed the parity sweep the phase itself mandates. **(4)** `outline/volume-06.md` called Mudmonth unfixed in §15 item 18, in §17's prose and in a table row while printing three rows that fix it at thirty. **(5)** Two soft attributions: the Block 4 card merged Alish Renn's want with Sarn Oyelaran's unsigned warrant into one woman, and §13's Batch 0004 row called Perry Hask the first person in the book to be handed the document that joins two things by accident while §5.2 and §8 Block 1 place that accident in Block 1 as a filing nobody made and nobody was handed. **The one ruled out was the review's finding that `outline/volumes/volume-05-close.md` §2.8 miscounts the age of a page: it holds that the fourteenth of Harvestmonth to the eighth of Embermonth is fifty-four days elapsed and fifty-five counting both ends, and the review said fifty-three and fifty-four. On the carried thirty-day month and the month order in `bible/terminology.md` — Thawmonth, Mudmonth, Greenmonth, Longlight, Rainmonth, Harvestmonth, Fallowmonth, Embermonth, Wolfmonth, Frostmonth, Hearthmonth, Goatmonth — the elapsed count is sixteen days to the end of Harvestmonth, one into Fallowmonth, thirty through Fallowmonth, one into Embermonth and seven more, which is fifty-four, and the close is right and the review was out by one. The review's own corroboration, that day 13 is Embermonth 8, is true and does not bear on the other date. Nothing in this block's repair changed §2.8, and the fifty-four propagated into item 647, the chapter-summaries note and the batch prompt is the correct figure.**

666. **WHAT THE REPAIR PASS DID NOT TOUCH, AND THE STANDING IT LEAVES.** It wrote no chapter prose and no scene and it made no line-level correction to any of the two hundred and fifty chapters, which are closed prose. **It changed no day number, no month, no weekday, no market-day count, no block boundary and no volume total; the manuscript stands at 926,261 words in two hundred and fifty chapters and every one of those five batch figures is unchanged.** It created no prompt and wrote no phase artifact, because the close phase had already written its one prompt at `workspace/volume-06/batch-0001/PROMPT.md` and the phase system requires exactly one per phase and this was a repair and not a phase. **And it did not settle the year question, which is still the one open label on the chain: `outline/volume-05.md` §17's day 0 is the twenty-fifth of Fallowmonth, YR 314, all fifty chapters of Volume 05 call that day YR 315, and Volume 06 follows the prose. A phase that settles it moves the two audited chains together, restates the last date of each volume, and says that it has done so, and nothing in this repair may be read as having settled it.**

667. **THE VOLUME 06 BLOCK FRAMES, RE-COUNTED, AS A FIGURE A LATER BATCH MAY INHERIT WITHOUT RE-DERIVING THEM.** Main world, five blocks, on the carried thirty-day month and a cycle of seven from day 150 a Thursday. **Block 1, days 150\u2013190, Goatmonth 25 YR 315 to Mudmonth 5 YR 316, Thursday to Tuesday, forty days elapsed and forty-one inclusive, twelve market days. Block 2, days 191\u2013231, Mudmonth 6 to Greenmonth 16, Friday to Monday, forty and forty-one, twelve market days. Block 3, days 232\u2013272, Greenmonth 17 to Longlight 27, Tuesday to Sunday, forty and forty-one, twelve market days, and the first of Longlight is day 246. Block 4, days 273\u2013313, Longlight 28 to Harvestmonth 8, Monday to Saturday, forty and forty-one, twelve market days, and the ninth of Rainmonth at day 284 is a Friday, is not a market day, and is the day the old hearing was entered for. Block 5, days 314\u2013390, Harvestmonth 9 to Embermonth 25, Sunday to Saturday, seventy-six and seventy-seven, twenty-two market days, and the volume's last day.** The four forty-ones and the seventy-seven foot at the two hundred and forty-one and the twelve four and twenty-two foot at seventy. **Thirty-five Saturdays, the first at day 152 and the last at day 390, and the volume's last chapter is a bench sitting on the last of them in a market morning.** The year turns at day 156, so days 150 to 155 are YR 315 and days 156 to 390 are YR 316, and the first of Mudmonth is day 186, the first of Greenmonth is day 216, the first of Longlight is day 246, the first of Rainmonth is day 276, the first of Harvestmonth is day 306, the first of Fallowmonth is day 336 and the first of Embermonth is day 366.

distinct, 27 distinct duplicated texts and 28 extra copies, and 0 of the new block's paragraphs are byte-identical to any of them; the month and weekday sweep returns twelve distinct tokens and no real-world month token anywhere; and the weekday check against `outline/volume-06.md` §17 counted from day 150 and not off the chapters returns all ten correct with all ten market flags right.**

669. **THE FRAME AS PRINTED, AND EVERY WEEKDAY CHECKED FROM DAY 150.** **Day 150, the twenty-fifth of Goatmonth, YR 315, a Thursday and a market day, to day 190, the fifth of Mudmonth, YR 316, a Tuesday and not a market day. Forty days and forty-one inclusive. The year turns at day 156 and every printed date from day 157 onward is YR 316.** The ten chapters and their days: 251 = 150, Thursday, market · 252 = 151, Friday, not a market day · 253 = 152, Saturday, market · 254 = 157, the second of Thawmonth, Thursday, market · 255 = 163, the eighth of Thawmonth, Wednesday, not a market day · 256 = 164, the ninth of Thawmonth, Thursday, market · 257 = 165, the tenth of Thawmonth, Friday, not a market day · 258 = 166, the eleventh of Thawmonth, Saturday, market · 259 = 169, the fourteenth of Thawmonth, Tuesday, not a market day · 260 = 190, the fifth of Mudmonth, Tuesday, not a market day. **All ten weekdays and all ten market flags were checked by counting forward from day 150 on a cycle of seven and against the thirty-day month and not by reading the chapters, and all ten are correct.** **The twelve market days the block carries are 150, 152, 157, 159, 164, 166, 171, 173, 178, 180, 185 and 187, and five of the twelve are printed on a dateline. The six Saturdays are 152, 159, 166, 173, 180 and 187, and two of them carry a chapter. There is no bench scene in the block, and the reason is not the one the phase prompt gave: the block carries six Saturdays and five market Saturdays, so a Saturday sitting was available, and the bench sits on Saturdays and on nothing else, no card wanted one, the volume's sitting is the last Saturday of the volume at day 390, the bench is asked nothing in this block, and the count on the page under that stair stays at eight. Mudmonth is carried at thirty days and the only Mudmonth date in the block is Chapter 260's fifth, counted from the row Mudmonth 1 = day 186, and no block boundary falls inside Mudmonth.**

670. **A BODY CORPORATE WITH A DOOR AND A NUMBER HAS BEEN SERVED, AND THE SERVICE CAME TO EIGHT PENCE, AND IT CAME TO A DOOR FORTY FEET FROM A HOUSE NOBODY KNOCKED ON.** **The Bellweather Claims Archive is named in a proceeding and served at its door on the twenty-fifth of Goatmonth, YR 315, and the service sheet is a sheet of the office's own printed series with the five heads and the form of oath printed on the back of it, so a person who swears in that proceeding is sworn on the back of a return.** The deed is thirteen words and names no officer, and **there is a line on the service sheet for the person served and a line for the office and both are ruled for a figure and neither is ruled for a name, and a keeper of records of twenty-nine entered the day, the hour and the door on the fair copy and did not enter a name and did not write *no person* either.** In four years and a half nobody had come up that lane with a paper in a hand, because a county of about four thousand people cannot be served with anything and has no writ and no seal and no office. **The not-askings stand at nine and this block entered no tenth. The breach is open. Nobody walks a road with anybody in this block. The nine words said in a wagon arch in Chapter 260 are not an apology, not a not-asking, and not a tenth.**

671. **THE COMPANION FILE HAS BEEN JOINED TO SOMETHING, AND THE JOIN IS A FILING AND NOT A HAND-OVER.** **On the twenty-sixth of Goatmonth, YR 315, at about the second hour and a half, a woman of about twenty-nine who is a clerk of the returns wrote a proceeding on the back of a form of the office's printed series, because the back of a form is where the form of oath is printed, and nobody in that room said what was on the sheet she was writing on.** Then at about the third hour a man of about sixty with a tray put the new file into the pigeonhole on the second shelf that already holds the standing hearing for the ninth of Rainmonth and the file of one sheet with a district on it that was opened beside that hearing on the fourth of Goatmonth, YR 315, **because the returns shelf is four inches deep and the second shelf was full and his hands were full, and the join took about four seconds.** The chain now stands: **a hearing entered for a delegation that cannot arrive, a file of one sheet with a district on it, and a proceeding against a body corporate in a county that is one of about nine market towns of that district.** **Nobody made the join, nobody was told about it, nobody has asked after it, and nobody in that building is going to.** The hearing is not adjourned, not refused, not retold and not closed, no delegation was put in the room, and the companion file was not removed, not corrected and not asked after. **No Volume 06 batch may merge the two hearings that sit on the ninth of Rainmonth into one hearing.** And **the woman of about thirty-three at the register is in none of the three papers and her name is not going to be in any of them.**

672. **THE TENTH LETTER WAS OPENED AND ENTERED, THE ELEVENTH DOES NOT EXIST, AND WHAT A CLERK DID WITH A DOCUMENT THAT ARRIVED WITHOUT A SENDER.** **On the twenty-seventh of Goatmonth, YR 315, at about the third hour, a second copyist of about thirty opened the tenth letter on the second shelf of the Bellweather Claims Archive, which had been there about two years, and it carried no sender.** Inside is one question of nine lines from a market town in the district: nine forms of the office's printed series went out, one came back, and the eight that did not come back have no register and no column in that office. The second half is one sentence: *And if there is a place on the sheet for the name of a person, will you tell me whether I am to write my own in it, or leave it, because I have left it, and I have left it nine times.* **A keeper of records of twenty-nine read that sentence over the copyist's shoulder, read it twice, and said nothing in the nine minutes she had, and did not answer the letter.** The copyist **entered it**, under a head of her own invention, *Received without a sender*, four words, in a fair hand a quarter of an inch smaller than the keeper's, with four items under it: the day, the hour, the town and the absence. **A thing entered in a day-book has a day against it, and a letter from a stranger entered under a head a copyist made up herself is a finding about a market town, and that office has never entered a finding in four years and a half.** The copyist's second thing in six years, in eleven words: *It was never going to be the eleventh that did it.* **The eleventh does not exist and the volume does not schedule one.** The letter went out on the ordinary post in about three weeks, **because a question is a thing that goes out and a finding is a thing that is produced, and there is no column in that office for a person who would rather not have answered it.** Alish Renn is not named in this block and a reader who has her from Volume 03 has to work out that the second copyist of about thirty is her.

673. **A CROWN OFFICER OF THIRTY-EIGHT HAS CONVENED A ROOM AND SAID WHAT SHE WANTS ONCE, IN NINETEEN SENTENCES, AND IT WAS ENTERED.** **Hester Cray, 38, of the Crown, convened a chamber on the second of Thawmonth, YR 316, at about the second hour and a half, and put her own name in the office line of a witness list of eight ruled lines for the first time on that sheet, and said her want once and nobody in that room improved on it and one of the two people in it wrote it down.** The want, in nineteen sentences and footed at nineteen: that a thing heard has to be entered, that an entry with a day on it in a proceeding with a date against it is a finding, that a finding is the only kind of paper in this kingdom that can be produced in a court four hundred miles off, that a question cannot be produced and she has had one refused by a clerk in four words and has carried the refusal for eleven months, that she has been in nine of these in nine years and every one of the nine is a figure and not one of the nine is a room, that she has never been in a room that could do it, and that she does not know whether it is possible. **She asked for the asking to be entered. The clerk entered it and read it back once and not twice. She said *That is right* and did not ask for it to be taken out.** A want with a day against it and a person against it is the thing she has just spent nineteen sentences saying cannot exist, **and nobody in that room said so and the clerk read it back once rather than twice and neither of those is an accident.** The chamber is a table of three, two chairs and a clerk's stool, a list of eight lines with four names against them and four lines empty, **and the oath is printed on the back of a return.** **She has a name on a page in this volume and that is new, and she does not get what she wants in this volume, and the volume's argument against her is that a room with a form in it is a column with a roof on it and the roof is what makes people go home believing they were heard.** The line for the body corporate is empty and she did not fill it in and did not write *no person* on it either, **and a woman of twenty-nine in a county two hundred miles off did the same thing to a different line on a different sheet on the twenty-fifth of a month, and the two of them are two hundred miles apart and neither has been told the other exists, and nothing has happened between them.**

674. **THE FIRST NAMED MEMBER OF THE CULLING ORDER IS ON A PAGE, AND HE IS A MAN OF FORTY-FOUR DOING THE OFFICE'S WORK, AND HE SAID THREE THINGS AND ALL THREE WERE ABOUT A COLUMN.** **Ansel Rudd, 44, a member of the Culling Order and a classifier, read a schedule of about two hundred classifications into a record in a chamber on the third floor at the second hour of the eighth of Thawmonth, YR 316, day 163, and the phrase is in the head of the record and was said out loud once, at the fourth hour, to a clerk about a tray, and not as a threat.** He is early, which is a thing about being afraid of a column and not of a person. He read about two hundred lines aloud for two hours and ten minutes, the object column first, **and about nine of the two hundred lines have the word *eastern* in front of the place name and the type for it has now been struck.** **He said three things and all three were about a column**: that the object column is the only one of the six a person can fill in alone and he is not going to write in it twice in a day; that the fifth head has been the same head for two years and a man who changes a head in his own hand has made a decision and he has not made one; and that the sixth has no head and so is not a column and anything put in it is a thing the building decided not to keep. **Nobody argued with him and nobody agreed with him.** His want, once, to a clerk who was about to leave, **in thirty-four words and footed at thirty-four**: *A classification that is late is a classification that can be argued with, and I have argued with nine of them in a year and I would rather be late than argue with ten.* **Nobody in that room asked him what is in the four places on the form and nobody noticed that nobody had, and about four people in that building noticed it afterwards, on the ninth and tenth of Thawmonth, YR 316, late and separately, in four rooms, about four hours apart, and did not know the other three had noticed.** He is not a speech, he does not explain himself, he does not confess, he does not lose an argument, and nobody in this volume says what the Order is for. **The debt is discharged and the discharge is a person on a page and the person is not a speech, and no later phase may treat its appearance here as spent a second time.**

675. **THE TYPE FOR *eastern* HAS BEEN STRUCK, ONCE, BY A PRINTER'S MATE OF NINETEEN, AND THE WORD IS NOW ON A SHEET IN AN OBJECT COLUMN.** **On the ninth of Thawmonth, YR 316, at about the sixth hour, a woman of about twenty-nine who is a clerk of the returns said *I want a word before the place and not a rule for the sixth*, in fourteen words and footed at fourteen, and a man of about fifty, clerk of the press, thirty-one years in that room and about eleven thousand forms entered, said *set it*, and a printer's mate of nineteen set it in about four minutes with a quad on either side.** The word had been in the fourth drawer down in a case against the north wall of a press room since the week the form was made, about two years ago, set in the line with the heads of the five columns, and the drawer does not lock and nine people in that building have known for two years that it is not to be used. **The mate asked whether it was a real word and was told that it is a word and that that is not the same as a word anybody uses, and he set it anyway and did not understand it and is not going to.** His own want is **eleven weeks and five days to the next sitting, in fourteen words to a man in a doorway, footed at fourteen, and the man said nothing and went down two flights.** He pulled the sheet at about the seventh hour, it came off wet at the fourth corner, he carried it up two floors on a board, **and he was not in that room when the room was told what it had done.** Four people looked at it for about nine seconds and one of them said *It has the word on it.* **The word is not defined in this block and is not defined in this volume, and there is no column in that office for the difference between a word that is used and a word that is set.**

676. **TWO OFFERS WERE MADE IN ONE WEEK, IN TWO ROOMS, BY TWO PEOPLE, AND BOTH OF THEM ARE REAL AND BOTH OF THEM ARE CORRECT, AND NOBODY IN THE VOLUME SAYS SO.** **First, on the eleventh of Thawmonth, YR 316, at about the third hour, in a room with no window on the ground floor at the end of the passage with the stove, a man of about forty offered a reduction of a sentence in exchange for evidence in the proceeding, and the sheet carries two prices of the same fine, a mark and a half and one mark, given in words and not in figures.** His one sentence about an offer, **twenty-four words and footed at twenty-four**: *A person who gives evidence in the proceeding is not sentenced for the matter the evidence is about. That is the whole of it.* His second thing, **twenty-four words and footed at twenty-four**: *If you do not take it the matter stands, and a matter that stands is a thing I carry, and I am carrying four.* He is carrying four matters in about nine years. **Aren said he would give evidence before he was asked. That is not the offer. The offer is the reduction**, ten words and ten. **He declined the reduction and offered his evidence anyway, and the man of about forty entered four lines in a book of which the fourth is not on any form in that office: *Witness attended. Offered reduction of sentence. Declined. Evidence offered before the asking.*** Second, **on the fourteenth of Thawmonth, YR 316, at about the second hour, in a room with no window on the third floor, the marshal offered access to sealed personal records, which is eleven drawers in four buildings and about nine hundred sheets, of which the marshal has read the eleven lines and not the eight hundred, on terms that are a condition and not a price: evidence in a proceeding he does not sit in, before a person who does not want him there, on a day he has not been told.** **He did not say yes and he did not say no, and that is the whole of the hour and a half, and the marshal said *That is the correct way to be in a room*, in ten words and ten, and the room then went on for about eleven minutes without anybody saying anything.** **The two offers are inside one week measured Saturday to Friday and nobody in the volume says the first one is correct procedure and it is, and nobody says the second one is a trade and it is.**

677. **THE SEALED RECORD'S LIST IS ON THE PAGE, AND IT HAS ELEVEN HANDS AND ELEVEN ROADS IN TWO PARTS AND NO COLUMN FOR WHAT BECAME OF ANYBODY, AND IT IS THE SAME LENGTH AS ELEVEN LINES IN HIS OWN NOTEBOOK, AND NEITHER PAGE KNOWS ABOUT THE OTHER ONE.** **In the marshal's room on the fourteenth of Thawmonth, YR 316, a sheet was taken out of a drawer and put on a table and did not leave the room.** It is a list of about eleven lines ruled in two columns in two parts, **a hand and a road, eleven of each, the same size and the same shape and not the same thing, the eleventh line with two marks on it, and about a year between the first of them going out and the eleventh coming back.** It concerns **a woman who went out of a valley in the year the Sundering happened with a boy of about one-and-twenty, and there is no name in it and there is a mark, and the two marks on the eleventh line are the only marks on the sheet.** The marshal said *You have a mother* in the plain way and did not raise his voice and did not stand up, **and he was never surprised and is never going to be, and he has had a copy of the list in a drawer in that building for about nine years and had never had a reason to open it until the man sat down.** Aren read the eleven lines in about a minute and a half and read them again and **said nothing**. **There is no third column and no column for what became of anybody, and the volume has not said why, and the reason is four hundred years old and belongs to Block 3 and is not spent here.** **A man of thirty-two with a limp wrote eleven lines with no words in them in a notebook in a city four hundred miles off in Chapter 227 and the two pages are the same length and neither of them knows about the other one, and the comparison of the two is Block 3's work and not this block's, and the line he has not finished is his.** **The unattributed two-line statement in this block is one and is at `259:55–56`, is in italics, has no number in either line, names no path, the roadmark, the light or the mechanism, and was written down by nobody, and he has had four of those in four years and has written one and that one has no hour against it and no name in it.**

678. **WHO KEEPS THE BELL, AND THE NO-ANSWER IS THE FINDING.** **On the fifth of Mudmonth, YR 316, at about the fourth hour and a half, the bell went at the Old Toll four hundred yards up the fen county's own road: nine stone of green-black bronze, a band of forty-one rivets, a dull red seam split lip to shoulder, rung by a boy who has been the steward's apprentice for two years and three months and is not good at it, and by a carpenter who is a hand and not a keeper, neither paid by the guild and neither a member of anything.** A man of thirty-two with a limp asked four people who keeps it, **at about the seventh hour, on the reach, after the bell had gone**: the mason of fifty and a half said the boy rings it and the carpenter rings it and that is the answer; a man of about twenty-six setting a course said that is the steward business and that he does not know; a carter of thirty said it has always been that pair and that he was not here before them; **and a man of forty-seven said the same four things he had said four times in a year, and none of the four was about the bell.** **Nobody in that county can answer, and that is the finding and not a gap: a bell rung by two people who are neither paid for it nor members of it is a bell nobody in that county can be asked about, and that is why it is rung.** **The bell is not explained, no device is named, no origin, maker or deathbed is scheduled, and the bell does not stop: it went on the Wednesday and it goes on, and Chapter 900 depends on it.** The tile on a coping is not mentioned once in Chapters 251 to 260.

679. **THE SIXTH LOOK AT THE SEVENTH LINE IS IN BLOCK 1 AND NOT IN BLOCK 5, AND `outline/volume-06.md` §4 STILL SAYS BLOCK 5.** **The separate leaf in the coat has a seventh line on it that says a person and has said it since a lane four hundred miles off, and it had been looked at five times in five months at the close of Chapter 250, and in Chapter 260, at about the fifth hour of the fifth of Mudmonth, YR 316, it was looked at for the sixth time and not finished, and the leaf went back flat with the first leaf turned to the first page.** `outline/volume-06.md` §4's last paragraph says the seventh line *has a sixth look at it in Block 5 and is not finished*, and the phase prompt for this batch places that look in the block's turn. **The prompt wins for Block 1 and the page now carries the sixth look. The consequence for the next batch is live and is the whole of this item: a Batch 0002 or later writer reading §4 will expect a look in Block 5 and must not write a seventh one, and if a look is wanted in Block 5 then §4's row needs correcting and the correction has to be recorded, because the plan and the page now disagree about a figure the reader can count.** **The four words he has had ready since the sixth day of a count of days he does not have are still ready in Chapters 258, 259 and 260 and are not said, and nobody in this block knows he has them, and the ninth words in Chapter 260 are a different nine words and are said to nobody in a wagon arch forty feet from a shut door and are not told to the reader.**

680. **THE MONEY, AND THE TWO PRICES OF THE SAME THING, IN THREE COLUMNS THAT ARE NOT ADDED TO ONE ANOTHER.** **Chapter 251, at a sill in a lane: a sheet a penny, a second sheet a penny, a carrier's hand for four miles twopence, a waggon kept an hour fourpence, footed to eight pence in front of the second copyist. Chapter 254, read out in a chamber: a sheet a penny, a sheet for the list a penny, a clerk's fee for entering a proceeding fourpence, a light kept burning in a room with no window for one day twopence, a carrier's hand for four miles twopence, footed to ten pence. Chapter 258, in a room with no window: a sheet a penny, a second sheet a penny, a clerk's fee for entering a witness fourpence, a witness's day eightpence, footed to fourteen pence, a shilling and twopence.** **The office is fourpence a year and the two rooms over the weigh-house are two shillings a month each and they are the salt merchant's and not the office's, and the two prices of the same two rooms are named and refused as a column in Chapter 251 and again in Chapter 260 and are never added to one another in either.** **Chapter 258's two prices of one fine are the hardest case in the block and the page says so: a mark and a half and one mark, in words, not added, not reconciled, and there is no column in that building for two prices of one thing.** **The bench's eight things asked in nineteen years is a count of askings and is added to nothing and does not appear in this block as an arithmetic term. About two hundred times a season in a *Keeper* column is a count of askings and is added to nothing and Chapter 257 says so in the sentence that gives it.**

681. **THE NAME BUDGET, AND THE ARITHMETIC, AND THE TWO NAMES.** **Two spent of six, four unfilled, against a volume plan of four of thirty across five batches: 2 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 4 and 4 + 4 + 6 + 6 + 5 + 5 = 30, which foots exactly at the cap.** **The two are Ansel Rudd, 44, in Chapter 255, and Hester Cray, 38, in Chapter 254. The marshal is a return, is named on the page in Volume 01 and Volume 02, and does not count; his name is written nowhere in Chapters 251 to 260 and in no state file this batch wrote, and the phase that eventually writes it checks thread 89 and the separate-sheet rule first.** No third face was spent and no slot was borrowed. **A sweep of the ten files for capitalised two-word sequences returns only Weir Street, Culling Order, Ansel Rudd and Hester Cray**, of which the first is a street and the second is the standing debt.

682. **THE TWENTY-SEVEN DUPLICATED PARAGRAPH TEXTS IN VOLUMES 01 TO 05, MEASURED ON A NAMED BASIS, AND NONE OF THEM IS IN THIS BLOCK.** **A duplicate-paragraph sweep across all two hundred and fifty chapter files on the basis blank-line-separated paragraphs of twelve words or more, excluding `---` and excluding the title line, returns 11,676 paragraphs and 11,648 distinct texts, and 27 distinct texts appear more than once, accounting for 28 extra copies.** **Nineteen of the twenty-seven are entirely italic, that is to say a quoted form or a quoted line standing whole as a paragraph, and they are a deliberate house habit of printing a document as its own paragraph, and the same paragraph recurring in two chapters of Volumes 01 and 02 is the same document being quoted twice in a volume that quotes its own paperwork.** Eight are plain prose, and they are: the bell report of the seventh of Greenmonth, filed as reported, with an hour, a direction and a tower sight-line; the seven-village figure line, *Alder Cross, two hundred. Saltbrim, ninety*, and so on; *Nobody in the gateway said anything, which is how a yard works*; the bell's description with the band of forty-one rivets and the dull red seam; a Monday arrangement on the Old Toll; *He put his hand flat on the book and left it there*; *The two are not added. There is no way on this earth to add them*; and **the paragraph the Volume 05 close found, the clerk who read that back and entered it and read it again, at `203:33` and `245:41`.** **The last of the eight is the house practice of reading a thing back twice and finding the second reading slower and not better, and it is the fifth whole-paragraph instance in the manuscript and a Volume 06 batch may not deliver it again, and this batch's `slower and not better` count is 0 on all ten files and a first draft of Chapter 254 held two instances and both were cut.** **None of the twenty-seven involves a Volume 06 chapter and 0 of the new block's 283 paragraphs are byte-identical to any paragraph of Volumes 01 to 05.** The twenty-seven are a finding for the Volume 06 close and not for this batch, and no chapter in Volumes 01 to 05 was touched.

683. **SIX FINDINGS ON THE PAGE THAT NO STATE FILE RECORDED, THREE OF THEM NEW TO THIS PROJECT, FOUND BY COUNTING AND BY READING, AND NONE OF THEM A CANON CHANGE.** One, **Chapter 244 says the man of about fifty's sentence about a district is about eleven words and the sentence is seventeen**: *A district is a set of market towns and I do not know what a district is*. **This is the sixth instance in the manuscript of the speech-length defect and the first one the Volume 05 close did not itemise, and this block records it in Chapter 252 and does not repeat the figure and does not repair Chapter 244.** Two, **the block's own `about` density is 20.1 per 1,000 words against Volume 05 Batch 0005's 18.8, and the block's shape is the finding: the four office chapters run 67, 71, 49 and 70 and the five room chapters run 48, 23, 52, 38 and 45, and Chapter 254's 23 is the lowest figure in two hundred and sixty chapters and it is the chapter that is a person saying nineteen sentences in a room.** Three, **the `wrote` figure is 26 against a baseline of 17 and twelve of the twenty-six are in Chapter 252, and the chapter is a filing chapter and the word is the trade there, and the figure is a finding about this block and not a defect.** Four, **`a man of sixty-one with a satchel` and `a lamp` are on `outline/volume-06.md` §15 item 1's barred-token list and the man of sixty-one with a satchel is Halven and is a main-world return, and this block refers to him as a man with a satchel and refers to the two room lamps as candles in tin holders, so that `fifty-two`, `sixty-six`, `sixty-one` and `lamp` are all at zero on the page; a later Volume 06 writer should know that the list is a token list and that two of its tokens are main-world figures the list was written about rather than for.** Five, **the house practice of reading a thing back twice and finding the second reading slower and not better is now a whole-paragraph repeat in the manuscript at `203:33` and `245:41` and this block came within two of adding a sixth, and the two are cut and the count is 0.** Six, **`have said since that` and `have said since` return the same figure for the first time in this project, 68 on both, and that is because no instance of the loose form was written without the exact one, and it is the smallest possible finding and it is recorded because the Volume 05 close recorded the two figures disagreeing and a reader of that item will want to know that they agree here.**

684. **WHAT THIS BLOCK DID NOT DO, AND WHAT IT NOTICED AND DID NOT DO, IN ONE LINE EACH.** The city is not on the page in any form and nothing was sent to it. The five refusal figures are not reconciled and none is added to a figure of persons. About four hundred doors is never added to about four hundred doors and no character said which county the older list is in. The four prints are not turned into a product. The bench's eight things asked is not a price and is added to nothing. The number of persons the office would not print is not printed and is not reconciled with the figure on a return. The marginal instruction is referred to as nine words in a smaller type and is not explained by anybody. The word *eastern* is not defined. The tile on a coping is not mentioned. The child is not named and is not in the block. The house practice of reading a thing back twice and finding the second reading slower and not better is not delivered. The seam in the fourth bay is not measured, ruled across or pointed at, and there is no second seam. The mechanism is not explained and no System panel is an explanation. The word *failed* is at zero and no drift figure is printed. No crossing is made and no door opens for him. The two crossings four hundred yards apart are not in one book and Chapter 260 does not go to the crossing. No apology in any form and the not-askings stand at nine and no tenth was entered. The word *brother* is not used in a room the two of them are in and the yard is off the page as a place. The name of the antagonist is not written. The hearing is not adjourned, not refused, not retold and not closed, and the two hearings are not merged. Nobody joins the four rooms in one sentence. **Noticed and not done: Alish Renn is not named although the tenth letter is hers; the clerk of the returns and the man of about fifty are given no names although both are established at length; Chapter 244's wrong speech-length figure is recorded and not repaired; the bell's provenance and its tile are not scheduled; the volume's argument in one sentence, a hearing is a column with a roof on it, is not said in this block and belongs to Nev Treen in an aisle in Block 3; and the eleventh letter does not exist and is not scheduled.**

685. **THE VOLUME 06 BATCH 0001 REVIEW REPAIR PASS, ITS FORTY-ONE APPLIED FINDINGS, ITS SEVENTEEN RULED, AND THE FIGURES RE-COUNTED AFTER THE PASS. THE FIGURES IN THIS ITEM ARE THE FIGURES OF THE PAGE AFTER THE FIRST PASS AND BEFORE THE SECOND, AND ITEM 689 SUPERSEDES EVERY ONE OF THEM.** **A review of Chapters 251 to 260 returned fifty-eight findings across seven categories and every category was checked by hand.
