696. **THE FORGED *Keeper* ENTRY, WHAT IT IS BUILT FROM, WHO BUILT IT, AND WHY THE PERSON IT WAS ABOUT DOES NOT FIND OUT IN THIS BLOCK.** **The record is a form of the office's own printed series, six columns and five heads, the fourth headed *Keeper*, and the classification it supports is a ford on a made road in a county two hundred miles off, entered in the object column because the object column is the only one that can be filled in without a person being in the room.** **The three real things are the form, a hand, and a date. The hand is the loop at the top of the fourth column on about four hundred forms a month for eleven years, filled in the same way by the same person in the same half-minute, and the hand is nine shapes. The date is somebody else's: it is taken off a tray of about eleven dates in about nine years in that building rather than copied from anything, and a man who takes a day off a tray of eleven has taken a date somebody else wrote and cannot afterwards say who put a given day where.** **The name that goes in is the name of the woman of thirty-three who fills that column, and the classification therefore says the keeper of a road in a county two hundred miles off is a woman at a register in this one who is not a keeper of anything and is not a member of anything.** **The man who assembles it is the man of about fifty, clerk of the press, thirty-one years in that room, about eleven thousand forms entered. He did it in about nine minutes in the ordinary way, and about four people in that building have said since that the villainy of this is thirty-one years of pressing type and that no man in that room did anything he had not done four hundred times before, and nobody in that building has ever asked him what is in the four places and he has never asked.** **He said one true thing about a column in that press room on that market Saturday and it was eleven words, footed at eleven, and he said it to a boy of nineteen and was not thanked: *A head on a column is what a court can use.* The boy asked about reality and the man answered about use and neither of them has ever said so to the other one. A true thing said to a boy of nineteen is not entered anywhere and is not going to be, and in Block 5 the same man is thanked and the thanks is worse. She does not find out in this block, nobody in that building is going to be the one to tell her, her note of nineteen words is face down on the second shelf of a case behind her and has been since the sixth of a month in a year before last, nobody turns it over, she is not thanked, not converted, not told she was right, not made the person who explains anything, and her want is not restated. She finds out in Block 4, from a piece of paper somebody else has carried in, and what she does about it is her own and is not a speech.**

697. **THE FOUR LINES AT THE HEAD OF THE FIRST SPREAD, AND WHAT READING THEM A SECOND TIME IN A DIFFERENT ROOM DID AND DID NOT COST.** **The four lines are printed word for word at `chapters/volume-06/chapter-0266.md:39`, `:41`, `:43` and `:45`, and they are byte-identical to the four at `chapters/volume-04/chapter-0173.md`, and the repeat is correct and is left standing: they are one document printed twice, and the second printing is a reading in the room over a cross that the four lines were written to be read in.** **This raises the manuscript's repeated-paragraph texts from 27 and 28 extra copies at Batch 0001 to 31 and 32 on 12,201 paragraphs, and the four new instances are entirely italic, which is the class Batch 0001 identified at continuity item 682 as a deliberate house habit of printing a document as its own paragraph. A Volume 06 writer may not alter a word of the four lines and may not re-derive them in Blocks 3, 4 or 5 and may not print them a third time.** **`outline/volume-06.md` §8 Block 2 and §10 both say the four lines are read out for the first time in a hundred and forty years in this block. `chapters/volume-04/chapter-0173.md:25` prints all four of them, read out in a room over a byre to a stranger by the man of fifty-eight, who had said three days before that he would not read them. The block's reading is that the first time is in that room over the cross, and Chapter 266 says *in that room on that evening*, and the reading was done to about thirty people, nine of them on benches and about two hundred of the ninth generation at the back, and it was slowed down for a man who was not on the bench with the hundred and forty on the end of it.** **And the aisle carries an unreconciled tension that this block prints and does not resolve. §3.9 and §5.3 say the aisle is four feet wide and has gone three generations without being used; `186:5` and `187:23` have a woman of the eighth generation asked what she swore forty years ago in that aisle and a man of fifty-five stand in it thirty-five years ago, and a generation is about fifteen and a half years in that valley. Chapter 266 prints the outline's sentence and prints the hundred and forty as a count of askings and says in the house clause that the two figures are about the same aisle and that nobody in the room has ever put them side by side and that the man of fifty-eight could do it in about a second and has not. THE FINDING IS RECORDED FOR THE VOLUME 06 CLOSE AND IS NOT REPAIRED HERE, because these are new chapters and closed prose in Volume 04 is not this phase's to tidy.**

698. **THE A FINDING IN THE WINTER BOOK, THE OATH, THE AISLE, AND WHAT THE GIFT COST.** **In `chapter-0267.md` a man of fifty-eight stands in an aisle four feet wide at fifty-eight years of age and is asked what he swore by a man of thirty-four with sixteen men and no work, who says *I am going to ask you what you swore and you are going to answer and I am not going to ask you anything else*. The answer is in the first spread in his own hand and is eighteen words, footed at eighteen: *I swear to keep the book, the room, the day, the mark and the hand, and nothing else.* He entered it in his own book, in his own hand, at the head of the first spread under the four lines, because the four lines are a rule about keepers and a fact about a keeper goes under the rule about keepers, and he ruled a line to do it, and that is the first line ruled across in that book in a hundred and forty years and the first finding in that book in a hundred and forty years. He offered it about four minutes after he had been asked and nobody had asked him to offer. Nobody in that room asked him whether he could stand it afterwards; there were about thirty people in it and two of them were strangers, and one of the strangers could have asked and did not.** **The fourth line at the head of the first spread is *Where a man is named in a book of this valley it is because he did it himself and not because anybody asked him*, and it permits the entry because he did it himself, and the block says so in the sentence that gives the fourth line.** **The block keeps Chapter 267's finding from contradicting `193:63`'s three figures in a hundred and forty years and from contradicting `196:47`'s four words, which went into a minute in a clerk's hand and are named on the page as not being in that book and as never having been copied into it.** **He is asked once and not twice. A finding cannot be asked a second time, and the volume's own mechanic is that a room hears a thing once and a person can be asked twice, and the room had just used up the once. A man of fifty-eight has wanted this for six years and said the six years out loud for the first time on that evening and nobody asked him anything about it.**

699. **THE SEVENTH COLUMN, AND THE SECOND NAME IN A COLUMN WITH A HEAD ON IT IN THIS BLOCK, AND THE FACT THAT NOBODY IN THE BOOK JOINS THE TWO.** **`chapters/volume-06/chapter-0270.md` puts a name in the seventh column of the county's own form, ruled in seven: *what is given. To whom, in the county's words. By whose hand. The day. The hour. A witness at this end. A witness at that end.* The seventh is a ruled space about two inches deep with nothing in it, its rule no more faded than the rule at the bottom of the third, in this office's use for four years and a half, and it has been filled with nothing on nine occasions. It gets the name of a man of fifty-eight four hundred miles off, entered by the second copyist of about thirty in about nine seconds, and he did not enter it. The keeper of records, who is twenty-nine, said one thing about it and it was fourteen words, footed at fourteen: *A name in a column of this office is a claim about a person*, and it was not a refusal and it was not an objection and it was about the office and not about the man, and it is the same sentence as `190:47`'s *a name in a column of this office is a claim about a person and this office has one of those already in a leaf in its press and it did not write it and it is not going to make another*, which is about a leaf in that press and not about the seventh column, and nobody in that room joined them.** **The third column says by whose hand and the hand is the second copyist, who has wanted a line in a book with her name in it since the summer before last, and about four people in that lane have said since that the difference between a hand and a person in a column is nineteen years old and is on a wall and has never once been read out loud in that room.** **So a name goes into a column with a head on it twice in this block: once at `263:24`, falsely, in the *Keeper* column of the office's own six-column series in a town two hundred miles off; and once at `270:63`, truly, in the seventh column of the county's own seven-column form in a room over a weigh-house. Two forms, two countries, two people, one false and one true, and no character in the book knows they are the same act and the reader can have it.** **And the block's cost, on the page and not explained: about four hundred people in a valley four hundred miles off went on that day as they go on every day of it, one of nine men on benches that are bolted to the floor in four rows is a man of fifty-eight who has entered one finding in a book that has had none in a hundred and forty years, he does not know that his name is in a column four hundred miles off, nobody in that valley is going to tell him, and a claim about a person is the only kind of paper in this kingdom that can be produced in a room a long way off, and there is no column in that office for what is done to a claim after it has been produced.**

700. **THE FOURTH REFUSAL IN A DOCUMENT IN FOUR VOLUMES, AND THE FIGURES ON IT.** **`chapters/volume-06/chapter-0268.md` and `chapter-0269.md` carry the fourth refusal. It is refused in writing for the third time; it is a fifth sheet of the kind of which four are in a press in a house on Weir Street that have not been sent for about two years and are not going to be; and it is the fourth refusal in a document in four volumes. THE TWO OF THOSE FIGURES ARE NOT THE SAME FIGURE AND THE PAGE SAYS SO AND NOBODY IN THAT COUNTY HAS EVER ADDED THEM. It is on the same office's own printed series, it names the crossing four hundred yards up that county's own road in the object column, and in front of the place name there is a word, printed once in the block, at `269:35`, and the word is in the same type as the heads of the five columns and was struck once about six weeks earlier by a printer's mate of nineteen who does what he is told. HE WROTE THE WORD IN BECAUSE IT IS THE WORD THAT GOES IN THAT COLUMN ON THAT SERIES AND HE DID NOT KNOW WHAT IT WAS, and there is no line on that sheet for a man to write down that he does not know what a column is for, and the word is defined zero times. The sheet goes out in the ordinary post in a bag, because a thing in a press in a yard cannot be served with anything and a thing in a bag in the ordinary post can, and a bag in the ordinary post is the first thing that has ever left that yard in the ordinary way. HE DID NOT PUT A HAND ON ANYTHING, in daylight, in front of about nine men, at the second hour of a wet morning while a man of about sixty was packing lime, and his left hand is warm at about the fourth hour every day and it was about the second hour and he did not put it on a sill, a gate, a bench-board, a stone, a wall, a door or a man. The page says that a man not putting a hand on a thing is not a thing anybody in a yard looks up for, and that about four of the nine men worked out what the hour was and about none of them worked out why the hour was not chosen. A yard on Weir Street is on the page in this volume for the first time since Volume 04 and it is nine men, a bench-board, a press that belongs to a yard and cannot be served with anything, and a man of about sixty packing lime who is not on the yard's book and is paid out of nothing, and the word *brother* is at zero on all ten files.**

704. **THE BATCH 0002 REVIEW REPAIR PASS, WHAT IT WAS ASKED TO DO AND WHAT IT WAS NOT ASKED TO DO, AND THE ORDER THOSE TWO THINGS ARE IN.** A review of the Volume 06 Batch 0002 writer phase returned seven findings and the last of them was a serious prose regression. **The repair pass was instructed to preserve good prose, not to restart the batch, and not to change the planned plot, and that instruction governed every decision below.** It edited Chapters 261 to 270, four state files and one prompt. **It wrote no new chapter and no new planned event, and it changed no day number, no month, no weekday, no market-day count, no block boundary, no name-budget figure, no money figure, no speech-length figure, no device position in the volume's plan, and the order of the ten chapters and their ten datelines. Every event the block planned is on the page in the order it was planned.**

705. **THE PROSE REGRESSION IN BATCH 0002, THE MEASUREMENT OF IT, THE BLOCK'S OWN VERDICT ON IT, AND THE REVERSAL OF THAT VERDICT.** Across Chapters 261 to 270 the narrator formula *about four people in that building have said since that* appeared **74 times in 23,184 words**, against **70 times in 25,990 words** in the larger and much more various Batch 0001, so the density rose by about a third while the block got shorter. Quoted dialogue across the ten chapters was **170 words**, a mean of 17 a chapter, against about 1,855 in Batch 0001. **Two chapters had no dialogue of any kind and no quotation mark of either style, Chapters 265 and 268, and two more had under ten words, Chapter 263 with twenty and Chapter 264 with nine.** The formula is a narrator move that asserts that a meaning exists; it cannot carry subtext, character thought or emotional consequence, and in Batch 0002 it had taken the place of all three. **Chapter 267 is the volume's emotional peak, a man of fifty-eight asked in an aisle what he swore, and it was delivered in thirty-three words of dialogue and a series of bolded assertions about what the room did not do.** Continuity item 693 recorded this density and called it *the block's own and is not a defect*. **That verdict was wrong and is reversed here. A volume about a form that is slow is not a defect. A volume in which a narrator formula has replaced the scenes is.**

706. **WHAT THE REPAIR DID TO THE PROSE, AND THE PRINCIPLE IT WORKED BY.** The formula was cut from **74 to 25** and *about four people* from **84 to 38**, and the recovered space was spent on what a room actually does. **The rule applied throughout was that an assertion of the form *somebody has said since that X* is replaced by the thing X is about, and the replacement must be observable, and if it is not observable then the sentence is kept and only shortened.** Concretely: the clerk's pen leaves a blot and his thumb smudges it into the ruled line and he leaves it, because a smudge in the margin of a schedule is a thing a clerk is not asked about. A boy of nineteen lets his hand come off a quoin. A man of fifty-eight rules a line with the straight edge off the back of a trestle because the book does not keep with the room, and the rule slips about a ninth of an inch twice and he does not rule a third and does not mention either. The man with a limp braces his left forearm along the top edge of a bench-board because a man cannot get at one at that height from a seat. A woman of about thirty with a pail says one sentence at a door and moves on before the knuckle has finished ringing in the frame. **Dialogue rose from 170 to 224 words, no chapter is now without dialogue, and the block grew by 1,326 words from 23,184 to 24,510. The added words are scene, not commentary.**

707. **THE SIX MALFORMED SECTION BREAKS, THE BELL STATED TWICE IN ONE CHAPTER, AND THE BELL STATED TWICE ACROSS TWO CHAPTERS.** A `---` rule immediately followed by a blank line and then another `---` rule leaves an empty section, and six of them were in this block: **`chapter-0262.md`, `chapter-0263.md` twice, `chapter-0265.md`, `chapter-0266.md` and `chapter-0267.md`.** All six are collapsed. The block's rule count falls from 61 to 55. **Chapter 0264 stated the bell's full specification, nine stone of green-black bronze, a band of forty-one rivets, a dull red seam split lip to shoulder, rung at the fourth hour and a half by a boy and a carpenter neither of them paid by the guild and neither of them a member of anything, at its ninth line and again in its last paragraph, with thirty-three shared distinct words between the two statements including every content word of the specification.** **Chapter 0268 stated it a third time.** The block is now one full statement, in Chapter 264's ninth line, and a reference in Chapter 268's, and **the specification appears exactly once in the block and the guild clause appears exactly once.** No plot moved: Block 2 still does not ring the bell, and the bell is still referred to as a standing fact of the county in both chapters.

708. **THE SWEEP THAT COULD NOT SEE THE DEFECT IT WAS BUILT FOR, AND WHY, AND THE BASIS THAT REPLACES IT.** Continuity item 702 reported duplicate paragraphs of twelve words or more at zero and a near-repeat sweep on an eight-word shingle returning 0.0 for every paragraph of the block. **Both are paragraph-scoped, and the defect they were supposed to catch was two sentences inside one chapter, which a paragraph-level basis is structurally incapable of seeing.** The replacement recorded for later blocks is a **clause-level comparison of a specific identified pair**, which found the bell at a 0.62 shared-distinct-word overlap between the two statements inside Chapter 264 and reduced it to a single statement. **A second finding about the same sweep is that an eight-word shingle against the prior two hundred and sixty chapters is too loose a basis for this manuscript.** Run properly it returns a hit on roughly one sentence in three, because the house voice is built from stock phrases that recur by design, among them *about four hundred people in a town of about four thousand people on a river who do not know*, *a man of thirty-two with a limp*, *a county that is not on any map*, *about four people in that lane have said since that* and *the marshal's own office's printed series*. **A later block should either lengthen the shingle or name the specific pair to be compared, and should not report a near-zero figure from a loose basis as though it were a clean sweep.** Item 702's duplicate-paragraph figure of zero **is** sound and still stands, and so is the byte-identical count of 31 repeated texts and 32 extra copies on 12,201 paragraphs, of which four instances are the four lines of the winter book at Chapter 173 and Chapter 266 and are correct.

The Saturdays are 236, 243, 250, 257, 264 and 271, six, all six market days, which is the six-Saturday figure and not §17's five, and continuity item 703 governs.** **The block has two bench scenes and both are Saturday sittings: Chapter 272's at the seventh hour on day 243 and Chapter 279's room on day 264, and the bench is asked nothing on either and the count on the page under that stair is eight before the block and eight after it.** Greenmonth is carried at thirty days and the four Greenmonth dates in the block were counted from the row Greenmonth 1 = day 216; the year label is YR 316 throughout on the convention Volume 05's closed prose established. **A defect in the Batch 0003 prompt itself is recorded and not followed: the prompt says the renewal falls on *the twenty-seventh of Longlight* and that day is 272 and is the block's last day, and §17's own table, its Block 3 header, and consequence 4 all fix the renewal on or about day 246, which is the *first* of Longlight. The document governs and the renewal is the first of Longlight. The prompt's *the cut is on day 253* is correct and the order is not reversed anywhere in the block.**

711. **THE BOUNDARY OATH-STONE IS RENEWED IN A FIELD ON THE FIRST OF LONGLIGHT, AND THE MINUTE IS THE SECOND KIND A CLERK OF ABOUT SIXTY HAS KEPT IN NINETEEN YEARS.** **The stone is a foot and a half and about nine inches square at the top with four letters cut into the face of it and a figure under them that is nineteen years old. It has been out of the ground and put back four times in nineteen years. The promise is four lines and is a copy of a copy of a thing this county has never had in its hand, and it was read out once in a field in the open by a magistrate of thirty and nobody read it a second time, and that was arranged before anybody came up the hedge and the arranging was done by the reeve and not by the clerk.** **A bench of nine was not asked, and about four people in that field worked out in the ordinary way that a bench of nine has no standing at a parish boundary and has never claimed any, and not one of the nine said it to the others, and the minute was kept anyway.** **The minute describes what is at that boundary and nothing else: a crossing with no owner and no money, a sill with nothing in it and no glass in it and no third seat, a dressed block in the abutment, squared, with nothing in the stone that anybody has ever read, and a bell a hundred yards off that goes at the fourth hour and a half. That is the first description of that crossing on the page in this volume and it is in Chapter 273, and no chapter before Chapter 273 describes the crossing.** The clerk of about sixty said one thing out loud in that field, in **thirteen words, footed at thirteen**: *A thing an office can enter is a thing an office can classify.* Nobody improved on it. **He has entered the absence of a vote once in nineteen years and he entered it by not entering it, and he entered nothing at all when a man asked him in writing what the bench had decided about a crossing, and the nothing at all is still in that book with no line where a line would go and the space the same depth as the spaces either side of it.** The sheet went down to the market in a bag in the ordinary post on the afternoon of the first of Longlight and that bag is the second thing that has ever left that county out of a field in nineteen years.

712. **THE WORD IN FRONT OF THE PLACE NAME IS PRINTED ONCE IN THIS BLOCK, IN A FIELD, AND IS NOT DEFINED.** **It is on the head of the minute's object column in Chapter 273, in the same type as the heads of the five columns, struck once about eleven weeks earlier by a printer's mate of nineteen in a press room two hundred miles off, and the clerk of about sixty read the line up before he entered it, as a line is read up, and read the word out loud with the rest of it, and about nine people in a field at a parish boundary heard a man say a word they had not heard before.** The magistrate asked where it was from, **once**, and was told *it is the word that goes in that column on that series, and if I left it off it is not a line of that series, it is a piece of paper with writing on it*, and nobody asked a second question. **The word appears once in this block and is defined zero times. In Chapter 274, where a sheet of the same series is put in a sill, the word is referred to and is not printed, so that the block's one printing is in a field as `outline/volume-06.md` §15 item 12 requires.** The volume's count of the word is now five printings and zero definitions, and the second of the two the volume still owes falls in Block 4 or 5.

713. **THE SHEET THAT WENT INTO THE SILL, THE LINK THAT WAS READ INTO THE RECORD, AND THE ORDER OF THE TWO EVENTS.** **The renewal is Chapter 273 at day 246. The link is read into the record in a chamber in the provincial town on day 250, at about the second hour and a quarter, by a man of forty-four who is a member of the Culling Order and is doing the office's work, and the line is a length of made road in a fen county, and the witness produced for the place at about the third hour is the forged *Keeper* entry built in Batch 0002 out of three real things by a man of about fifty in about nine minutes in the ordinary way.** **Nobody in that chamber asked him what is in the four places and he has never asked and nobody noticed that nobody had.** **The name in the fourth column is the name of a woman of thirty-three at a register on the first floor of that building two floors below, and it is read out because a name in a column is read out when the column is read, and nobody in that building went up or went down on that Saturday, and her leaf on the second shelf is still face down, and she did not turn it over, and she finds out in Block 4 and not before.** **A man of about thirty-one with a satchel carried about two hundred sheets of that series through the market in a fen county on the afternoon of the same Saturday and said the true thing about the four places a third time, to a woman buying salt, in the tone of a man saying a price.** A carrier of about fifty with a firm of two carried a bag up that county's own road himself because his firm were at a market four miles off, and put one sheet of the office's own printed series in the sill of a crossing, weighted with a stone off the bank, and did not ask anybody what to do with it and nobody in that lane was there to tell him. **A carrier is not a man of letters and a crossing that carries nobody is not a place a bag is brought to, and that is the only reason the sheet was not taken in the rain.**

714. **THE CUT IS NOT WRITTEN, AND THE BLOCK WRITES THE THREE DAYS BEFORE IT AND THE FOURTH DAY AFTER IT.** **The moment is not on the page and nothing in the block is a substitute for it.** The three days before are day 250, day 251 and day 252 and the volume prints day 250 and day 252. 715. **THE MAN OF FORTY-SEVEN'S FOUR THINGS STAND AT FIVE OCCASIONS AND THIS BLOCK DID NOT ADD ONE.** **He is asked one question on day 252, at a crossing, about the sheet, and he answers in forty-six words that are not the four things, and the page says so. 716. **THE REVERSAL, AND IT IS A COMPLICATION AND NOT A VINDICATION.** **In a room over a smithy on day 259 a man of thirty-two with a limp puts three pieces of paper on a table: a sheet of the office's own printed series out of a sill with the name in the fourth column gone soft in the weather, a blank form of the same series out of a coat, and this county's own form ruled in seven with a name in the seventh column entered by a second copyist in about nine seconds.** The second column of the first is the same width as the second column of the second, and the fifth of the first is the same width as the fifth of the second, and the sixth column of both has no head on it and is the same width as the fifth, and about four of the six on both are ruled for a figure and there is nowhere on the whole of either for the name of a person. **That took him about four minutes and it is on the page.** **The fourth thing is not on the table: a list of eleven lines in a drawer in a building two hundred miles off, ruled in two columns in two parts, a hand and a road, eleven of each, the eleventh with two marks on it and about a year between the first of them going out and the eleventh coming back, and no third column and no column for what became of anybody, which a man said out loud before he was asked and the not asking took about four seconds and that man is not asked again and is not going to be and the not-asking is not a decision anybody took.** **The finding, in the block's own words: the first column of that list is a hand, and a hand is not a person, and a hand is what a person is when a column has a head on it and the head is *Keeper*; 717. **HIS MOTHER IS ON THAT LINE AND THE VOLUME DOES NOT RESOLVE IT.** **It is the eleventh line, it has been the eleventh for about four months, he did not find that out on the fourteenth of Longlight and he knew it in a room with no window in it, there is no name in it, and the eleventh line has a woman's mark and a boy's mark on it. 719. **THE STANDING LIMIT IS ON THE PAGE ONCE, IN A ROOM, ON THE ELEVENTH DAY AFTER THE CUT, AND HE TELLS ONE PERSON.** **The eleventh day after the eighth of Longlight is the nineteenth of Longlight, day 264, and that is the day the sentence is spent, and the two things sit in the same room an hour apart.** **A version of the last eight months in which he does not do it reads to him as the reasonable one, and he can see the shape of it, and the shape is the shape of a thing that would have worked: the sheet in the sill for nine more days and then the weather, the forty yards of hemp in the dressed block four feet down, no line in that block at all, a man of fifty-eight in a room over a cross with a trestle against a wall at the ninth hour, **a sheet of eleven lines staying in a drawer in a building two hundred miles off with his mother on the eleventh of them and no three forms on any table in this county and nobody in either county telling him that**, a bench of nine asked nothing that month or the next, a man of fifty-five saying the same four words to about four hundred more people, and a man of thirty-two with a limp in a room over a smithy who cannot get up a bank and does not try to, because there is no reason on that side of it to try. 720. **THE FEE IS ANOTHER CROSSING AND IT IS REFUSED, IN A YARD, OUT LOUD, TO NINE MEN WHO WERE NOT LISTENING.** **The price of the thing done at the second hour of the eighth of Longlight is another crossing, and the man of thirty-two with a limp said so at about the fifth hour of the twenty-seventh of Longlight standing at a bench-board in a yard on Weir Street, in twenty-seven words, and about nine men in that yard heard it and about four did not and neither of those four has ever mentioned it.** **The reason is in the block's own trade terms and it is the volume's argument: a crossing is a claim, a road that has been claimed can be claimed again by somebody else with a different column and a different hand, and the sheet in the coat has four places ruled for a figure and a name in the fourth column and a word in front of the place name and no head on the sixth column at all, and a man who makes a second crossing on a road is a man who has put a second name on it in a column nobody is keeping. 726. **THE THREE PLACES WHERE THIS BLOCK CAME CLOSEST TO A DOCUMENT BLOCK, AND WHETHER EACH HELD, AND THE CHAPTER THAT SHOULD HAVE BEEN A ROOM WITH A PERSON IN IT.** **One, Chapter 273. The minute is the volume's most elegant page and it is a document, and it held, because the four lines of the promise are read out loud by a woman in a field in the open in front of about nine people, and the field, the lime, the barrow, the wet ground, the two men who dug and the mason who argued with the clerk about wet and dry lime are all on the page, and the document is the fourth hour of a morning that went wrong about the weather. Two, Chapter 274. A link is read into a record in a chamber and a sheet arrives in a sill, and it held, barely, and it held because two rooms on one day are given about nine people between them and about six speeches, and because a market goes on in the county with a salt waggon and a man with a satchel saying the true thing about the four places a third time to a woman buying salt, and because the whole of the money and the whole of the carrier and the whole of the stone off the bank are on the page. Three, Chapter 279. A minute is kept and a sentence is entered in it and a version of eight months is seen in a room, and it held, because the room has nine people in it and a salt item that takes eleven minutes and a hedge argued about for twenty minutes and a clerk with two books, and because the two documents in that chapter are a spoken sentence and a minute nobody reads twice.** **The answer the block was asked for: none of the three failed, and the block is the first in the volume with no document chapter in it at all, and the answer is that the chapter which came closest to needing to be a room with a person in it is Chapter 275, the day before, and it did need one, and it has one, and the person in it is a man of forty-seven with a hod he is not carrying anything in, who is asked one question and answers in forty-six words that are not the four things.** **The finding is that the two-card problem Batch 0002 named was not a document problem at all. It was that a block whose cards are a field and a chamber and a book has no room in it, and the fix was not to make a document a room but to find the room the county already has, which is the long room over the wharf with an aisle four feet wide in it, and to spend the volume's one sentence there.**

## Canon established by the Volume 06 Batch 0003 review repair pass

728. **WHAT THE REVIEW OF BATCH 0003 FOUND, WHAT THE REPAIR PASS CHANGED, AND WHAT IT LEFT.** A review of the Volume 06 Batch 0003 writer phase returned ten findings, of which the first two were the ones a reader would have hit in the first three pages of Chapter 279, and the pass applied all ten, applied six further repairs of the same classes that the recount surfaced, and changed no day number, no month, no weekday, no market-day flag, no block boundary, no name-budget figure, no money figure, no speech-length figure, and no sentence the volume spends. **It did not write a chapter, did not replace a scene, and did not restart the batch.** Twenty-one paragraphs were changed across nine of the ten chapters, two of them datelines, and Chapter 273 was not touched, and the block's three cards, its ten chapter shapes and its ten endings stand.

729. **THE VOLUME'S ONE SPEAKER IS A WOMAN OF SEVENTY-TWO, AND THE BATCH PRINTED HER AT SIXTY-SIX, WHICH IS ANOTHER WOMAN.** **The finding: `chapter-0279.md` gave the volume's one sentence to a woman of sixty-six, seated at the end of a bench for the fire, standing in an aisle four feet wide, in a room in a building in a county, and the woman of sixty-six in the valley four hundred miles off has a bench, an aisle, a fire, a room in a building in a county and a want, at `chapter-0266.md` and `chapter-0267.md`, and no reader can be expected to hold two of them.** The repair: **she is a woman of seventy-two at all three printings in `chapter-0279.md`, in the dateline, in the paragraph that has her stand up, and in the last paragraph of the chapter, and in items 718 and 722 and 727 and in `state/current.md`, `state/chapter-summaries.md`, `state/batch-summaries.md`, `state/open-threads.md` and the Batch 0004 prompt.** Nothing else about her changed. She is unnamed, unasked, without a want, without a history and gone by the end of the chapter, she is not a name and spends no slot, and the volume's arithmetic is 2 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 4 of thirty and unmoved. **The lesson for the next block, and it is a rule now: a returning character is identified by age in this volume, and an unremarked body may not be given a returning character's age. The ages in this volume's returns list are spoken for, and a new body takes an age that is on nobody's list, and the review repair pass checked the whole manuscript for the age it gave her and found it at zero outside the three printings it changed.**

730. **THE DATELINE OF CHAPTER 279 CONTRADICTED THE CHAPTER ON THE ONE POINT A READER CHECKS FIRST, AND THE CHAPTER WAS RIGHT.** **The dateline said the tenth person in the long room over the wharf has a seat on the roll of the bench of nine; eighteen lines later the chapter said she has no vote, no office and no place on any roll, and the dateline is the one line every reader of that chapter reads before anything else.** The repair: the dateline now says the tenth person in that room is on no roll of anything and has never once spoken in that room, which is what the chapter says and what item 718 has always said. **The rule for the next block, and it is the same rule the volume's own line-number warning exists for: a dateline in this book restates the page and it is written first, and if a dateline and its chapter disagree the dateline is the one that is wrong, because the dateline is what the reader holds in their head while they read the rest of it.**

731. **THE FEVER HAD THREE INCOMPATIBLE END DATES AND NOW HAS ONE, AND THE WHOLE RUN IS ON THE PAGE IN THREE PLACES.** **As written, Chapter 278 put the fever on its sixth day on the seventeenth of Longlight, Chapter 279 said it was out of him two days before the nineteenth, and Chapter 280 said it was over on the nineteenth and that he had been up five days by the twenty-seventh, which are three statements and no two of them can be true.** The run as it now stands: **the fever began on the ninth of Longlight, day 255, and was over on the seventeenth, day 262, and it runs about nine days, and the fourth day of it is the twelfth, which is the day a man of thirty-two with a limp got about two feet up a bank and sat down on a dressed block, and the third of it is the eleventh, on which he could not get out of bed, and the fifth is the thirteenth, on which a man of about thirty came up a flight of stairs with a pail and was not asked a question, and the ninth is the seventeenth, on which he was out for about two hours and then was not.** Chapter 280's ten days up by the twenty-seventh and Chapter 279's two days before both follow from that and both are unchanged. **A man of fifty-five's four hundred figures were corrected in the same pass and the corrected figures are here so that no later phase has to guess: about four hundred people is the number he has said the four words to in nineteen years and it is the same four hundred in Chapters 275, 279 and 280 and in item 715, and about four thousand is the number of people let through the barrier in nineteen years and the number of times the three bars have gone up and come down, and about nine is the number of people he turned round on the twelfth of Longlight. He is a man who has spoken to about a tenth of the people who have gone past him and the two figures have never been added to one another and are not to be.**

732. **THE BLOCK'S THREE DATE ARITHMETICS THAT WERE OFF BY ONE OR BY NINE ARE CORRECTED, AND NO DATE NUMBER MOVED.** **One, `chapter-0271.md`: the chapter is the twenty-fourth of Greenmonth and the clerk reads the day off the inside cover of his book and said it aloud as the first of Longlight, seven days forward, in the future tense, with the stone standing in the field behind him; he now says the twenty-fourth of Greenmonth, and names the first of Longlight as the day they are all coming back for, and the chapter's closing paragraph already separated the two dates correctly and was the only correct account of them. Two, `chapter-0276.md`: the thing done at the second hour of the eighth of Longlight was said to have been done eight days after the promise was said in a field, and the renewal is the first of Longlight and the eighth is seven days after it, and the block's own convention, the eleventh day after the eighth being the nineteenth, is exclusive. Three, `chapter-0280.md`: a man who has not gone up a bank since the seventh day of the month and is writing on the twenty-seventh was credited with nine days of thinking about it, and the twentieth day is the right figure. And the day-book figures in Chapter 278 moved with the fever and the yard: a man last seen at the bench-board on the fifteenth has not been there two days, not six.** And the fourth date error is not on a page at all and is recorded here because the Batch 0004 prompt cites an item for it and the item it cited did not contain it: **the Batch 0003 prompt itself called day 246 the twenty-seventh of Longlight, when `outline/volume-06.md` §17's table, its Block 3 header and consequence 4 all fix the boundary oath-stone renewal on or about day 246, which is the first of Longlight, and the Batch 0004 prompt's third standing defect names it correctly and its list of standing defects pointed at item 725, which is the sweeps item and never recorded it. The prompt now points at this item.**

733. **THE SEAM, AND THE FALSE PREMISE THE BLOCK BUILT ON IT, AND WHAT A NEXT WRITER IS ACTUALLY FORBIDDEN.** `outline/volume-06.md` §15 item 9 requires that the seam in the fourth bay and the second seam in the dressed block four hundred yards away not be joined, that the two sills and the two crossings not be put in one book by anybody, that no character be allowed to use either as a door, a key or a mark, and that no character point at the first one. **The block did all of that. Chapter 276 says, in the narrator's voice, that a line about nine inches long in a dressed block is the same length as a line about nine inches long in a stone course in another structure in this county, and that this is a fact about two pieces of work done by the same hands in the same trade, and that no person in that county knows of the other one, and that the two have never been in one book and are not going to be, and that sentence is the volume's echo and not a violation of it.** What was wrong was the ledger: **item 714 said the block does not mention the first seam once, item 727 said the seam in the fourth bay is not mentioned once in the block, and requirement 13 and inherited item 6 of the Batch 0004 prompt repeated it, so a writer reading the handoff would have been told that Block 3 never touched the other structure when Block 3 refers to it once, in narration, by saying that nobody in that county knows of it.** All four are corrected. **What Block 4 is forbidden is narrower and is now stated correctly: it may not name the reach, the bay or the first seam, may not place the second seam and the first one in one sentence by a character, may not measure, rule across, point at or use either, and may not repeat the sentence in Chapter 276, which is the volume's single printed reference to the two and is spent.**

734. **THE DEVICE LEDGER WAS NOT REPRODUCIBLE AND THE BATCH'S OWN FIGURES WERE WRONG IN FOUR PLACES.** `about` was 459 and not 460, the per-chapter list gave Chapter 275 as 45 where the file has 44, `three` was 31 and not 30, and Chapter 275 was 2,375 words where `state/batch-summaries.md` and the Batch 0004 prompt both said 2,375 and continuity item 724 said 2,370, so two files in one commit disagreed. **Item 724 now carries a full recount made after the repair pass: 23,267 words for the block, 1,000,028 for the manuscript, `about` 461 and 464 case-insensitive at 19.81 per 1,000 words, `nine` 148, `two` 172, `three` 33, `cut` 9, `the whole of` 25, `in nine years` 2, thirty-five `---` rules, eighty-seven bolded line-openings on both bases and twenty-seven quote-wrapped dialogue openings, 2,276 words of quoted dialogue across 111 speeches, and the narrator reporting clause at 12 and `about four people` at 20.** The two figures the next block is told to watch did not move: **the reporting clause is 12 and the dialogue count is 2,276, against Batch 0002's 74 and 224.** The lesson is the one the block itself wrote at requirement 9 of its own prompt and it is now a finding: **a block that counts its own devices at the end of the batch, on a basis it names, and reports them in three files, will still get one or two of them wrong, and the only defence is that the next phase counts again and believes the count.**

735. **THE DOUBLED SECTION BREAK IN CHAPTER 274 IS THE SIXTH OF SIX IN THE MANUSCRIPT AND FIVE OF THEM ARE NOT IN THIS PHASE.** **`chapter-0274.md` had two `---` rules with a blank line between them, which produces an empty section, and the same sweep finds five more: `chapter-0189.md` in Volume 04 and `chapter-0203.md`, `chapter-0204.md`, `chapter-0205.md` and `chapter-0207.md` in Volume 05.** The one in this phase is fixed and the count of rules in Block 3 is thirty-five. **The five in Volumes 04 and 05 are not this phase's to fix, are recorded here so that they are not found a second time, and are of the same class as the six the Batch 0002 review pass fixed in Batch 0002's own chapters.** The batch's own ledger reported thirty-six rules and a clean count with no doubled-rule check, and the check is now in the sweep list for the next block.

Chapter 290 is the eighth of Harvestmonth, day 313, a Saturday and a market day.** Every year label in the ten files is YR 316 and no year was re-labelled. **Seven of the block's twelve market days are chapter dates, 278, 283, 285, 292, 299, 306 and 313, and five market days are not, 276, 290, 297, 304 and 311. All six of the block's Saturdays are chapter dates, 278, 285, 292, 299, 306 and 313, and the six non-Saturday chapter dates are 273, a Monday, 283, a Thursday, 284, a Friday, 286, a Friday, and 283 is a market day. No chapter is dated day 271 and no chapter is dated a day outside 273 to 313.** **The block has one bench sitting and it is Chapter 282, on day 278, a Saturday, a market day, the ordinary seventh-hour sitting, and it is asked nothing, and the count on the page under that stair stays at eight. There is no other bench scene in the block and no special sitting and nothing was put to the bench of nine in ten chapters, and the ninth ask remains Block 5's.** The three standing outline defects are unchanged and are not this phase's to repair: item 692, item 703, and the Batch 0003 prompt's own slip about the date of the renewal.

738. **THE CROWN'S PROCEEDING SAT ON THE NINTH OF RAINMONTH, YR 316, IN THE SAME ROOM AS A STANDING HEARING FOR A DELEGATION THAT CANNOT ARRIVE, AND THE TWO ARE NOT JOINED IN ONE SENTENCE BY ANYBODY.** **The delegation does not arrive, is not sent for, and is not in that chamber, and there has not been one in that building on the ninth of a month in four years. The matter it was entered for is on a board at the end of that chamber in a folder with a card on the front of it and the card has one word on it and the word is *stood*, and it has been *stood* four times. The Crown's proceeding is a second folder on the same board a foot away, with a card of its own, and the word on that one is *sat*. The two are never put in one sentence by any character and no character in Chapter 284 joins them.** **The reason the chamber was free on that date is shown on the page as an object and is never said in one sentence by anybody: four cards of the same colour and the same hand and the same word for the ninth of a month in four consecutive years, on a booking board in a passage on the second floor, and a fifth card of a different colour taken off that board on the fourth of a month by a woman of thirty-eight who did not come down to the board and did not look at it and has not asked about the four.** The hearing is not adjourned, not refused, not retold and not closed, and the companion file of one sheet with a district on it is not removed, not corrected, and not asked after by anybody who knows what is in it, and a second clerk of the returns entered that sheet as a sheet on the Thursday before and nobody in that building has asked him about it.

739. **THE WITNESS LIST HAS EIGHT NAMES AND SIX PEOPLE IN THE CHAMBER, TWO OF THE SIX ARE THERE BECAUSE THEY ARE CLERKS, AND A SECOND COPYIST OF ABOUT THIRTY CAME TWO HUNDRED MILES AND WAS IN THE ROOM AS A WITNESS AND NOT AS A COPYIST.** **Eight lines on the wall and a nail through the top corner of the sheet. Seven of the eight are people and one is a body corporate with a door on a lane and a year against a number at fourpence and a deed of thirteen words that names no officer, and there is no person against that line. Six of the seven people are in the chamber. The seventh, a keeper of records of twenty-nine in a fen county, is two hundred miles off and was not sent for, and her name is on the list in a hand that is not the office's, and a clerk of the Crown entered it in about four seconds and did not say when. Two of the six in the room are there because they are clerks: a clerk of the Crown on a stool, and a second clerk of the returns. The other four are the woman of thirty-eight in the office line, a man of about fifty who has been a clerk of a press for thirty-one years, a man of about thirty-one with a satchel, and the second copyist.** **A man of thirty-two with a limp is in that chamber because his name is on the sixth line in a hand that is not his and is not the office's, and nobody in that chamber has said when that was done and nobody is going to.** **Alish Renn, thirty, a second copyist in a room over a weigh-house with a door on a lane, came two hundred miles on a warrant to produce that names a room and a day and does not name a person, was put in a room at the end of a second-floor passage because a building of four floors and seven presses had nowhere to put a person, and is in that town from the ninth of Rainmonth to the first of Harvestmonth, about four weeks, and no third sitting was ever entered and nobody in that building ever said otherwise and nobody said anything about it at the time.** The day-book's third post is on a warrant held by a second keeper of twenty-six and is not signed, and the want for a line in that day-book is the second copyist's and belongs to her alone, and the two women have never spoken about either and did not speak about them in this block.

740. **PERRY HASK, 34, A SECOND CLERK OF THE RETURNS IN THE PROVINCIAL TOWN, IS THE BLOCK'S ONE NEW NAME, AND HE DOES NOT GET THE COLUMN.** **One name of six spent and five unfilled, and the volume's cumulative arithmetic is 2 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 4 of thirty, with 4 + 4 + 6 + 6 + 5 + 5 = 30, which foots exactly at the cap.** A sweep of the ten files for capitalised two-word sequences returns five hits and every one of them is accounted for: **Alish Renn** and **Perry Hask** are people, **Weir Street** is a street, **Culling Order** is the standing debt, and **And Hask** is a sentence opening. The marshal is a return, does not count, and his name is written in no chapter of Volume 06 and in no state file this batch wrote. **Hask's want is said once, in eleven words, to a man of about fifty at a stone, and the eleven words are in the chapter and are eleven: *I would like there to be a column for a sheet.*** The man of about fifty gives him back none of it and does not thank him and does not refuse him, contradicts himself once at the stone about whether a column exists, retracts it, is told *You did*, and goes down two flights. **Hask entered the companion sheet as a sheet, on the line for the district, and the book now carries a line that is not a return for as long as the book is kept, and nobody in that room will ever look at that line again and the line will be there. The volume does not tell the reader whether that was right.** **The accident he was handed is not the accident that made this volume turn, and the two are not the same event: the accident that turned the volume is a filing in Block 1 and nobody made it and nobody was handed it, and what Hask is handed on the Thursday is a sheet with a district on it that is not a return, and there is no column for it, and the two accidents are nowhere near each other on the page and no character in that building joined them.**

741. **A WOMAN OF THIRTY-THREE FOUND OUT ON THE TENTH OF RAINMONTH, IN A ROOM, FROM A COPY CARRIED IN BY SOMEBODY ELSE, AND SHE SAID THREE THINGS, AND THE THIRD IS THE VOLUME'S THIRD REFUSAL OF KINDNESS.** **The paper is a copy, and it came down two flights on a tray carried in by a man of about sixty with a tray, who has carried trays in and out of that building for twenty-two years, and the man with the stick is not the carrier and is not in that room. The copy was made on the ground floor at about the third hour on the Friday before by the man of about fifty who has been a clerk of a press for thirty-one years, by putting a filled sheet face down on a clean one and ruling the six columns again over the top of it and going along the lines with the same hand, in about nine minutes.** **The name in the fourth column, headed *Keeper*, is hers, and the nine shapes in it are the nine shapes she puts in that column when she fills it from a roll in about a minute and a quarter without looking up, and a stroke is left short at the top the way she leaves it short, and the weight of it is wrong. That is the whole of what she had in about two seconds, and a copy of a hand is the right shapes at the wrong weight.** Her first thing is her want, unchanged, and it is the same sentence and has not got one word more in it than it had in the month she was twenty-two. Her second thing is a question, and it is the first question anybody in that building has asked about that column in eleven years, and nobody answered it, and the clerk of the returns answered a different question and said so. Her third thing is the block's own words and is printed word for word in `chapters/volume-06/chapter-0286.md` and is not improved on, softened, shortened or staged: *I have been afraid of that column since I was twenty-two and I filled it in this year in about a minute and a quarter without looking up, and you have now put my name in it again, and both of those are the same hand, and neither of them is mine. Do not thank me. I would like somebody to write down that I did not stop it and there is nobody in this building I can ask.* **Nobody thanked her, nobody told her she had been right, nobody told her it was not her fault, nobody improved on any part of it, and nobody in that building asked her anything, and a second clerk of the returns offered her a form and was refused and was told he had had to ask and was told he did not.** **Her want does not change. Her note of nineteen words stays face down on a shelf in a case behind her and is not turned over and nobody asks her to. She is not the person who explains anything, and the marginal instruction is not quoted, not referred to and not explained in this block. A kind thing has been refused once at that table and is not offered at it again, and a table where a kind thing has been refused once does not get one offered at it again, and nobody in that building has worked out how to do that on purpose and nobody has had to.**

742. **THE ELEVEN SENTENCES, THE FOUR WORDS THAT WERE NOT SAID, AND THE TWELFTH THAT WAS NOT SAID, AND THE REASON HE WENT FIRST IS NOT GIVEN AND NOT REPLACED.** **On the twenty-fourth of Rainmonth, YR 316, day 299, at the second hour of the second sitting, a man of thirty-two with a limp was sworn on the back of a return and nobody asked him anything for about a minute and a half, and then he said eleven sentences before anybody asked him for any part of it and before the order of the marshal's office was read.** The eleven are in `chapters/volume-06/chapter-0288.md` and the chapter is counted: **eleven sentences, and a clerk of the Crown made a stroke in the margin against each of them, and there are eleven strokes, and the space after the eleventh is ruled and empty, and there is no rule after a twelfth because a clerk of the Crown does not rule a space for a thing that has not been said.** The eleventh sentence announces that he has one more and is not going to say it. **He did not say a twelfth. The four words he has had ready since a day he cannot count were not said, and the chapter says that they were ready in a room with no window in it in a town in this province in the winter before last and were not said in that room and are not said in this one, and does not print them.** **The reason he went first is a sentence a woman of twenty-nine said in a room with a door on a lane in another month, and it is not in this volume, and this block did not invent a substitute and did not paraphrase it, and the only thing on the page about it is that nobody asked him why he began the way he began, and nobody is going to, and there is no line in that proceeding for a reason a witness had before he stood up.** The woman of thirty-eight entered the room as a room in the minute in her own hand on that afternoon, and had asked for exactly that in nineteen sentences in Thawmonth, and watched the best possible version of it performed by a witness, and it did not work, and she was told by her own clerk that the ninth line of the minute already said what she had said and that she had not heard the ninth line, and she believed him and did not ask.

743. **A TEMPORARY INJUNCTION AGAINST FORCED CULLING WAS ACCEPTED ON THE FIRST OF HARVESTMONTH, YR 316, WITH A DAY ON IT, AND THE CULLING ORDER WENT UNDERGROUND, AND NEITHER IS AN ENEMY AND NEITHER IS GIVEN A WANT.** **The court accepted the injunction at about the fourth hour and a clerk of the Crown read the term out at about the fourth hour and a half: it holds to a day and after that day it holds if a local council renews it in public. Nobody in that chamber said anything about the renewal and nobody in that chamber has any power to renew it and no council is in the room and no council was written to and nothing in that proceeding asks anybody in a county to do anything.** The minute was made up and read back once and only once, and the four sentences in it are the term, the date, that a thing asked in that chamber was entered as a thing asked, and that a witness had spoken before he was asked. **Two floors up, in the chamber with the long table, the second hour came and went and the third hour came and went and nobody read anything into the record, and the head of that record still says a schedule is to be complete before a date, and the date went by a month ago, and a schedule that cannot be complete before a date that has been is not a schedule that is late, it is a schedule that has stopped.** The clerk with the bad wrist had about two hundred and thirty lines to copy and nothing to copy and sharpened the pen twice. **The man of forty-four, a member of the Culling Order and a classifier, is not in that room, his room is two doors down it with a cold stove, he has not been in the building since the Friday before, and nobody in that building has asked him where he is and nobody is going to, and about four people have noticed the cold stove and two of them have not connected it to a man.** His want was said once, in thirty-four words, to a clerk carrying a tray out of a room on the eighth of a month in the year before, it is that a classification that is late is a classification that can be argued with, and it is spent and was not said again in this block and is not going to be said again. **A woman of thirty-eight's last page in this volume is a clerk of the Crown asking her whether a certain column is a column and her saying yes.** The second copyist went down two flights and out of the front door with a bag of her own, and nobody in that building said that the reason she was able to go was that the thing that was being held was over.

744. **A COUNTY OF ABOUT FOUR THOUSAND PEOPLE LEARNED IT FROM A COURIER TWO HUNDRED MILES OFF, AND DOES NOT KNOW WHETHER TO BE GLAD, AND A SHEET THAT SAYS SO IS IN A PRESS THAT NOBODY CAN BE SERVED WITH.** **On the eighth of Harvestmonth, YR 316, day 313, a Saturday and a market day, a courier came up the county's own road at about the second hour with about four hundred people in the market and did not stop in the market. A courier is not a carrier: a carrier has a round and a firm and a rate that is not printed in the county he is standing in, and the two of them have been in that county four times between them in about nine years and have never met and are not going to.** The sheet is a copy of a minute of a court, one sheet, with a number of an office on the head of it, the seal of that office and the word *copy* in the corner, and it says four things: that a temporary injunction has been accepted against forced culling, that it holds to a day and after that day if a local council renews it in public, that the classifications already entered are not taken back by it, and in one line at the foot of a sheet of the office's own printed series with no name against it and no office to ask, that the office has gone out of the ordinary way and will not be circulating the schedule. **The county read it in a room over a weigh-house at about the third hour on a market Saturday, and it does not name a bell and it does not name a crossing and it does not name that county at all. A reeve came up two flights and got to a true thing by saying the wrong one first. The magistrate was not told and is not going to be until a bench of nine sits at the seventh hour on a Saturday, and a courier with a bag is not a thing anybody has ever put to a bench of nine and is not going to be, and she has a construction ready and did not use it on a courier. The not-askings stand at nine and this block entered no tenth.** The keeper of records is twenty-nine and has run that office four years and a half out of a deed of thirteen words, and the office pays fourpence a year, standing alone in that chapter with no second price anywhere near it. The second copyist put the courier's sheet into the press in that room, which can be served with anything by anybody who walks up that lane, and a man of thirty-two with a limp took it out of that press, put it in his coat, did not ask what he was going to do with it, went down the lane and up a street to a yard, and put it into a press in a room at the end of that yard that belongs to the yard and cannot be served with anything, and the man of twenty-five who owns that yard said eight words about it, which are *It goes in on the shelf and not on the book, and I have never asked you to take anything out of it and I am not asking you now.* **The sheet is the one a man with a satchel put in a sill at the toll house on the twenty-eighth of Longlight and took out of it on a collection on the third of Rainmonth and which has been in and out of two buildings and a satchel since, and nobody in any of them has ever asked where it has been, and the last page of the block is a man looking at it in a press in a room where nobody knows what he is looking at.**

745. **THE TWO MONEY COLUMNS OF BLOCK 4, FOOTED ON THE PAGE, AND EVERY FIGURE THAT IS NOT ADDED TO ANYTHING.** **Chapter 284, the ninth of Rainmonth, the second sitting's costs, and the items are added in pence and the total is said after the addition and not before.** A clerk's fee for entering a sitting is fourpence. A sheet of the office's own printed series for the list on the wall is a penny. A second sheet of the same series, which that office prints itself and charges for anyway, is a penny. A light kept burning in a room with no window for one day is twopence. A second copyist of about thirty two hundred miles in a cart and four days on the road, and there is no rate for a cart in this county and there is not going to be one, and a man who travels on a warrant is paid his wages and not his road, and his wages are on a sheet in a drawer in that building and the sheet is not one of the five items and the five items are not added to it. *Fourpence and a penny is fivepence. Fivepence and a penny is sixpence. Sixpence and twopence is eight pence.* **Total: eight pence.** **Chapter 289, the first of Harvestmonth.** A sheet of the office's own printed series for the injunction is a penny. A clerk's fee for entering an injunction is fourpence. A light kept burning in a room with no window for one day is twopence. A messenger's hand for two hundred miles, and there is no rate for a messenger for two hundred miles printed in this county. A copy of a schedule of about two hundred and forty lines for the Crown, and there is no rate for a copy of two hundred and forty lines in this county. *A penny and fourpence is fivepence, and fivepence and twopence is seven pence.* **Total: seven pence.** **The two are not added to one another and neither is added to Batch 0003's fourteen pence and six pence.** The office's fourpence a year is printed in Chapter 290 standing alone with no second price anywhere near it, and also in the datelines of Chapters 282 and 284 as part of a door and a number, and in each case no second price is within reach of it. **The two shillings a month that a salt merchant charges for each of the two rooms over a weigh-house is named once in this block, in Chapter 289, only to say that it is not in that column, and the fourpence a year is named in the same sentence and the two are not added there either.** The two prices of one fine on one sheet in Chapter 258 are not reprinted, restated or referred to as a pair. The bench's eight things asked in nineteen years and the valley's hundred and forty on the end of a bench are two separate counts of askings, neither is a price, neither is a count of persons, neither is added to the other and neither is added to anything; **the eight is restated in this block twice, in the dateline of Chapter 282 and in its body, and the hundred and forty not at all, because the block does not go to the valley.** A figure of persons that the office would not print on an offer is not printed, the figure now on a return is not reconciled with it, the figure of persons against a district is not printed, and no character in any room in this block put the two together. The five refusal figures are not reconciled and no two of them are added. About four hundred doors is never added to about four hundred doors, the two carriers never meet, and no character in this block says which county the older list is in, and the block introduces the courier who is not one of them and keeps him apart from both.

760. **THE MAN OF ABOUT FIFTY IS THANKED, AND THE THANKS IS WORSE, AND HE GOES BACK TO THE PRESS.** **In Chapter 293, at about the third hour of the seventeenth day of Harvestmonth, a woman of thirty-eight came down two flights to a press room and said thank you to a man of about fifty for a true thing about a column, and the true thing is twenty words and foots at twenty: *A figure of persons stands under a head that says Date, and there is no place here for a name.*** **A clerk of the Crown wrote the thanks in a margin in about four seconds in a hand that is not the office's, and a thing in a margin can be produced, and a true thing said in a room and thanked by the office now has a day on it and a person against it, and that is a finding.** **He has waited about two years to be thanked for that column and has not been thanked for it at any time before this.** He put a sheet under the press and said nothing else about it and that is the last time anybody in that building has said anything to him about a column. **The printer's mate of nineteen with eleven weeks to serve before the next sitting and who wants to be a journeyman is not in that room when the room is told what the drawer held, and the sort is not struck again, and the nine copies went out with the space in the first column empty in front of the name of the place.**

761. **THE BENCH OF NINE IS ASKED A NINTH THING AND SAYS NO IN ELEVEN WORDS, AND THE COUNT GOES FROM EIGHT TO NINE.** **In Chapter 300, on day 390, the twenty-fifth of Embermonth, YR 316, a Saturday and the volume's last day, at about the seventh hour in the long room over a wharf, a woman of thirty-eight who is of the office that convened the proceeding put the term of the injunction on the long table and asked the bench to renew it in public, there and that morning, as a matter of the county's own record and not of a court two hundred miles off.** The ask is a thing and is not a figure of persons, and the county can refuse it. **The magistrate said the no and it is eleven words and foots at eleven: *No, because we have never been asked for anything at all.*** **The reason is on the page twice and no more: once in the mouth of the bench and once in the ink of the clerk of about sixty, who entered it under the line for a thing that was not decided and entered on the same line that the bench did not vote.** Nobody improved on it, nobody thanked her for asking, nobody thanked her for being answered, and nobody in that room said the county was right. **The magistrate's construction, which she has had ready for about a year, was not used and nobody wrote it down for her and nobody is going to.** The reeve sat next to her and does not vote on the guild's own matter and has not for nine years. **At about the eighth hour the clerk of about sixty went down four steps and put a ninth mark under eight on a page about nine inches by six under that stair, and he did not enter the number nine anywhere else, and nobody in that hall has ever entered that count on a form, and there is no line in that minute for what the count is a count of.** The count is a count of askings and is not a price, is not a count of persons, and is added to nothing, and the valley's hundred and forty is a first count of the times anybody has stood in an aisle to be asked and is not a count of persons either, and the two hundreds and forties were not added to each other anywhere in the block.

762. **THE MAN OF FORTY-SEVEN, HIS FIFTH OCCASION, AND THE COUNT THAT TWO CHAPTERS DISAGREE ON.** **In Chapter 300, at about the fifth hour, a man of forty-seven was at the end of a bench-board four feet off the ground in a yard on a street four hundred yards up that county's own road, with a man with a stick about nine feet off him, a yard wall behind one of them and nobody else in the yard. He said the four things. A man with a stick asked him the same thing he has asked four times and got the four things and asked nothing else.** He is on the roll of a bench of nine with a vote and not an office, is not on a trade, has not used his vote since the day he was elected and did not use it then, has been the witness at two ends of two crossings in a year, is paid fourpence a week out of a private box and not out of the chest, and does not hold the reach, the Old Toll or the crossing. **At the seventh hour he sat on that bench and was asked nothing, and the chapter has no further page about him.** The block printed the four things once as a description and did not reprint them, and the four things are not printed in this block at all. **The count is a defect and it is recorded rather than resolved: `outline/volume-06.md` §3.5 and the Batch 0005 prompt both say the same four things have been said four times in a year and that this is the fifth, and `chapters/volume-06/chapter-0276.md` says in its own text that the four things have been said five times in a year and that there is no sixth occasion on any list anybody keeps. This block printed the fifth occasion because the outline and the prompt both fix it and because a sixth is forbidden, and the Chapter 276 figure is left unrepaired, because no batch phase repairs a prior chapter.**

763. **BESSA QUILL, 36, A BRIDGEKEEPER IN THE NINEFOLD WINTER, IS THE ONLY NAME THIS BLOCK SPENT AND HER WANT IS SAID ONCE, IN A YARD, TO A BOY WITH A BARROW.** **She is first named in prose in Chapter 298 and the name is said by the man of thirty-four with sixteen men and no work.** She keeps a bridge over the river with about two hundred and forty feet of stone on it and is thirty-six. **She got up before the mill on the eighteenth day of Fallowmonth, YR 316, rode about four hundred yards down a made road nobody has come down, stood at a standing finish on the end of it for about as long as it takes to look at nine feet of grass twice, and came back up with nothing.** **She said her want once, to a boy of about nine with a barrow and not to the yard and not to a stranger, and it is the only time she has said it, and the boy carried on to the mill and nothing is asked of him and he is not named.** **She was not thanked, was not comforted, was not given a reason, and was not put in a record, and the day-book forty feet from a wagon arch did not get a tenth entry on that day and is not going to get one.** **Seven words were said to the man of thirty-four after that, and the seven foot: *Nobody is to be told I went.*** **The volume does not say that this is the last time any of them looks for him, and the narrator does not say it, and about four hundred people in that valley go to bed not knowing that the road was gone down and came back from.** The want is not connected on the page to the finding in the winter book and the finding is not re-entered and is not asked about.

766. **THE TWO CROSSINGS, THE TWO LINES, AND THE VOLUME'S LAST LINE, AND WHAT MAY NOT BE DONE WITH ANY OF THEM.** **The line in the third course of the fourth bay of the reach, under about half an inch of lime, is about nine inches long, in the stone and not across a joint, has not moved, and nobody has measured it, ruled across it, laid a rule on it or put a finger on it. The line in the face of a dressed block in the abutment of the crossing a hundred yards from the end of the market is about nine inches long, in the stone and not across a joint and not in a joint, under no lime of its own, has not moved, and nobody has measured it and nobody is going to.** **The word *seam* is used nowhere in this block of either of them; the one occurrence of the word in the ten chapters is in the bell's own specification in Chapter 299, where it is the seam in the metal where the band was closed.** **The two are never in one sentence by a character, the two sills and the two crossings are never put in one book by anybody, and the sentence in Chapter 276 that first put the two in one narrator's sentence is neither repeated nor varied: Chapter 299 says only that not one person in that county has ever put a thing seen at one of those places into the same sentence as a thing seen at another of them.** Forty yards of tarred hemp went into that abutment four feet down on the fourth of a month in the year before and **nobody has dug for it and nobody is going to dig for it in this volume either.** The volume's last line is not about a man and is not about a city: it is a county of about four thousand people with two crossings in it, the county's own figure that the two of them are four hundred yards apart, a line in each, both about nine inches long, neither measured, nobody knowing of the other one, and the fact that **there has never been a book in this kingdom with the two of them in it and there is not going to be one**, and that fact is the last line and is not a thing anybody says.

780. **THE FOUR ROOMS AND FOUR PEOPLE, OR FIVE, AND THE RULING THE CLOSE HAS TO MAKE.** **The Batch 0005 card requires *four documents and four rooms and four people noticing four separate wrongs*, and the page carries five rooms in which somebody notices something: Chapter 293, a press room, where a figure of persons stands under a head that says *Date*; Chapter 294, a room with a stove in it, where a clerk of six years worked out that her room's habit and another room's habit are two things; Chapter 295, a chamber, where a card says a matter was sat and nothing ever was; Chapter 296, two rooms over a weigh-house, where a figure is read that the county cannot refuse and cannot check; and Chapter 300, a long room over a wharf, where there is no council in the county that could renew an injunction.** The block recorded a deliberate decision, that a fifth noticing would be a fifth person and the block is four, and that 293 and 296 are two different wrongs rather than one wrong noticed twice, and that is defensible and it is not a repair. **The state sentence and the page are in tension and this pass does not resolve it, because the close is where a volume's shape is ruled on and a batch phase may not rule on it.** **What the close has, in one place: five rooms, five noticings, five different wrongs, no two of them joined by anybody, one new name in the whole block and it is four hundred miles off in a yard; and one room, Chapter 294's, whose noticing is not about a document at all and which may be the reason the count of five is the right count.**

798. **THE RULING ON THE FOUR ROOMS AND FOUR PEOPLE, OR FIVE, WHICH IS THE ONLY QUESTION A BATCH PHASE COULD NOT SETTLE.** **The card held.** Four documents in four rooms with one person in each and four separate wrongs and nobody joining them: a contested record in a press room on the ground floor, an injunction's expiry in the room over a weigh-house, a schedule gone underground with a district that has not in the room with the stove, a companion file of one sheet in the chamber on the third floor — and the Crown's acknowledgement is the contested record and not a fifth document. **Item 759 is true as written and stands.** **The page also has a fifth room in which somebody notices something**, and it is Chapter 300's long room over a wharf, **and it is not a fifth instance of the block's shape, because a document can be produced in a room and a refusal cannot, and that room contains a bench, nine men, a woman, two clerks, a page under a stair and eleven words and no document anybody can act on.** **The block's method was not four rooms with one each: it was four documents kept in four rooms, plus two rooms where the volume's argument actually happened and neither of them is a document room — Chapter 293, where a true thing is thanked and the thanking turns it into a finding, and Chapter 300, where a refusal with a reason in it is entered and a count goes from eight to nine — and the fourth document room leaked, because Chapter 294's noticing is a clerk working out that her room's habit and another room's habit are two things, and that noticing is not about a document and is the first in the manuscript that is about a room.** **The ruling is four documents and five noticings, and the state sentence and the tension are both right and the tension is not a defect and is not a repair, and what a Volume 07 writer inherits is the distinction: a noticing about a document can be had in a room by one person, a noticing about a room cannot be had by anybody, and a block of four documents that produced a fifth noticing in a room where nobody was looking at a document is a different shape from four rooms with one each — and the different shape is the finding.** The count a Volume 07 prompt may carry is **five rooms and five noticings and four documents**, and a Volume 07 block may produce a fifth noticing and that is the finding and not a breach, **provided the fifth room contains no document anybody can act on.**

The bell is not explained, no device is named, and it does not stop. The two lines in two stones are not named, not measured, not joined, and the two crossings have never been in one book and are not going to be.
