The valley's eleven weeks is said in the valley's own mouth and is converted by nobody and cannot be true of any date in Block 5 on the audited chain. The mechanism is not explained. The not-askings stand at nine. The breach is open. **And the city four hundred miles off is behind the reader, and this volume sent it nothing, and the volume's last word on it is that it is four hundred miles off on a shelf.**

802. **THE PROMISES VOLUME 06 DID NOT KEEP, COUNTED, INSTEAD OF THE ONES IT DID.** **The rotation row's recovery anchor for Volume 6 — the injunction is won, the cost is processed — is not kept: the injunction is won and the cost is not processed**, and the volume is right not to process it, and the plan's claim that it is processed in Block 5 is not on the page. **The public is not in the volume at all**, so the promise that the public cannot erase the Sundering is kept in its negative form and fails in its positive one. **Reaching the upper end of Threadkeeper is delivered as a fact and is invisible to a reader**, and `bible/power-system.md` puts Stage 3 at Volumes 4 to 6 and Stage 4 at Volumes 7 to 10, **so no stage is crossed in this volume and the ledger's row is a position within a stage and not a promotion.** **The spent sentence was said once, correctly, by the right person in the right room, and the plan attributes it to the wrong woman in the wrong county and says it was referred to twice when the volume refers to it zero times.** **The testimony lag of two to six weeks is unspent and is a plan figure**, and the only lag on the page is nine days each way to a valley, which is a body's travel and not a letter's. **The protagonist is on the page for about a quarter of an hour in five of the last ten chapters**, and that is a cost and not a defect, and the plan's own table gives him forty-eight chapters and Volume 06 gave him about six.

805. **THE RELATIONSHIP STATE AT THE END OF CHAPTER 300, AND THE STATE OF THE MANUSCRIPT AT THE CLOSE OF VOLUME 06.** **Aren and Mara: on opposite sides of a public proceeding, and the breach open and not repaired, and the not-askings at nine.** She proposed nothing in this volume; he asked her for a sheet in a room over a weigh-house and she gave it to him and did not ask him what he was going to do with it, **and the not-asking is not a courtesy and is not a rule and is the ordinary habit of a room, and a room hears a thing once.** He put the sheet in his coat, went down the lane and up a street and put it into a press in a room at the end of a yard, **and nobody asked him to and nobody in that room knows what he is looking at, and the yard's rule is that nothing that belongs to a man goes in that yard's book and only a thing set, and the word *brother* was not used in that yard.** She is a woman of twenty-nine who has run that office four years and a half out of a deed of thirteen words at fourpence a year, **who is a body corporate that can be served with anything at all by anybody who walks up a lane, and whose not-askings cannot be served with, and who has a want of four or five words that is not printed and has not changed since she was twenty-two.** **Aren and the bench of nine: he is on the roll with a vote and not an office, he does not vote, and on the last day of the volume he stood in a yard four hundred yards up the road while the man of forty-seven said the same four things a fifth time and did not write them down, and four hours later he sat on that bench and was asked nothing.** **Aren and the woman of thirty-three two hundred miles off: he is in her office at about the sixth hour, about a quarter of an hour, and asked nothing in it, and there was nothing in it he had come for, and he took a sheet out of a coat, looked at a leaf with a seventh line that says *a person* for about a minute and a quarter, put it back, and left, and she did not ask him a question and has not asked him one.** **Aren and the valley: a man of thirty-two with a limp took a sheet out of a sill on the fourth day after a cut, and it was a sheet with a woman's name in the fourth column of it, and he put a hand on a crossing on the strength of a line somebody else wrote, and a man of fifty-eight four hundred miles off is not coming back.** **Aren and the woman of thirty-eight: she thanked a man of about fifty for a true thing about a column and the thanks is a finding, and she was refused in eleven words by a bench of nine and was not thanked for asking and was not thanked for being answered, and she went down the outside stair without staying to see it written, and the last page of hers in the volume is a clerk asking her whether a certain column is a column and her saying yes.** **Aren and the man of fifty-eight and the book: one finding entered in a hundred and forty years, on a line he ruled himself, in his own hand, under four lines read out for the first time in a hundred and forty years, and nobody asked him whether he could stand it afterwards and nobody is going to.** **Aren and a man of about thirty-four with sixteen men and no work, who dug a road about four hundred yards long with a standing finish on it that does not go anywhere, who said *A line that is late can be argued with* to a room with nobody in it, and who said the four words of a man of thirty-four's own want about the road to a man with a bag and was answered with a different question, and who asked the man of fifty-eight whether the man who came up a road nine days was coming back and was told that if he asked a second time in that room he would not be answered in that room.** **And the power state, held and not advanced: Stage 3, Threadkeeper. Two paths he can reach and one he cannot, and the one he cannot is not closed and is not lost and a crossing that carries nobody carries nobody and carried nobody for four years before anything happened to it, and the word *failed* is at zero in the volume.**

806. **AND THE VOLUME'S LAST IMAGE, IN A COUNTY, AND IT IS STILL THERE.** **Two crossings four hundred yards apart by the county's own figure, a line in the third course of the fourth bay of the one that carries a road over a river and a line in the face of a dressed block in the abutment of the one a hundred yards from the end of that market, both about nine inches long, neither measured, neither moved, nobody in that county knowing of the other one, and there has never been a book in this kingdom with the two of them in it and there is not going to be one.** Forty yards of tarred hemp four feet down under the dressed block, and nobody dug for it and nobody is going to, and a man with a stick is the only man in that county who could ever have got at it and he has a permanent limp. A bell a hundred yards up that road that goes at the fourth hour and a half and goes on, rung by a boy and a carpenter, neither paid by the guild and neither a member of anything, **and nobody in that county can be asked who keeps it, and the answer nobody can give is the finding.** About four hundred people in a street four hundred yards long who went home on the last day of that year not knowing that there are two.

812. **THE ROLL, THE TWO ROLLS, AND THE GAP OF NINE DAYS, AND WHAT IS AND IS NOT IN THEM.** The roll of the valley is a long sheet folded in four and ruled in three columns: **a day, a name, and a mark that is either a gate or a market or a cross. There is no fourth column and there never has been one.** It carries about four hundred people in about nine hundred lines. It is kept by **Marek Ollen** in a room at the top of a lane, and the room over a cross is nine days' walk and four hundred miles off any county that is on a map, and it is a path. **A second roll exists and is a copy of the first, made by Marek Ollen himself once a season for about nine years, about thirty-six times, and kept because the first gets wet at the low end when the water comes up, and the two sit in the same box within a hand's width of each other and have never been compared in a room.** In nine places a season they differ, and the difference is **nine days ruled across in the day column with nothing in them in the first roll and not ruled and not empty in the copy**, and he has ruled them about four times in nine years and cannot say which of the two books he was right about. **The forgetting is not entered anywhere, and the reason is not a decision: the roll has a day and a name and a mark and no column for it and never has had one, and Marek Ollen said so on the page once and the sentence is *It does not go in,* and about two hundred people of the ninth generation in that valley are in the state of being a person on no instrument at all.** **Nobody in that valley is told why the road was severed, and this block does not tell them and does not send anybody to find out, and the answer to a question about the nine days was *I do not know* and was given once, on the day he arrived, and has not been given again.**

813. **THE WOMAN OF ABOUT THIRTY WITH THE SLATE, HER WANT, AND THE THREE FORGETTINGS.** **Her want is said once, to the roll and not to a person, in Chapter 303, and it carries no length figure on the page, following the Batch 0004 and Batch 0005 precedent for a want.** It is that her son's name stay on the roll. **On the ninth day of Wolfmonth she lost a name in a yard in front of two people, at the fourth hour, and had it back inside about a minute and a quarter, and the man she was writing it for did not notice, and about four of two hundred people in that yard noticed a pause and about nine had noticed it before and about four had noticed it twice. Nobody in that valley asked her about it then or since, and nobody asked her whether the third one was going to be different, and the volume does not say and does not have anybody ask.** The woman of thirty-three in the provincial town two hundred miles off is a different person and **is not on the page in this block at all** and was not asked and was not thanked and had her want and her face-down leaf untouched.

814. **THE COPY THAT WENT OUT, THE SHEET IT WENT OUT ON, AND WHAT IS ON IT.** **A sheet of that office's own printed series stood in a box at a gate in that valley for about two months in the ordinary post and was picked up by the man of about sixty who keeps the roll of the crossing, who did not know what office it came from, did not know the town, and had never asked.** It is ruled in six spaces, five of them with a head over them, the sixth the same width as the other five with nothing at the top, about four of the six ruled for a figure and one for a person, and **nowhere on the whole of it is there the name of a person.** He put the valley's name in the first column in that office's own way of writing a place, and a figure in the second column under a head that says *Date*, and **the figure is four hundred and four and it is the last line of his own roll and not a count of anything, because a roll of nine hundred lines is not a count of four hundred and four people.** He copied his own half of the record as well and rolled it and put it in the same bag with the sheet, because a man who sends a figure sends the thing the figure came from. **It went out on an ordinary round at the ninth hour on the nineteenth day of Wolfmonth and nobody in that city knew that it had ever arrived and nobody in that valley was asked about it and the second keeper and the first keeper are both in that valley and neither of them knows.** The word in front of the name of the place was not printed, is not defined, and the type was not struck; the copy went out with the first column empty in front of the place, and **a man at a stone in a provincial town two hundred miles off looked at a drawer at the fourth hour of the second day of Frostmonth and did not open it, and one of the nine sheets going out that afternoon had something in the space in front of the name of the place in a hand that is not the press's, and nobody in that building knows whose hand it is and the sheet went out on the cart with the other eight.**

832. **THE PROPOSAL, WHAT IS ON IT, THE FIRST MISTAKE, AND THE REFUSAL, AND WHAT THE INSTRUMENT WOULD NOT TAKE.** **A proposal for a public-copy network, made by the keeper of records, twenty-nine, on the sixth of Frostmonth, YR 316, at about the second hour, in a room over a weigh-house with a door on a lane, at fourpence a year, out of a deed of thirteen words, *for the keeping of what this county cannot be shown it has lost*.** Her want is not a column and is not the Crown: **that a thing heard in this county be entered as a thing asked, and that anybody who asks one be given a copy of it.** She has asked for nine years, **and in the spring a witness performed the best possible version of what she wants in front of her in a chamber two hundred miles off in eleven sentences and it did not work, and the space after the eleventh stroke in the margin of that minute is ruled and empty.** **The proposal is written on that office's own printed series because there is no other series, and about four hundred of that series go out of a building about two hundred miles off into nine counties every month and about four hundred of them come back in a month, and a thing written on anything else stays where it is written.** **The first mistake is in the first line of it: a figure of persons goes into the second column, and the head over the second column says *Date*, and she knew that when she sent it, and there is no column on the whole of that sheet that will take a day, and the second column is the only place on it where a thing can be dated and that place is for a count of people.** **She put her own trade in the third column, and the third column is the only one on the whole of that printed series that will take a person at all, and it takes him by what he does and not by what he is called, and she wrote *keeper of records* in it.** **[CORRECTED IN THE BATCH 0002 REVIEW REPAIR: the person column is the THIRD, not the fifth. See item 840.]**  The sheet went out in the ordinary post in a bag with about four hundred others of the same thing and nobody in that county was told that it had gone. **She said the mistake out loud in the room at about the second hour and a half, which is the first time in four years and a half that she has said anything about a sheet in that room, and the second copyist of about thirty heard it from the third step.** **The refusal is the reeve's, and it is short, and it is the reason and not a reason, and nobody improved on it. *No, this is a body corporate and it has spent four years and a half refusing to be one, and the first thing that makes a county a thing anybody can act on is a copy of what it has been asked, and I will not have this room be the place it happens in. 834. **THE COPY, THE FAIR COPY, THE RETURN WITH NOTHING IN THE SECOND COLUMN, AND THE DECISION, IN THE ORDER THEY ARE ON THE PAGE.** **A fair copy of the register, made on the eleventh of Frostmonth at about the second hour and finished at about the fourth hour and a half by the second copyist, six years in that room, out of her own trade and not her own name at the foot of it, and it is the first fair copy that office has made in four years and a half and nobody had asked for it.** A fair copy in that county carries the person by what she does and has never carried a name. **The cost is that a county that cannot be sued for a question is now producible out of a question twice instead of once, and that the second copyist put her trade in the one column on the whole of that series that will take a person, and said out loud in the room why she would not put her name in it, and that the day-book cannot be copied at all because a not-asking is not a place and not a figure and not a person and not a keeper and not a frequency and the sixth column has no head and a column with no head is not a column.** **A return came back up the lane on the sixth of Hearthmonth, a Sunday, with a place in the first column and nothing at all in the second, and it is the only time in four years and a half that anything from that office has come up that lane with nothing on it that anybody had to answer, and the discovery is that a place with nothing against it is the only paper that machine has ever sent anybody that a county can carry without answering anything, and neither woman said that out loud.** **And on the fifteenth of Hearthmonth, a Tuesday, the keeper of records decided to answer, and the instrument did not take what she put in it: there is no column on that series for an answer, and a sheet with a place in the first column and her trade in the third and nothing in the other four is a sheet that says nothing, and it will go round and come back about two months from now and nobody in that county will be there when it does, and neither of the two women has ever been in that building. The decision stands and it is entered in the register as a question and not as a finding, and the register stands at seven questions and no finding, and the day-book was not opened and does not get a tenth and a tenth would not be a gift if it came.**

835. **THE VALLEY CHAPTER, THE COPY OF THE WINTER BOOK, AND WHAT IT COST, AND WHAT WAS NOT DONE IN IT.** **Chapter 316 is the sixth of Hearthmonth and is a valley dateline, and it is the only chapter in this block set in a path, and no month name and no weekday is spoken in its body — a sweep of nineteen calendar tokens over the body returns zero.** **Chapter 316 is one span of four days, the first of Hearthmonth to the Friday, and its dateline says so, and day 460 is unused and the chain allows it.** A man of thirty-four with sixteen men and no work copies the winter book on a trestle in the corner at the back of a room over a cross, four days, with a rule and a straight edge, and the copy is good work, **and the trestle was carried in on the first morning and the copy went into the press on the fourth morning.** **The book is forty leaves tied with a piece of tarred hemp and nine spreads, one to a generation, and there is a finding in it, and nobody in that room said anything about where the finding is or how many there are, and nobody asked, and the man of thirty-four did not copy the head of the first spread out loud to anybody and did not look at it while he was working, and the four lines at the head of the first spread are not reprinted and not re-derived and not improved on.** The man of fifty-eight was in that room for about two hours on the first of the four days and about half an hour on the last, **the bar was already across the press, he did not go to the press and did not go to the trestle**, did not ask, and **is not coming back, and about four hundred people in that valley are not told why, and this block does not tell them and does not send anybody to find out.** **A man of thirty-four who does not keep a book will not sign a copy of it, in the ordinary way, and a woman with a slate was in that room for about an hour on the third of the four days and carried no slate and asked for nothing, and her want is not said and nobody asks her about it.** The copy went into a press with a door and a bar and no shelf anybody looks at, and the original went back under the trestle **on a board of its own, where it had lain for nineteen years before that trestle was carried in**, and **the two of them are in the same room within about six feet of each other and there is no line in the room and no line in either of the two books that says which of them is the one that happened.** `Marek Ollen`, about fifty, keeper of the roll of who is in that valley, is in the room for about an hour on the second of the four days, has kept that roll for nineteen years, is a different man from the keeper of the winter book, and **has not been asked about the copy and is not going to be.**

836. **THE TWO CORRECTORS ARE TWO REFUSALS, AND WHAT EACH COST.** **A woman of thirty-eight was refused the second time on the sixteenth of Frostmonth, a Monday, in a vestry behind the choir of a church four hundred yards from the front of a building of four floors and seven presses in a provincial town, by a churchwarden of about fifty who has kept that minute book eleven years and who signs the rate and has lent the parish against it.** His reason is his own and is not about her: a question in that book is a question out here, it is read out in that church once a year in front of about four hundred people, a parish that cannot answer a thing is a parish that is asked it again, and the rate is settled at the quarter-day and comes back to him on that morning. **She put her want down once, was refused once, did not put it down a second time, and he did not give the rate a second time, and nobody in that room improved on anything.** **And the cost of the second refusal is that he asked her a question — what the figure under the head that says a day on a sheet of that series is a count of — and she could not answer it, and about four seconds of that vestry are on the page because a woman of thirty-eight who has spent nine years asking rooms to show what was asked could not answer the ordinary question, and the ordinary question is the only question anybody in this kingdom has ever asked about a figure on that printed series, and it has been asked three times in about four years and answered once, and that answer is in a county two hundred miles off and the man who gave it is not in that room.** The refusal was entered in his own hand in about four seconds in the middle of a page and was not read again and she was not asked to stay and see it written. **Nobody thanked her for asking and nobody thanked her for being answered and nobody told her she was right, and she is not redeemed and is not converted, and the second refusal cost her something the first one did not and is not improved on by the first one.** **And the aphorism that being correct is the most expensive thing available to a person in a chamber is printed once in this block, in Chapter 313, in its own words, and the volume's standing was four printings and is now five, at Chapters 288, 289, 293 and 300 of Volume 06 and at 313 of this volume.**

847. **THE CURE, AS IT IS ON THE PAGE, AND WHAT IT IS NOT.** **It is a thing nine men in a glass works in a valley four hundred miles off filled into a trough behind that works about four months before day 471, on nine days, with a board and a piece of wood across it, and it is called *a clear*, and the name is a word those nine men already used about a piece of glass with nothing wrong in it that can be seen from outside, and the trade has about four words in it for a fault nobody standing outside the shed could see and *a clear* is the one that means the absence of a visible fault and not its presence.** **It was named once, at `chapter-0321.md`, by a man with his hands in a cooling box, in the second hour, and it was not said again that day and it has not been said since by anybody in that valley.** **And that is the whole of it: the mechanism is not explained, no man in that works was asked to say more, a thing with only a trade name cannot be argued about in a room, and about four people in that valley have said since that a cure in a valley of about four hundred people has a trade name and no other name.** **It is not a mechanism, not a device, not a power, not a System panel, and not a second office, and nobody stops anybody taking it, and it was refused by a room and then taken by about nine people in the same room five days later, and the volume does not resolve that and does not have the council resolve it and does not have the person who took it speak again.** The word *bloom*, the glass-trade word Batch 0001 spent at `chapter-0304.md`, is **not** printed and not used again.

848. **THE COPY OF THE ROLL, WHERE IT WENT, WHAT WAS NOT ENTERED, AND WHY, AND WHERE IT WAS ON DAY 508.** **A roll of about nine hundred lines folded in four twice, being a copy made by a man out of his own half of a roll of about four hundred people in a valley four hundred miles off, came up the stairs of a building of four floors and seven presses in the ordinary post about two weeks before day 508, with a strip of paper round it and no head on the strip, and a man of thirty put it into the returns press because a press is a press.** It is ruled in three narrow columns, a day, a name, and one of three marks, a gate, a market or a cross, and there is nothing else on it and there never has been, and it has nine ruled days in the day column with nine names in them in a hand that is not the hand of the man who ruled them, and the ruling of that gap is older than most of the page. **At `chapter-0324.md` a clerk of the returns, a woman of about thirty with six years in that room, reads it in about four seconds and does not enter it, and the reason is a shape of book: the returns book under her arm is ruled nine inches by six, takes every form as a line, has about eleven lines in it in about nine years, is written by a room and not by a press, and is the only record in that building with a person at the front of every line, and there is no line in it for a copy and there never has been.** **The copy went into the returns press because a return is a return, and about four hundred a month go out of that building and about nine come back, and everything else in that drawer is still in that drawer when the building closes.** **It came out of that drawer on day 508 because a drawer gets emptied, and about two hundred of that office's own printed series crossed the same table that afternoon wanting a keeper, and a woman of thirty-three filled the fourth column off that roll in about a minute and a quarter without looking up, and the person she was writing down was on a list she had never seen and is four hundred miles off in a valley that is not on any map.** **Nobody thanked her, nobody asked her why, her want did not change, her leaf is still face down, and the returns book has no line for a copy and the copy is not in the returns book.** **And the strip of paper came off it when the drawer was shut on it and a woman of about thirty picked it up off the floor of the returns press room and put it in her pocket, and it is not on any form and it is in no book and there is no line in that office for a piece of paper a person has put in her pocket.**

849. **THE COUNTY'S REGISTER AT SEVEN, ITS DAY-BOOK AT NINE, ITS FOUR THINGS ON THE SHELF, AND THE PRESS, WHICH IS A FIFTH THING AND IS NOT ON THE SHELF.** **The register stands at seven entries, all of them questions, none of them a finding, the fifth about four months old and the sixth and the seventh both dated in the same month, and it was read aloud once in that room at about the seventh hour of day 504 by the keeper of records and nobody asked for it and nobody was offered it again, and the reading took about a minute and a quarter.** **The day-book stands at nine entries of a thing that was not asked and was not opened on any day of this block and does not get a tenth, and a tenth would not be a gift if it came.** **The shelf carries four things: the contested sheet with a figure of persons against this county under a head that says a day, a fair copy of the register carrying the second copyist's trade and not her name, a sheet that came back up that lane with a place in it and nothing in the second, and the answer that went out on day 470 in the ordinary post with four of its six columns empty.** **And at about the fourth hour of day 504 the keeper of records opened a press in the corner of that room for the first time in about four years and a half, and at the bottom of it, folded once, under a bundle of papers about a hedge and a piece of a letter on the back of a sheet about a wall, was a copy of the contested sheet, and nobody in that county can produce the hand that put it there, and a courier who came up that lane with it did not give a name and was not asked for one, and it went into a press because a press is a press.** **And on day 510 the press is standing open and has not been shut, and the reason the keeper of records gives for not shutting it is that a shut thing in that room can only be broken and an open thing can be looked in.** **A press is the only instrument in that room that works and cannot be checked, and it can be served with and emptied by anybody who walks up that lane, and about four people in that lane have said since that a woman of twenty-nine has left an instrument open on purpose for the first time in four years and a half and that the only office in that county with anything anybody else can use is the one that has answered a figure it cannot refuse with nothing since the day it was a thing that could be named.**

850. **THE TWO CORRECTORS, AND THE REFUSAL THAT IS THE MORE USEFUL OF THE TWO.** **A woman of about thirty at a steading up the water, whose mother died in the winter before last, told a man of thirty-two with a limp the account of that mother's last month at about the fourth hour of day 490, for about nine minutes, and he was in the middle of it in about a minute and a half and he said so at the ninth minute: *I do not know whose that is*, and he said that he had been in the middle of it for about a minute and a half and it was not his and that he could not tell her when it stopped being his.** **She did not believe him, said so in about nine seconds, and gave the reason: he has not been in that house and he has not been in that room, and her mother is not his, and if he is telling her he does not know whose grief he is carrying then he is telling her a thing she has no way of checking, and she had just said out loud the one thing she has said out loud about her mother since she died, and she is not going to have said it to a man who was somewhere else at the time, and the part she would have believed is the part he did not say.** **She said one thing afterwards and she said it to a woman coming down the water, and he was nine feet off and heard it, and it was that she told it to a stranger who was somewhere else at the time and that is the whole of what she got out of it and she is not going to do it again.** **The second corrector is a man of thirty-four with sixteen men and no work, who has known him nine days, and at the fourth hour of day 495 he told him in a yard that he has watched him do that twice, that the first was on the second morning the man was in that valley when somebody asked what he did before he was a man with a stick and he answered with a woman's hand, that the second was five days before at a gate up the water with a cart, that he did not need to hear a word of it because he has seen sixteen men do that in about a year and it looks the same every time, and that the second one was worse and the man did not know it was the second one.** **And the refusal is the more useful of the two, and the volume does not improve on it and does not repair it: the man with the limp did not say he was right and did not say he was wrong, and he asked one question, and it was *why is the second one worse*, and the answer was that the first one you find out and the nine men in a yard now have a woman in their heads that they cannot put down anywhere, and that the instruction was to ask out loud what is his before answering the next man and to accept that the room will not answer it, and that he did not ask anybody anything.** **Nothing was written down in either case, there is no line in that valley on which either of the two things can be put down and got back out of, and the woman with the slate was not told and has not been asked.** **This is the volume's relationship beat and it is not a scene with the woman of twenty-nine and it is not a scene about the two of them, and nobody walked a road with anybody in any of the ten chapters and the word *brother* is at zero across the ten files.**

858. **THE ELEVENTH STANDING CLAUSE, AND IT IS ABOUT THE INSTRUMENTS AND NOT ABOUT THE PROSE.** A containment-over-the-smaller-set shingle basis divides by the paragraph. **One verbatim clause of twelve words sitting inside two otherwise unrelated paragraphs of fifty and sixty words is one shingle in forty-nine, which is 0.02, and a basis with a 0.40 threshold cannot see it at all.** That is why both shingle bases returned zero on all four of this block's real defects while Jaccard returned two of them, and it is the same shape as the failure seven blocks in a row have been recording in the other direction. **So: a sweep is a report about a basis and a run, and a clean return is a statement about the instrument and not about the book; name the basis before the run; run a basis that respects no paragraph boundary; compare a block's own frames with each other; and do not print the word *zero* about a basis unless that number came out of that basis on the text as it stands, after the last edit.** The three bases in this project's list are not three views of one thing. Jaccard sees vocabulary overlap in a paragraph. The shingle bases see near-duplicate paragraphs and are blind to a single reused clause inside a long one. The raw-token basis sees repeated wording anywhere, including inside a house frame, and reports the volume's own dateline formula at thirty-four words by construction.
